Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- unbond (ServiceManager)
- create (ServiceManager)
- update (ServiceManager)
- registerAgents (ServiceManager)
- terminate (ServiceManager)
- Description
- Multiple ServiceManager flows perform side-effecting external calls (token-utility transfers, ETH forwarding, or token bookkeeping) before invoking the authoritative registry action, and they frequently ignore boolean success returns or fail to validate input array invariants. This pattern yields: (1) irreversible transfers occurring even when the registry later declines/fails the logical operation (unbond/terminate/registerAgents), (2) permanent desynchronization between token-utility and registry state (create/update flows), (3) inconsistent/ambiguous refund reporting (refund values overwritten or denominated in the wrong units), and (4) reentrancy/DoS opportunities because untrusted external helpers are called without protections.
- Root cause
- Repeated unsafe design choices in ServiceManager: (A) performing side-effecting external calls (token-utility transfers, ETH forwarding) before the authoritative, state-changing registry call instead of after verifying success; (B) treating downstream registry functions as if they always revert on failure and therefore ignoring their boolean success returns (no require(success)); (C) mutating and splitting input arrays in-place and failing to validate that related arrays (agentIds, agentParams, agentInstances) are equal length and positional, making multi-call protocols fragile and prone to misalignment; and (D) trusting a token-utility address only by non-zero check at construction, yet invoking it without reentrancy guards or additional runtime validation.
- Impact
- High: attackers or faulty downstream implementations can cause direct financial loss and persistent state corruption. Concrete impacts include:
- Refund extraction while remaining bonded: callers can receive token refunds from the token-utility even when IService.unbond later fails (returns false), allowing repeated extraction of funds while the registry still marks bonds as active (IDs 0, 11, 12).
- Lost funds on non-atomic registration: token deposits and ETH forwarded to the registry can be irrecoverably transferred even if IService.registerAgents returns false, leaving callers out-of-pocket with no registration (ID 4).
- Permanent desynchronization and misattributed bonds: create/update sequences that split bond data across two external calls (IService and IServiceTokenUtility) without enforcing array length/ordering or checking IService’s boolean return can leave token-utility state changed while registry state is unchanged, producing misaligned agent↔︎bond mappings, locked funds, or theft (IDs 1, 2).
- Inconsistent/ambiguous refunds: terminate/unbond overwrite or mix refund values from token utilities and registry without preserving units or verifying success, causing callers and integrators to observe (success == false, refund > 0) or token-denominated refunds where ETH was expected (IDs 8, 10, 12).

## [F-388] null
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-388](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-388)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Reward accrual ignores availableRewards cap leading to checkpoint DoS
- Targets
- _calculateStakingRewards (StakingBase)
- Description
- _calculateStakingRewards sums rewards for every eligible service as rewardsPerSecond * ts without constraining the result to the availableRewards pool or otherwise signaling that the sum exceeds what can actually be distributed. When the system has accrued more theoretical rewards than tokens available, the subsequent checkpoint flow will attempt to distribute totalRewards (and each eligibleServiceRewards value) that are larger than availableRewards, which causes subtraction/transfer logic in checkpoint to revert. Once this occurs, checkpointing cannot succeed until additional rewards are deposited, effectively bricking the reward distribution process.
- Root cause
- The function computes rewards purely from elapsed time and per-second emission rate, never enforcing totalRewards <= availableRewards nor capping per-service rewards to the remaining reward budget.
- Impact
- Reward allocations become greater than the remaining reward pool, causing checkpoint executions to revert and halting the reward distribution mechanism until the pool is refilled.
- Incorrect index used when removing service from setServiceIds
- Targets
- _unstake (StakingBase)
- Description
- The function locates the position of the service being unstaked inside the array returned by checkpoint(). It then reuses that index to mutate the persistent setServiceIds array. This assumes that the ordering of the checkpoint() serviceIds array always matches the ordering in setServiceIds, which is not guaranteed. If the two arrays differ (e.g., checkpoint() returns service IDs sorted or otherwise rearranged), the swap-and-pop removal will target the wrong index, unintentionally deleting a different service ID from setServiceIds while leaving the unstaked service ID behind.
- Root cause
- Using the index of serviceId found in the checkpoint() return array to update the distinct storage array setServiceIds without ensuring both arrays share identical ordering.
- Impact
- Corrupts the setServiceIds storage array: the wrong service can be removed from the active set, losing eligibility for rewards and activity checks while remaining staked in mapServiceInfo, and the intended service ID stays in the set with an empty ServiceInfo entry, breaking accounting and downstream logic.
- Stale index from checkpoint() lets swap-and-pop target wrong array slot
- Targets
- _unstake (StakingBase)
- Description
- _unstake relies on the index of serviceId inside the serviceIds array returned by checkpoint(), and then uses that index on the storage array setServiceIds to swap-and-pop the element. This only works if checkpoint() leaves setServiceIds unchanged. As soon as checkpoint() mutates setServiceIds (for example by evicting/inactivating other services and performing its own swap-and-pop), the ordering/length of the storage array no longer matches the memory copy. The idx found in serviceIds can then be greater than or unrelated to the actual index in storage, causing the write setServiceIds[idx] = … to revert with Panic(0x32) or to remove the wrong service entry. A legitimate owner can therefore be permanently blocked from unstaking, or another service can be inadvertently removed from the active set.
- Root cause
- The code assumes the memory array returned by checkpoint() remains index-aligned with the storage array setServiceIds even though checkpoint() is allowed to mutate the storage array (reordering or shortening it).
- Impact
- Honest stakers can be griefed into a denial-of-service when attempting to unstake (panic due to out-of-bounds) or the contract can silently remove an unintended service from the active set, breaking accounting invariants.
- tsCheckpoint not updated when no services leads to reward inflation
- Targets
- checkpoint (StakingBase)
- Description
- The checkpoint routine only refreshes tsCheckpoint when serviceIds.length > 0. When a checkpoint occurs during a period where no services are returned by _calculateStakingRewards, tsCheckpoint remains at its previous value. Later, when at least one service becomes active again, the next checkpoint computes epochLength using this stale timestamp, effectively treating the entire elapsed time since the last non-empty checkpoint as if the service(s) were active. This causes reward and inactivity calculations to apply to a time interval during which those services were not actually staked, allowing new or returning services to capture rewards for idle periods.
- Root cause
- tsCheckpoint is updated only inside the branch that requires serviceIds.length > 0, leaving it unchanged during empty-service checkpoints.
- Impact
- Attackers can wait for all services to exit, let time elapse, stake a service, and immediately run a checkpoint to obtain rewards corresponding to the entire downtime, draining the reward pool and corrupting inactivity metrics.
- getNextRewardCheckpointTimestamp can return a timestamp in the past
- Targets
- getNextRewardCheckpointTimestamp (StakingBase)
- Description
- The external view function returns tsCheckpoint + livenessPeriod without comparing that value to the current block.timestamp. tsCheckpoint is set only in _initialize and updated in checkpoint(). There is no enforcement that checkpoint() is called regularly, so if more than livenessPeriod seconds pass without checkpoint() being invoked, tsCheckpoint + livenessPeriod can be less than block.timestamp. As a result callers expecting the returned value to represent the next eligible (future) checkpoint time can receive a timestamp that already lies in the past.
- Root cause
- The function blindly returns tsCheckpoint + livenessPeriod and the contract does not maintain or enforce an invariant that tsCheckpoint is advanced such that tsCheckpoint + livenessPeriod >= block.timestamp. There is no max(tsCheckpoint + livenessPeriod, block.timestamp) or other guard, nor a mechanism that guarantees checkpoint() is executed in a timely manner.
- Impact
- Off-chain callers (UIs, schedulers, monitoring services) can be misled about when the next checkpoint will be eligible, causing incorrect displays or scheduling decisions. This is a correctness/logic bug rather than a direct on-chain exploit: contract state and reward calculations remain protected by internal time checks (e.g., _calculateStakingRewards uses block.timestamp - tsCheckpoint >= livenessPeriod), so it does not by itself enable reentrancy or fund theft. However, depending on how callers use the value, user experience or automation may break, and integrations that assume the value is always in the future will behave incorrectly.

Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Proxy constructor delegatecalls implementation during construction -> initializer executes with code size 0 and msg.sender = deployer
- Targets
- constructor (ServiceManagerProxy)
- Description
- The constructor stores the provided implementation (serviceManager) address into the PROXY_SERVICE_MANAGER storage slot and immediately delegatecalls serviceManager with serviceManagerData while the proxy is still in its constructor. Because the proxy contract has no deployed bytecode at this point (extcodesize/address(this).code.length == 0) and the external caller is the deployer EOA, the implementation’s initializer executes under delegatecall with those semantics. Initializer logic that depends on extcodesize/address(this).code being non-zero, that calls Address.isContract(address(this)), or that expects msg.sender == address(this) will behave incorrectly (return false or be different) or will revert. The proxy does not adapt or enforce any initializer semantics, so implementations that do not explicitly support being invoked via delegatecall from a constructing proxy can fail deployment or be misconfigured.
- Root cause
- The proxy performs a delegatecall to the implementation from inside its constructor (after writing the implementation slot). This runs the implementation’s initializer in the proxy’s storage context while the proxy’s code size is zero and with msg.sender set to the deployer EOA. Implementation initializers that assume they are executing in a fully-deployed contract (or assume msg.sender semantics) are incompatible with this execution environment.
- Impact
- Possible consequences include:
- Deployment failure if the implementation’s initializer reverts when extcodesize == 0 or when address(this).code is empty (causing the proxy construction to revert).
- Incorrect initialization: ownership/roles/storage may be set to unexpected addresses (e.g., msg.sender becomes the deployer EOA instead of the intended proxy or caller), creating security or access-control issues.
- Incomplete or insecure configuration: initializers that bail out when they detect no contract code (common anti-constructor checks) may skip critical setup, leaving logic in an uninitialized or unsafe state.
- Denial-of-deployment (DoS) for implementations that cannot be initialized via constructor-delegatecall.
- Any downstream assumptions about the proxy/implementation state can be violated, potentially leading to lost funds or broken access control.
- getImplementation reads non-canonical storage slot (wrong EIP-1967 slot) in proxy
- Targets
- getImplementation (ServiceManagerProxy)
- Description
- The getImplementation function loads storage at the PROXY_SERVICE_MANAGER constant (bytes32 0xe39e69948a448ce9…). That constant does not equal the canonical EIP-1967 implementation slot (bytes32(uint256(keccak256(‘eip1967.proxy.implementation’)) - 1) = 0x360894a13b…2bbc). Because the proxy’s implementation address is commonly stored at the canonical slot, reading the incorrect slot causes getImplementation to return an incorrect address or zero. This breaks any logic or tooling that relies on getImplementation to report or manage the actual implementation address (e.g., upgrade checks, admin UI, management scripts), and can lead to inconsistent or broken upgradeability and management flows.
- Root cause
- A wrong storage slot constant is used: PROXY_SERVICE_MANAGER is defined as a different bytes32 value instead of the canonical EIP-1967 implementation slot. The assembly sload uses that wrong constant, so the function reads the wrong storage location.
- Impact
- Management and upgradeability may fail or behave inconsistently: callers will receive an incorrect implementation address (or zero) even when the real implementation is stored at the canonical slot. Consequences include failed or undetectable upgrades, admin/operator confusion, broken integration with tooling that expects EIP-1967, and the potential for Denial-of-Service of upgrade paths. While not directly an immediate theft vector, this can severely impair contract maintenance and recovery and may be leveraged in complex scenarios where inconsistent implementation assumptions are exploited.

## [F-390] null
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-390](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-390)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Missing success check after serviceRegistry.update allows inconsistent state
- Targets
- update (ServiceManager)
- Description
- The function forwards update requests to the external serviceRegistry and stores the returned boolean in the local variable`success`. However, it never validates the return value before proceeding to interact with the serviceRegistryTokenUtility. If`serviceRegistry.update`returns`false`instead of reverting while having already failed (or not applied the update),`ServiceManager.update`will still execute the subsequent token-utility operation (`resetServiceToken`or`createWithToken`). This causes the ServiceManager to commit token-utility side-effects even though the registry update failed, leading to mismatched service state and potentially mis-accounted collateral.
- Root cause
- `serviceRegistry.update`return value is ignored for control flow; the function continues execution even if the call returns`false`.
- Impact
- An adversary or faulty registry that returns`false`without reverting can cause ServiceManager to mutate token-utility state (e.g., reset or recreate token deposits) while the underlying service update is not applied. This desynchronizes registry and token-utility state, which can result in incorrect bond accounting, stuck collateral, or loss of service funds.
- Token refund is triggered before confirming unbond success
- Targets
- unbondWithSignature (ServiceManager)
- Description
- The function calls the token-utility’s`unbondTokenRefund`before confirming that`serviceRegistry.unbond`actually succeeds. If the registry call fails gracefully (returning`success == false`instead of reverting), the token utility can already have released the bond refund while the operator remains bonded in the service. This breaks the intended invariant that refunds are only released after a successful unbond, letting a cooperating service owner/operator withdraw bonds without unbonding the service.
- Root cause
- `IServiceTokenUtility.unbondTokenRefund`is invoked prior to observing the boolean result of`IService.unbond`, so refunds are issued even when`unbond`reports failure.
- Impact
- Operators (or colluding service owners) can reclaim their bonded funds while the service still treats them as bonded, undermining the bonding/slashing model and allowing premature withdrawals of escrowed value.
- ETH creation path skips agent bond validation, allowing zero-bond agents if registry doesn’t enforce bonds
- Targets
- create (ServiceManager)
- Description
- ServiceManager.create has two code paths depending on the token parameter: an ETH path (token == ETH_TOKEN_ADDRESS) and a token-backed path (token != ETH_TOKEN_ADDRESS). In the token-backed path the function extracts each agentParams[i].bond into a local bonds array, enforces that each bond != 0 (reverting otherwise), replaces agentParams[i].bond with a BOND_WRAPPER placeholder, calls IService.create, and then calls IServiceTokenUtility.createWithToken to store the real bonds. In the ETH path the function simply forwards the provided agentParams to IService.create without validating agentParams[i].bond or replacing bonds with BOND_WRAPPER. If the IService implementation (the registry) does not itself enforce non-zero bonds for agents, an attacker can call create with token == ETH_TOKEN_ADDRESS and supply agentParams that set bond == 0 for agents expected to require collateral. The registry would then create a service whose agent definitions contain zero bonds, enabling subsequent low-cost or zero-collateral agent registration and Sybil attacks.
- Root cause
- Asymmetric handling of bond validation: the token-backed branch explicitly validates and extracts non-zero bond values and replaces them with a wrapper, while the ETH branch omits these checks and forwards agentParams unchanged to the registry. The code implicitly assumes the registry enforces non-zero agent bonds for ETH-backed services, but this invariant is not enforced by ServiceManager.
- Impact
- If the registry (IService) does not validate non-zero agent bonds for ETH-backed services, an attacker can create services whose agents have zero bond requirements. Consequences include: low-cost or zero-collateral agent registration, enabling Sybil-style attacks, degraded network security/trust, malicious or spam agent instances participating in the service, and financial exposure for honest participants who expect bonded agents. The severity ranges from lost economic guarantees to protocol-level disruption, depending on how critical agent bonds are to security/economic design.
- Token-utility refund can be returned even when IService.unbond reports failure
- Targets
- unbondWithSignature (ServiceManager)
- Description
- The function reads a refund value from the token-utility (tokenRefund), then calls IService(serviceRegistry).unbond(…) which returns (bool success, uint256 refund). After the call it unconditionally replaces the returned refund with tokenRefund when tokenRefund > 0, but it does not check the success flag. If IService.unbond fails by returning success == false (instead of reverting), the function will return success == false together with a positive refund value. This violates the expectation that token-utility refund responses should only be exposed when the service unbond actually succeeded, and can mislead callers and downstream logic about the actual outcome.
- Root cause
- tokenRefund is fetched before calling IService.unbond and then is unconditionally used to overwrite refund whenever tokenRefund > 0, without verifying that IService.unbond succeeded (success == true). The code assumes either that IService.unbond always reverts on failure or that success is always true, but neither is enforced.
- Impact
- Callers may receive a response indicating a non-zero refund while the unbond operation actually failed. This can lead to: incorrect accounting and state assumptions in callers or downstream contracts; refunds being treated as available when they are not (potentially enabling incorrect token transfers); inconsistencies between service registry state and token-utility state; and in some contexts, exploitable discrepancies if an attacker can trigger IService.unbond to return false while tokenRefund > 0.
- Nonce consumed before confirming successful registration (registerAgentsWithSignature)
- Targets
- registerAgentsWithSignature (ServiceManager)
- Description
- The function increments and stores the operator-service nonce immediately after signature verification and before calling the external IService.registerAgents. If the callee can fail without reverting (i.e., return false), the nonce is still consumed even though the registration did not succeed. This breaks the intended property that each operator-service nonce increments only on successful registrations and allows an attacker or an accidental failure to consume nonces (griefing / denial of service).
- Root cause
- The implementation updates the nonce (state change) before performing and verifying the result of an external interaction. The code assumes registerAgents either always reverts on failure or that the call cannot fail silently; it does not handle a non-reverting failure case and does not follow checks-effects-interactions for this operation.
- Impact
- An adversary (or an innocuous failing condition) can cause registerAgents to fail while still consuming the operator-service nonce. Consequences include: replaying prevention being misapplied (signatures/nonce pairs are wasted), denial of service for the operator-service pair (legitimate future signed registrations require new nonces or fresh signatures), potential griefing where many nonces are consumed, and operational disruption of agent registration. If callers pay deposits or values that are tied to successful registrations, funds or state may become inconsistent depending on callee behavior.

## [F-392] null
Severity: `Low`

Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`

Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Judge Comments. Invalid, the mentioned timestamp overflow is unrealistic
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Invalid, the mentioned timestamp overflow is unrealistic
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- getNextRewardCheckpointTimestamp (StakingBase)
- Description
- The function returns tsCheckpoint + livenessPeriod without any bounds checks or use of a checked-arithmetic library. The provided StakingBase snippet contains no pragma specifying Solidity >=0.8.0 and no SafeMath/checked-add usage. If the contract is compiled with a Solidity version that does not perform automatic overflow checks (Solidity <0.8.0) or if unchecked arithmetic is otherwise in effect, the addition can overflow and wrap around, producing a tsNext smaller than tsCheckpoint. Because tsCheckpoint is set from block.timestamp and livenessPeriod is populated from initialization parameters, a maliciously large livenessPeriod can cause wraparound.
- Root cause
- Unchecked arithmetic: the implementation performs a raw uint256 addition (tsCheckpoint + livenessPeriod) with no overflow checks, and the contract snippet lacks a pragma enforcing a compiler with built-in overflow checks (Solidity >=0.8.0) or any validation of livenessPeriod at initialization.
- Impact
- If overflow occurs, the returned next-checkpoint timestamp can be less than the last checkpoint (tsNext < tsCheckpoint). Any logic that assumes the returned timestamp is monotonic or >= tsCheckpoint (e.g., reward release windows, liveness checks, gating or time-based permissions) can be bypassed or behave incorrectly. Potential consequences include incorrect reward calculations, bypassing timing restrictions, unexpected state transitions, or denial-of-service in time-dependent flows. The exploitability depends on whether an attacker (or untrusted initializer) can supply or influence livenessPeriod during deployment/initialization.

## [F-394] Constructor Misconfiguration (Registries)
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-394](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-394)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Judge Comments. Invalid, OOS, assumes malicious deployment input parameters by trusted admin/deployers
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Invalid, OOS, assumes malicious deployment input parameters by trusted admin/deployers
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Unsafe proxy initialization and baked-in implementation state break per-proxy configuration and enable takeover
- Targets
- constructor (ServiceManager)
- constructor (ServiceManagerProxy)
- Description
- Two related, high-impact issues in the proxy/implementation deployment flow can cause deployed proxies to behave incorrectly or be maliciously controlled. First, the implementation contract embeds collaborator addresses as immutable variables in its constructor, which are compiled into the implementation bytecode and therefore cannot be changed by proxies that delegatecall into it — preventing per-proxy configuration and potentially routing proxies to wrong or attacker-controlled collaborators. Second, the proxy constructor writes the implementation address into the proxy storage slot and immediately delegatecalls an untrusted initializer on that implementation; because delegatecall executes in the proxy’s storage context, a malicious initializer can overwrite the same implementation slot (e.g., setting it to address(0) or an attacker address). The constructor performs no post-initializer verification, so the proxy may be left pointing at a wrong or attacker-controlled implementation.
- Root cause
- Use of immutable state for collaborator addresses in the implementation constructor. Immutables are embedded into the implementation bytecode and are not stored in proxy storage, so delegatecall/initialize() cannot change them per-proxy. (2) Unsafe ordering and trust in the proxy constructor: it sstores the implementation slot before executing initializer code via delegatecall, and there is no validation after delegatecall to ensure the implementation slot still contains the expected value. The initializer therefore has the ability to modify proxy storage, including the implementation slot.
- Impact
- High — combined effects can break availability, integrity, and allow full takeover:
- Proxies will use the implementation’s baked-in collaborator addresses rather than per-proxy-configured addresses. This can cause misrouting of calls, broken functionality, or implicit trust in contracts chosen by the implementation deployer (centralization/trust issue).
- A malicious initializer supplied at deployment can overwrite the implementation slot to address(0), bricking the proxy (denial-of-service), or to an attacker-controlled implementation, enabling full takeover of proxy logic and any privileged functionality mediated by the implementation address.
- Because the constructor does not verify slot integrity post-initializer, deployments can silently produce proxies that report or forward calls to unexpected addresses, undermining system assumptions about upgrades, admin controls, and collaborator relationships.
- Unsafe constructor assumptions for baseURI — external call unchecked and missing input validation allow deployment-revert or broken initial state
- Targets
- constructor (ComplementaryServiceMetadata)
- constructor (HashCheckpoint)
- Description
- Multiple contracts assume that constructor inputs or external calls used to initialize baseURI are well-formed and succeed. These assumptions manifest as two related classes of issues: (A) the constructor makes an unchecked external call to an untrusted serviceRegistry and directly ABI-decodes the result, which can revert deployment if the registry address is malformed, absent, or behaves maliciously; and (B) constructors accept and persist an empty baseURI without validation, producing an initial state that the contract’s own setters disallow (invariant violation) and leading to malformed URIs at runtime.
- In ComplementaryServiceMetadata, the constructor performs a high-level call to IServiceRegistry(serviceRegistry).baseURI() and immediately decodes/assigns the return value to baseURI with no extcodesize check, try/catch, or low-level staticcall handling. If the provided address has no code (EOA), if baseURI() reverts, or if it returns malformed data, the constructor call reverts and the contract deployment fails.
- In HashCheckpoint, the constructor writes baseURI = _baseURI without validating that the string is non-empty. Later, an owner-only setter (setBaseURI) explicitly rejects empty strings, indicating an intended invariant that baseURI must be non-empty; the constructor’s lack of validation allows deploying an instance that violates that invariant and may remain in that broken state if the owner never sets a valid value or the owner key is lost.
- Root cause
- Unsafe constructor assumptions and missing validation: constructors assume external contracts exist and return well-formed data, and constructors accept unchecked input (empty baseURI). There is no defensive coding (extcodesize checks, low-level staticcall with success checks, try/catch, or require on bytes length) to guard against absent/malicious registries or invalid constructor parameters.
- Impact
- High for ComplementaryServiceMetadata (deployment-time denial-of-service) and Medium for HashCheckpoint (invariant violation leading to malformed URIs and degraded functionality):
- Deployment can be reverted: a malicious or misconfigured serviceRegistry address can cause ComplementaryServiceMetadata’s constructor to revert (denial-of-deployment). This breaks deployment pipelines and allows griefing by supplying an EOA or a contract that reverts or returns bad data.
- Broken/invalid initial state: HashCheckpoint can be deployed with an empty baseURI despite the contract’s later API forbidding empty values. This yields malformed URIs (CID_PREFIX + hash but no baseURI), can break frontends and integrations, and may be permanent if the owner does not update the value. While not directly enabling theft, it undermines correctness and availability of metadata resolution.
- Silent failures: Both issues are constructor-level and thus result in either a non-existent contract (in the revert case) or a contract that starts in an invalid state, making runtime detection and mitigation difficult.

## [F-395] Admin-Only/Privileged Access (Registries)
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-395](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-395)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Judge Comments. The determination of whether the service Id is token secured or if ETH secured is determined within the ServiceRegistryTokenUtility.registerAgentsTokenDeposit, function via the service id, and as such, do not need to be encoded in the signature
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: The determination of whether the service Id is token secured or if ETH secured is determined within the ServiceRegistryTokenUtility.registerAgentsTokenDeposit, function via the service id, and as such, do not need to be encoded in the signature
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- registerAgentsWithSignature (ServiceManager)
- Description
- The registerAgentsWithSignature flow in ServiceManager has multiple related weaknesses that together allow a service owner (or caller) to deviate from the operator’s intended registration semantics and to consume operator-signed nonces even when registration does not succeed. Specifically:
- The operator-authorized signature (getRegisterAgentsHash) does not include a deposit mode flag (token-secured vs native-ETH) or any expected native-ETH deposit amount. The function defers the bonding-mode decision to a runtime call (IServiceTokenUtility.registerAgentsTokenDeposit) and then either forwards a fixed wrapper amount or msg.value to IService.registerAgents. Because the signed payload does not bind the payment mode or amount, an attacker can choose a different payment path or supply arbitrary msg.value (including zero), causing registrations to proceed with incorrect, missing, or underpaid deposits if downstream logic does not strictly validate amounts.
- The function updates and persists the per-operator-service nonce (mapOperatorRegisterAgentsNonces) immediately after signature verification and before calling the external IService.registerAgents. If the external call fails by returning false (rather than reverting), registerAgentsWithSignature completes and the incremented nonce remains consumed. This allows operator-signed nonces to be spent without resulting in successful registrations.
- Combined, these issues enable misuse of operator-signed intents: a malicious service owner with a valid operator signature can (1) register agents without providing the operator-intended collateral or using an alternative payment path, and (2) grief the operator by consuming signed nonces through failing external calls, preventing reuse of those signatures.
- Root cause
- The signed authorization does not cryptographically bind critical runtime choices (deposit mode and expected native-ETH amount), and the implementation mutates nonce state prior to an external call whose failure mode may be a non-reverting false return. In short: (1) operator intent is not fully specified in the signed payload, and (2) state is advanced before the external operation is confirmed successful.
- Impact
- High: An attacker who is the service owner (msg.sender) and holds a valid operator signature for registering agents can bypass bonding guarantees by supplying arbitrary or zero ETH when native bonding was intended, or by forcing inconsistent token/native flows. This can lead to unauthorized registrations without proper collateral, misallocation or loss of funds, and weakened security assumptions for consumers relying on bonded operators. Additionally, signed nonces can be consumed without successful registrations, enabling denial-of-service or griefing against operator workflows and requiring operators to re-issue signatures.
- Unchecked assumptions about caller identity and external interfaces enable DoS and permanent state corruption
- Targets
- forcedUnstake (StakingBase)
- create (RecoveryModule)
- Description
- Two separate contracts contain related classes of mistakes where the code makes hard assumptions about caller identity or the behavior/shape of external contracts and then performs state-changing operations without appropriate validation or correct access gating. In StakingBase._unstake, an unconditional owner-only check is executed before honoring an enforced/forced-unstake path, preventing privileged actors from evicting stakes. In RecoveryModule.create, the function constructs and executes batched delegatecalls that assume precise multisig/multisend parameter ordering, owner ordering, and specific add/remove/threshold semantics; these assumptions are not validated, risking DoS or irreversible corruption of multisig control.
- Root cause
- Both issues stem from brittle control-flow and trust assumptions: (1) access-control checks are applied unconditionally in an internal unstake routine rather than being conditional on an ‘enforced’ flag or exposing a privileged path, and (2) recovery logic performs delegatecalls to external multisig/multisend targets relying on exact owner ordering, parameter order, and call semantics without verifying interfaces or outcomes. In each case the contract advances or expects critical state changes without enforcing or validating the preconditions required for those changes to be correct and safe.
- Impact
- High: These mistakes enable denial-of-service and in one case potential permanent loss of control. For StakingBase, privileged eviction flows (governance/registry/eviction actors) cannot forcibly remove misbehaving or inactive service owners; callers simply revert and eviction cannot proceed, allowing stuck or malicious owners to retain stakes and break eviction/reward accounting. For RecoveryModule, benign differences or maliciously crafted implementations of multisig/multisend can cause the recovery sequence to revert (blocking recovery) or to partially succeed leaving the multisig with incorrect owners or threshold—potentially locking governance or funds irrecoverably.

## [F-396] Zero Value Guard Failure (Registries)
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-396](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-396)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- RecoveryModule.recoverAccess — validation, locking, and unsafe multisig assumptions can block or break recovery
- Targets
- recoverAccess (RecoveryModule)
- Description
- recoverAccess in RecoveryModule contains multiple, related reliability and correctness issues that together can (1) cause immediate revert/DoS when the target multisig has zero owners, (2) create a fragile/manual reentrancy-lock that could block the function in some failure scenarios, and (3) rely unsafely on multisig implementation semantics (atomic multi-send and owner-change guarantees) without verification. These defects prevent the intended recovery flow from completing and risk permanent or partial corruption of multisig owner state.
- Root cause
- Missing defensive validation and unsafe assumptions: the function assumes IMultisig.getOwners() returns a non-empty, head-first-ordered owners array and that the multisig will execute a concatenated multi-send payload atomically and with expected module semantics. It computes numOwners - 1 and indexes multisigOwners[numOwners - 1] without checking numOwners > 0, uses a manual _locked flag pattern that depends on all failure paths reverting to reset it, and performs owner surgery via execTransactionFromModule without verifying postconditions or constraining multisig behavior.
- Impact
- High availability and integrity risks: if getOwners() returns an empty array, recoverAccess will revert (underflow / out-of-bounds) and the recovery cannot complete — effectively a denial-of-recovery. The brittle manual reentrancy-lock is fragile and could lead to DoS if future code paths fail to revert while leaving the lock set. Unsafe reliance on multisig atomicity/semantics can result in partial application or unexpected rejection of owner-change operations, producing inconsistent owner lists or loss of control. Overall, owners may be unable to regain access, or the multisig may be left in an incorrect or unrecoverable state.
- Missing validation of external deploy return value — CreateMultisig emitted for address(0)
- Targets
- deploy (ServiceManager)
- Description
- ServiceManager.deploy calls IService(serviceRegistry).deploy(…) and immediately emits CreateMultisig(multisig) using the returned address without validating it. If the registry returns address(0) (to signal a failure) or any other invalid address (e.g., a non-contract address or a deliberately bogus value from a malicious/buggy registry), ServiceManager will emit an event indicating a multisig was created even though no valid multisig exists. The function performs no storage updates, no further interaction with the returned address, and contains no error handling around the external call.
- Root cause
- The function assumes the external registry call always returns a valid, non-zero multisig address. There is no defensive programming: no require(multisig != address(0)), no address.code.length check, and no try/catch to handle revert/failure cases from the registry.
- Impact
- Off-chain consumers (indexers, UIs, other services) that rely on CreateMultisig will be misled into believing a multisig contract was deployed. This can cause failed interactions (attempts to call address(0) or a non-contract), broken UX, and downstream logic errors. If an attacker controls or compromises the registry (or if the registry is buggy), they can cause many false-positive CreateMultisig events, disrupt onboarding flows, or create conditions that enable further exploits in systems that trust the event. At minimum this causes incorrect state reconstruction off-chain; at worst it can be weaponized by a malicious registry to confuse or disrupt the protocol.

## [F-398] null
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-398](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-398)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- _evict (StakingBase)
- Description
- The _evict helper builds a compact list of services to evict (using sCounter) but then performs removals using the caller-supplied numEvictServices. If numEvictServices is larger than the number of non-zero entries actually collected (sCounter), the removal loop will read default-zero entries from serviceIndexes for the extra iterations. Those zeros are interpreted as index 0 and cause repeated swap-and-pop removals at setServiceIds[0], unintentionally evicting unrelated services and corrupting the active service set. The function never verifies that the counted evictions (sCounter) equals numEvictServices before mutating state.
- Root cause
- Reliance on an external caller-provided count (numEvictServices) for the number of removals without validating it against the locally-computed sCounter; default-zero values in serviceIndexes are consumed as valid indices when sCounter < numEvictServices.
- Impact
- Unintended removal of unrelated services from the active set (setServiceIds), leading to state corruption. Potential consequences include unexpected loss of staking positions, incorrect reward accounting, denial-of-service for evicted service owners, mis-specified event data, and broader protocol consistency/balance errors. If an attacker or a caller bug can cause numEvictServices to exceed the real count, they can trigger arbitrary removals (by index 0) and disrupt staking state.

## [F-399] null
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-399](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-399)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- _checkRatioPass (StakingBase)
- calculateStakingLastReward (StakingBase)
- Description
- The staking-preview and eligibility logic (_calculateStakingRewards / calculateStakingLastReward and the _checkRatioPass helper) depend on mutable external inputs and internal state in ways that produce non-deterministic or incorrect results. Specific issues observed: (1) a hard-coded return-data length check rejects valid ABI encodings of empty uint256[] from activityChecker.getMultisigNonces, causing ratioPass to remain false for multisigs with legitimately zero nonces; (2) calculateStakingLastReward invokes external activityChecker calls, reads mutable availableRewards, and is gated by a time window (livenessPeriod), making its preview non-deterministic for identical checkpoint/elapsed-time inputs; (3) the preview logic trusts internal arrays (setServiceIds / mapServiceInfo) without re-checking membership with the authoritative service registry, so deregistered or stale services can be included in eligibleServiceIds and shown non-zero previews.
- Root cause
- The reward-preview and eligibility implementation mixes runtime/external state with preview computations and applies brittle decoding assumptions: it (a) relies on current external activityChecker responses (including decoding its returned bytes) and live multisig nonce state rather than a deterministic snapshot; (b) uses a hard-coded returnData.length > 63 check that can reject valid ABI encodings of an empty dynamic array, skipping isRatioPass and leaving ratioPass false; and (c) builds eligible service lists from internal storage without validating against the authoritative registry. Combined, these design choices make previews dependent on mutable, possibly spoofable inputs and can produce false negatives for activity checks or include stale services.
- Impact
- Multiple correctness and integrity issues arise:
- Valid multisigs with zero recorded nonces can be treated as ineligible for rewards because _checkRatioPass may skip decoding and never call isRatioPass, leading to permanent false negatives until state changes; this can block onboarding/staking or other flows gated by activity checks.
- The reward preview returned by calculateStakingLastReward is not a pure function of checkpoint + elapsed time. UIs and integrators cannot trust previews: values can change if activityChecker behavior, multisig nonces, availableRewards, or the livenessPeriod flip. This enables confusion and potential manipulation: an actor who can influence activityChecker responses or availableRewards could change eligibility or allocation amounts.

## [F-400] Initialization Validation
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-400](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-400)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- serviceRegistry not validated as contract — external calls may revert and cause DoS
- Targets
- _initialize (StakingBase)
- Description
- The initializer (_initialize) ensures serviceRegistry != address(0) but does not verify that the provided address actually contains contract code or implements the expected ERC721 / IService interface. Multiple internal functions make direct high-level external calls to serviceRegistry (e.g., IService(serviceRegistry).getService, safeTransferFrom, transferFrom, getAgentParams, getAgentInstances, mapAgentInstanceOperators) without try/catch or interface checks. If serviceRegistry is an EOA or a self-destructed address, these external calls will revert when invoked and bubble up, breaking stake/unstake/claim/reward flows and rendering the staking contract unusable.
- Root cause
- Missing validation in _initialize that _stakingParams.serviceRegistry.code.length > 0 (or equivalent) and/or that the address supports the required ERC165/ERC721 interface. The code only checks activityChecker.code.length but not serviceRegistry.
- Impact
- Denial-of-service: staking-related functions may always revert, preventing staking, unstaking (NFT transfers back to users), and reward calculations. Users could be unable to recover tokenized service NFTs or claim rewards. If a malicious or mistaken initialization uses an EOA or destroyed address, the system becomes inoperable until redeployed or otherwise fixed. Severity: High.
- Missing module argument in Safe.setup calldata — recovery module may not be enabled or Safe creation may fail
- Targets
- create (SafeMultisigWithRecoveryModule)
- Description
- The create() function composes calldata for Gnosis Safe.setup that calls recoveryModule with only the 4-byte selector 0x24292962 (ENABLE_MODULE_SELECTOR) and no ABI-encoded arguments. The canonical Safe method enableModule(address) uses the same selector but requires the module address as an argument. By sending only the selector, the code instead expects recoveryModule to implement a non-standard no-argument callback that, when invoked by the Safe during setup, will enable the module via a callback. There is no runtime validation that recoveryModule implements this no-arg callback. If recoveryModule does not implement the expected no-arg callback (or if it reverts), the Safe will either be created without the recovery module enabled (silent failure) or the Safe.setup call will revert and Safe creation will fail.
- Root cause
- Incorrect construction of the Safe.setup payload: the module address is omitted and only the 4-byte enableModule selector is provided. The implementation assumes a non-standard no-argument callback on recoveryModule instead of invoking the canonical enableModule(address) or encoding the module address in calldata. No validation or fallback is performed to ensure the module was enabled.
- Impact
- High — either (1) the deployed Safe is created without the intended recovery module enabled (silent misconfiguration), breaking intended recovery guarantees and misleading users, or (2) Safe creation may revert if recoveryModule does not implement the expected callback or intentionally reverts, causing denial-of-service during Safe creation. An attacker or integrator could supply an incompatible or malicious recoveryModule to cause either outcome.

## [F-401] null
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-401](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-401)

Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Judge Comments. Invalid, the exact bond value is enforced in the following check within`ServiceRegistry.registerAgents`
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Invalid, the exact bond value is enforced in the following check within`ServiceRegistry.registerAgents`
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- registerAgentsWithSignature (ServiceManager)
- Description
- When`IServiceTokenUtility.registerAgentsTokenDeposit(…)`returns true,`registerAgentsWithSignature`calls`IService.registerAgents`forwarding exactly`agentInstances.length * BOND_WRAPPER wei`and ignores the caller’s`msg.value`. In the observed code`BOND_WRAPPER`is a constant equal to 1, and`ServiceManager`has no`receive()/fallback()`payable handler nor any withdraw/sweep function. As a result, if the caller (typically the service owner) supplies msg.value larger than the computed bond, the surplus ETH remains in the ServiceManager contract balance and cannot be recovered by the caller or owner through any available function in the contract.
- Root cause
- In the token-secured execution path the function uses a computed fixed value (agentInstances.length * BOND_WRAPPER) when forwarding ETH to IService.registerAgents and does not (a) validate that msg.value is zero or exactly the expected amount, (b) forward the full msg.value, or (c) provide a refund/sweep mechanism. This logic mismatch (ignoring msg.value in one branch) combined with the absence of withdrawal code causes any surplus ETH to be trapped.
- Impact
- Accidental or defensive overpayments by service owners (or callers) result in permanent locking of Ether in the ServiceManager contract. Funds cannot be refunded to the sender nor withdrawn by an owner because no withdraw/escape hatch exists in the contract. While this is not a direct theft of third‑party funds, it leads to unrecoverable loss of ETH for honest callers and can be trivially reproduced by calling the function with`msg.value > agentInstances.length * BOND_WRAPPER`when the token-utility returns true.

## [F-402] processBridgeData may indirectly read/modify contract state via opaque _verifyData callee

- Targets
- processBridgeData (ProcessBridgedDataOptimism)
- Description
- processBridgeData itself performs only decoding and validation of an incoming message and then calls _verifyBridgedData, which iterates over embedded entries and invokes _verifyData(target, payload, chainId). The implementation of _verifyData is not provided. Because _verifyData could perform SLOAD/SSTORE, emit events, or perform external calls (including calls to ‘target’), the property that “processBridgeData does not rely on or modify persistent contract state” cannot be guaranteed from the available code. A malicious or state-changing _verifyData (or any functions it calls) could cause state changes, depend on storage values, or trigger reentrancy or external effects when processBridgeData is executed.
- Root cause
- processBridgeData assumes (implicitly) that its callee chain is side-effect-free, but it calls into an opaque function (_verifyData) that is not shown. This missing guarantee (no purity/view annotation or visible implementation) allows _verifyData to read/write storage or perform external calls, invalidating the stated property.
- Impact
- If _verifyData or functions it calls perform state changes or external calls, then:
- processBridgeData may indirectly modify contract storage (SSTORE) or read sensitive state (SLOAD), breaking invariants and leading to incorrect logic elsewhere.
- External calls can enable reentrancy or interaction with malicious contracts.
- Unexpected event emissions or state writes could be used to manipulate off-chain systems or monitors.
- The function may be exploitable depending on the semantics of _verifyData (e.g., unauthorized state mutation, denial of service, or bridging logic corruption). The concrete severity depends entirely on _verifyData’s implementation.

## [F-403] Self-call gated changeSourceGovernor can be invoked during message processing allowing unauthorized governor update
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-403](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-403)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- changeSourceGovernor (WormholeMessenger)
- Description
- changeSourceGovernor requires that msg.sender == address(this) (i.e., only self-external-calls can invoke it). receiveWormholeMessages authenticates incoming Wormhole messages (checks wormholeRelayer, sourceChain, and that sourceAddress == sourceGovernor) and then calls _processData(data). If _processData (or any callee reachable during processing) executes a self-call to this.changeSourceGovernor or directly writes to sourceGovernor without additional authorization checks, the contract will update sourceGovernor while processing a Wormhole message. This is safe only if _processData enforces the same strict authentication guarantees — namely that the instruction to change the governor actually originated from a message that was authenticated as coming from the current sourceGovernor. The provided code does not include _processData, so whether this safety property holds is unknown. If _processData (or other code reachable from external callers) can trigger a self-call to changeSourceGovernor based on unauthenticated/forged input, an attacker could set sourceGovernor to an attacker-controlled identity.
- Root cause
- Separation of concerns and implicit trust: the state-changing function (changeSourceGovernor) is protected only by a self-call gate rather than explicit authentication, and authorization is performed outside of that function (in receiveWormholeMessages). This design assumes that any self-call path into changeSourceGovernor is only reachable from properly authenticated code paths, but the implementation of those paths (_processData and its callees) is not enforced by changeSourceGovernor itself.
- Impact
- If an attacker can cause the contract to call changeSourceGovernor without the instruction being authorized by the current sourceGovernor, they can set sourceGovernor to an attacker-controlled bytes32. Consequences include: future Wormhole messages appearing to originate from the new (attacker) sourceGovernor will be accepted, enabling arbitrary administrative actions mediated by messaging, potential irreversible misconfiguration, loss of protocol control, and downstream fund or asset exfiltration depending on what messages the messenger controls.

## [F-404] Constructor sets sourceGovernor without emitting SourceGovernorUpdated
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-404](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-404)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- constructor (OptimismMessenger)
- Description
- The contract’s constructor assigns the storage variable sourceGovernor directly (sourceGovernor = _sourceGovernor) but does not emit the SourceGovernorUpdated event. The changeSourceGovernor function emits SourceGovernorUpdated when it updates sourceGovernor, so the property “Changing the source governor must emit the SourceGovernorUpdated event” is expected to hold for all writes to sourceGovernor. Because the constructor performs an initial write without emitting the event, that property is violated (unless the constructor assignment is intended and documented as an explicit exception).
- Root cause
- An event-emission was omitted in the constructor: the contract updates the sourceGovernor state variable during initialization but fails to emit the SourceGovernorUpdated event, unlike the runtime setter changeSourceGovernor which correctly emits the event.
- Impact
- Low-to-moderate operational impact: this is primarily a transparency/logging/invariant issue rather than an immediate access-control break. Off-chain monitors, indexers, or other contracts/tools that rely on the SourceGovernorUpdated event to observe changes to the source governor will not see the initial assignment. This can lead to inconsistent state tracking, missed alerts, or incorrect assumptions by off-chain tooling. It is unlikely to be directly exploitable for theft, but it violates an expected invariant and may impair security monitoring or automated checks.

## [F-405] Reentrancy lock sticks on external call failure
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-405](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-405)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- burn (Burner)
- Description
- If the external`IToken(olas).burn(olasBalance)`call reverts, the state variable`_locked`remains set to`2`. Subsequent calls to`burn()`will then always fail the`_locked > 1`check, permanently disabling burning.
- Root cause
- The reentrancy guard`_locked`is set to`2`before the external call and is only reset to`1`after the call succeeds, with no`try/catch`or`finally`-style reset on failure paths.
- Impact
- A single failing burn attempt bricks the contract’s burn functionality, preventing any future burns and locking the token balance inside the contract.

- The contract assumes an external burn(amount) call atomically reduces the caller’s balance by exactly amount and provides no verification.
