## [F-407] null
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-407](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-407)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Judge Comments. The Olas token does not implement a transfer hook that allows such reentrancy to occur
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: The Olas token does not implement a transfer hook that allows such reentrancy to occur
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- burn (Burner)
- Description
- The burn() function reads this contract’s olas token balance, calls IToken(olas).burn(olasBalance), immediately emits a Burned event, and releases its reentrancy lock. It never re-checks the contract’s token balance or otherwise enforces that the external burn call actually reduced this contract’s balance. Because olas is an external token contract, a malicious or nonstandard IToken implementation (or a third party acting during the call) can cause the balance to remain or be restored, making the emitted event misleading and the burn ineffective.
- Root cause
- The function trusts an external side-effect without verifying the post-condition. It assumes IToken.burn(amount) will irrevocably reduce address(this)’s balance but does not read balanceOf(address(this)) after the burn call nor enforce an invariant (e.g., resulting balance == 0).
- Impact
- Off-chain observers and other contracts relying on the Burned event or on the contract’s reduced olas balance can be misled. Possible consequences: incorrect accounting, broken protocol invariants, and economic exploits where tokens thought to be destroyed are reused or double-counted. An attacker controlling the token contract (or a buggy token) can make burn() a no-op, burn from a different account, or burn then re-mint/transfer back during the burn call — leaving tokens available for abuse while the protocol believes they were destroyed.

## [F-408] null
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-408](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-408)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- checkTransaction / unpause (GuardCM)
- pause (GuardCM)
- Description
- The GuardCM contract contains two related flaws in its pause/unpause and role-check logic that together subvert the guard protections intended to validate transactions. First, the paused state variable is used with inverted semantics and is never initialized to the protective value at deployment, leaving the guard checks disabled by default. Second, role checks in pause() are ordered such that if the owner and multisig are set to the same address, the owner branch is taken and governance preconditions for the multisig branch are bypassed. Both issues allow transactions to execute without intended validations or permit unilateral pausing that should be constrained by governance.
- Root cause
- Logical inversion and missing initialization: paused defaults to 0 in Solidity and the contract never initializes it to the protective value. The unpause() function sets paused = 1 (which enables checks), meaning the safety checks are disabled by default until someone calls unpause(). 2) Role- and flow-control issue: constructor allows owner == multisig and pause() checks the owner branch before checking multisig/governor conditions, so a single address in both roles can pause without meeting the governor defeat requirement.
- Impact
- High — In the default (deployed) state the guard validations in checkTransaction (e.g., blocking delegatecall, preventing self-call to the multisig, enforcing owner schedule checks) are skipped, enabling unauthorized or dangerous transactions including delegatecalls and self-calls to the multisig. Additionally, if owner and multisig are the same address, that single address can pause the contract without the intended governor constraint, undermining separation-of-powers and enabling denial-of-service or administrative misuse.

## [F-409] GuardCM issues (lower confidence)
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-409](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-409)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Chain ID truncation when stored as uint64
- Targets
- setBridgeMediatorL1BridgeParams (GuardCM)
- Description
- The function accepts arbitrary 256-bit chain IDs but stores them in the BridgeParams struct’s uint64 chainId field. Although it checks chainId == 0 and chainId <= MAX_CHAIN_ID, there is no guarantee that MAX_CHAIN_ID is <= 2^64 - 1. If a value greater than 2^64 - 1 (but still <= MAX_CHAIN_ID) is provided, the cast to uint64 silently truncates the most significant bits, causing a different ID to be stored than the one validated. Subsequent logic consuming BridgeParams can then operate on an unintended chain ID, undermining the guard’s enforcement assumptions.
- Root cause
- Lack of validation that chainIds[i] fits within uint64 before assigning to BridgeParams.chainId.
- Impact
- Attackers who can influence owner inputs (or a misconfigured owner) can register bridge parameters for a high chainId that truncates to another value, potentially bypassing or corrupting bridge validation logic that depends on accurate chain IDs.
- Targets
- pause / unpause / checkTransaction (GuardCM)
- Description
- The guard can be permanently left in the paused state because the multisig is able to set paused to the paused value, while only the owner (set to the timelock contract at construction) may restore the active state. When paused, the guard prevents or rejects transactions targeting the owner/timelock, so the timelock cannot later call GuardCM.unpause. As a result, if the multisig triggers pause, there is no path for the owner/timelock to call unpause and restore normal monitoring.
- Root cause
- A logic combination error: pause() permits the multisig to set paused to the paused state, but unpause() can only be executed by owner. The owner is the timelock contract, and the guard’s transactional checks prevent calls directed at the owner while paused, creating a circular dependency that leaves paused permanently set when triggered by the multisig.
- Impact
- Permanent denial of the guard’s active monitoring and validation. The system remains in the paused state indefinitely: scheduled/monitored operations and guard-enforced protections cannot be restored by the legitimate owner. This can disrupt protocol operation (failed schedule verification, inability to reconfigure allowed selectors/bridges via owner), hamper upgrades or emergency responses, and may require privileged out-of-band recovery (contract redeploy, multisig/owner replacement) to restore functionality.

## [F-410] GovernorOLAS issues (lower confidence)
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-410](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-410)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Judge Comments. As mentioned in the issue, the legacy population is no longer required, so there is no impact here.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: As mentioned in the issue, the legacy population is no longer required, so there is no impact here.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Missing compatibility metadata when using 4-argument propose in GovernorOLAS
- Targets
- propose(address[] targets, uint256[] values, bytes[] calldatas, string description) (GovernorOLAS)
- Description
- Proposals submitted via the 4-argument propose(…) path do not populate the compatibility/legacy metadata stored in _proposalDetails (signatures, legacy calldatas, descriptionHash). The GovernorOLAS override for the 4-arg propose simply delegates to super.propose(…), and that code path does not call GovernorCompatibilityBravo._storeProposal which is responsible for recording legacy proposal fields. Only the 5-argument compatibility overload (the Compound-style propose that accepts signatures) calls _storeProposal, so proposals created with the 4-arg interface leave the compatibility fields unset.
- Root cause
- GovernorOLAS’s 4-argument propose delegates to the base 4-arg implementation and never calls the compatibility helper _storeProposal (implemented in GovernorCompatibilityBravo). The only code path that invokes _storeProposal is the 5-argument compatibility propose, so the 4-arg path omits populating _proposalDetails.
- Impact
- Functional/compatibility breakage: on-chain or off-chain tooling and any contract code that expects signatures, legacy calldatas, or descriptionHash to exist in _proposalDetails will find those fields unset for proposals created via the 4-arg route. This can break proposal decoding, UI displays, legacy tooling integration, and any backward-compatibility logic that relies on the stored legacy data. It does not directly enable bypass of voting checks or asset theft, but it can lead to incorrect behavior in systems that assume those fields are present.
- Governor constructed with zero governance token or timelock
- Targets
- constructor (GovernorOLAS)
- Description
- The constructor does not validate the governanceToken and timelock addresses. Supplying address(0) for either parameter succeeds, leaving the governor configured with a non-existent voting token or timelock. Subsequent governance operations that rely on these components will fail, effectively bricking the governor once deployed with bad inputs.
- Root cause
- Missing zero-address validation for critical constructor arguments (governanceToken and timelock).
- Impact
- Governor cannot execute proposals or compute voting power, resulting in a permanent denial of service for the governance process.

## [F-411] Admin-Only/Privileged Access (Governance)
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-411](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-411)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Owner-controlled verifier delegatecall enables arbitrary GuardCM storage corruption and invariant breakage
- Targets
- checkTransaction / _verifySchedule (delegatecall path to verifierL2 → IBridgeVerifier.processBridgeData) (GuardCM)
- _verifySchedule (GuardCM)
- checkAfterExecution (GuardCM)
- changeGovernorCheckProposalId (GuardCM)
- Description
- GuardCM’s _verifySchedule executes external verifier contracts using delegatecall into an owner-configurable verifierL2 address (mapBridgeMediatorL1BridgeParams[].verifierL2). Because delegatecall executes callee code in the GuardCM storage context, any storage writes performed by the verifier modify GuardCM’s own state. VerifierL2 is settable by the owner (only validated as a contract) and _verifySchedule can be triggered by any caller who submits a scheduled SCHEDULE/SCHEDULE_BATCH transaction. There is no sandboxing, no post-execution snapshot/validation in checkAfterExecution (it’s a no-op), and _verifySchedule does not re-validate critical storage after the delegatecall. Together these design choices allow a malicious or buggy verifier (or an owner-registered malicious verifier) to permanently corrupt GuardCM storage and break vital invariants.
- Root cause
- Using delegatecall to run owner-controlled external verifier code in the GuardCM storage context, combined with (1) owner-controlled verifier registration with only a code-presence check, (2) lack of post-execution validation or state snapshot/compare (checkAfterExecution is a no-op), and (3) allowing any caller to trigger the delegatecall via scheduled payloads. Critical invariants (owner, paused flag, mapBridgeMediatorL1BridgeParams entries including chainId, governorCheckProposalId, allowed-target mappings, etc.) are enforced only at setters or assumed to hold, but delegatecalled code can overwrite them unchecked.
- Impact
- High. A malicious or compromised verifierL2 (or an owner who registers a malicious verifier) can: (a) overwrite ownership or governance-related storage (owner, governor, governorCheckProposalId), enabling takeover or governance subversion; (b) flip or clear paused flags and disable guard enforcement, bypassing protections; (c) modify bridge parameter entries (mediator addresses, verifier pointers, chainId) to corrupt routing or bypass chainId bounds checks, causing misrouting, silent no-op mediators, or loss/misprocessing of cross-chain messages; (d) corrupt mappings that gate allowed target/selector/chainId checks; and (e) perform arbitrary storage writes to other slots, enabling broad privilege escalation or denial-of-service. Because any external caller can cause _verifySchedule to run for a scheduled payload, these storage modifications can be triggered without owner involvement once a malicious verifier is registered. Many of these modifications are persistent and are neither detected nor reverted due to the empty checkAfterExecution hook.
- Owner-controlled governor/proposal state and inconsistent pause logic enable governance subversion and multisig DoS
- Targets
- changeGovernorCheckProposalId (GuardCM)
- pause (GuardCM)
- unpause (interacts with pause and checkTransaction) (GuardCM)
- changeGovernor (GuardCM)
- Description
- Multiple related issues allow the owner to (a) unilaterally control or block the multisig/governor path for pausing, (b) set stored governor/proposal state to values that make multisig pause unusable or trivially satisfiable, and (c) exploit inconsistent paused encodings so operator actions have inverted effects. The contract relies on a stored governor address and a stored governorCheckProposalId when deciding whether a multisig caller may set paused state, but these values can be set or left stale by the owner without validation. Additionally, pause()/unpause() treat owner and multisig differently and write numeric encodings that do not match the guard’s check semantics. Combined, these flaws let a single owner key either permanently disable the guard’s protections, prevent multisig/governor from exercising emergency pause, or cause pause/unpause to behave opposite to operator intent.
- Root cause
- Design and implementation mistakes in governance-related state management and pause logic: (1) owner-only setters (changeGovernor, changeGovernorCheckProposalId) accept values without verifying the governor address implements IGovernor or that the stored proposal id is meaningful for that governor; (2) pause() calls IGovernor.state(governorCheckProposalId) without try/catch, so incompatible/stale ids or non-compliant governor addresses can cause reverts; (3) the owner branch of pause() omits the governor-proposal check enforced for multisig, and unpause() is owner-only; and (4) the numeric encoding used for paused is inconsistent (pause sets 2, unpause sets 1, but checks treat 1 as the paused/restricted state), producing inverted semantics.
- Impact
- High. The combined effects let the single owner address gain effective unilateral control over emergency pause/unpause and block the multisig/governor recovery path. Concrete consequences include:
- Multisig/ Governor DoS: The owner can set governorCheckProposalId to an arbitrary or incompatible id (or change governor to an EOA/non-compliant contract) causing IGovernor.state(…) called by pause() to revert or return a non-Defeated state; this makes the multisig branch unusable and prevents multisig from pausing the guard in emergencies.
- Governance subversion: The owner can point governorCheckProposalId to a proposal known to be Defeated (or change it later) enabling pause() when governance did not authorize it, or conversely pick a non-Defeated/stale id to prevent legitimate governance from pausing.
- Permanent owner lock-in: Because unpause() is owner-only, the owner can set paused to a value that disables guard enforcement (or exploit the inverted encoding) and refuse to restore normal operation, leaving multisig/governor powerless to recover on-chain.
- Input validation and key-packing errors allow mapping collisions, misrouting, and owner-misconfiguration of bridge mediation
- Targets
- getTargetSelectorChainId (reads); setTargetSelectorChainIds (writes) (GuardCM)
- setBridgeMediatorL1BridgeParams (GuardCM)
- Description
- GuardCM accepts owner-controlled inputs (chainId and bridgeMediatorL1) and uses bit-packed composite keys and stored mediator entries to gate and route schedule verification and execution. Two classes of validation failures allow the owner (or a compromised owner) to create silent collisions or misconfigurations that break access-control and routing invariants:
- ChainId packing / masking bug: chainId is accepted as a uint256 and packed into bits 192–255 of a 256-bit composite key (target | selector | chainId<<192) without enforcing a 64-bit bound or masking. If chainId >= 2^64, left-shifting it by 192 wraps modulo 2^256 and high bits are lost — e.g. chainId == 2^64 yields a zero contribution — causing different chainId values to map to the same key. The getter and setter use the same flawed packing, so writes by the owner can silently overwrite or collide with other entries.
- Missing mediator code validation: bridgeMediatorL1 addresses are registered by the owner without verifying that those addresses have runtime code. The mapping is used to identify schedules that should be validated by a configured verifierL2, but a mediator entry may point to an EOA or destroyed contract. In that case, an approved schedule that was meant to invoke mediator logic can execute a no-op at runtime while still being allowed by the guard.
- Together these issues undermine the guard’s guarantees about which targets/selectors/chainIds are allowed and whether registered mediators actually execute the intended logic.
- Root cause
- Insufficient input validation and incorrect assumptions about fixed-width fields when constructing packed mapping keys, combined with lax registration checks for mediator addresses. Specifically: chainId is not masked or bounded to 64 bits before left-shifting into the packed key; and setBridgeMediatorL1BridgeParams does not verify that bridgeMediatorL1 has deployed runtime code.
- Impact
- Medium-High. Practical consequences include:
- Mapping collisions and silent overwrite: Owner writes using an out-of-range chainId (>=2^64) may unintentionally collide with existing entries (including producing a zero contribution), corrupting mapAllowedTargetSelectorChainIds and breaking intended allow/deny rules. This can cause incorrect acceptance or rejection of scheduled calls for certain chainIds.
- Misrouting and access-control confusion: Callers relying on getTargetSelectorChainId can observe misleading results (false positives/negatives) for large chainId inputs, potentially allowing or denying actions incorrectly.
- Approved no-op executions: If the owner registers a mediator address without code (EOA or destroyed contract), GuardCM can approve and route a schedule as if it will be mediated, while the on-chain execution of the scheduled call performs no mediator logic. This can silently disable expected bridge behaviors (e.g., transfer finalization), disrupt cross-chain flows, and create false assurances.
- Increased blast radius if owner key is compromised: Because only the owner can write these mappings/registrations, a compromised owner key can weaponize the above flaws to alter routing, create collisions, or configure mediators to be inert, causing denial-of-service or loss of expected cross-chain operations. Even without compromise, inadvertent owner misconfiguration can have significant downstream effects.
- Mutable external sender checked once before unprotected external calls (reentrancy / mutable-state trust issue)
- Targets
- processMessageFromSource (OptimismMessenger)
- Description
- processMessageFromSource performs a single equality check of ICrossDomainMessenger(CDMContractProxyHome).xDomainMessageSender() against the contract’s stored sourceGovernor, then calls _processData which performs arbitrary low-level external calls (target.call) in a loop. There is no reentrancy guard or mechanism to freeze/snapshot the messenger-reported sender while _processData executes. Because the messenger-reported sender value is read from an external contract and can be mutated by external calls, a called target (directly or indirectly) can change xDomainMessageSender during processing, breaking the implicit invariant that the reported sender remains equal to sourceGovernor for the entire processing flow.
- Root cause
- Relying on a one-time equality check of a mutable value owned by an external contract and then performing arbitrary external calls without reentrancy protection or locking. _processData executes target.call{value}(payload) in a loop with no reentrancy guard, allowing external code to mutate external-contract state (including xDomainMessageSender) mid-execution.
- Impact
- An attacker can craft a target payload that, when called by _processData, triggers calls that mutate the messenger proxy’s xDomainMessageSender (or related state). This breaks assumptions made after the single check and can lead to: unauthorized actions attributed to the original sourceGovernor, inconsistent state changes, privilege escalation, theft of funds via manipulated logic, or causing the contract to accept/execute actions from a different sender than originally validated. Events emitted after processing (e.g., MessageReceived) may also be misleading.

## [F-412] Timestamp width mismatch breaks same-block update detection in validatePrice
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-412](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-412)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Judge Comments. uint32 is more than sufficient to represent current timestamps, so this issue is only technicallly correct but realistically not going to occur.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: uint32 is more than sufficient to represent current timestamps, so this issue is only technicallly correct but realistically not going to occur.
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- validatePrice (UniswapPriceOracle)
- Description
- validatePrice reads the pair reserves via getReserves() and compares the returned blockTimestampLast to block.timestamp to detect same-block updates. getReserves() (Uniswap V2) stores blockTimestampLast as a uint32 (timestamp % 2 32). validatePrice assigns the returned value into a uint256 and compares it directly to block.timestamp (uint256) without truncating or casting. Because blockTimestampLast is effectively a 32-bit timestamp (wraps modulo 2 32) and validatePrice does not normalize widths, the equality check can be incorrect (notably once the 32-bit value differs from the full 256-bit timestamp). As a consequence the function may incorrectly treat a pair that was updated in the current block as if it were updated in a prior block, causing the oracle to continue and accept a price computed using reserves that could have been manipulated within the same block.
- Root cause
- Type/width mismatch: blockTimestampLast originates from a uint32 in the Uniswap pair but is read into a uint256 and compared against block.timestamp without casting/truncation. The code fails to normalize the timestamps (e.g., uint32(block.timestamp) vs uint32(blockTimestampLast)), so wraparound or differing bit-widths break the intended same-block detection.
- Impact
- If validatePrice misdetects a same-block reserve update, the oracle will compute a time-weighted price using a maliciously-updated reserve snapshot from the same block. An attacker can perform swaps or other reserve-manipulating actions and have those changes reflected in getReserves() within the same block; because validatePrice can fail to recognize the update, it may accept a manipulated price. Practical exploitability today is low because the classic wraparound (2**32 seconds) won’t occur until far in the future; however the logical bug reduces robustness and could become exploitable after wrap or if any environment produces mismatched timestamp representations. Fixes should be applied proactively.

## [F-413] getPrice depends on mutable pair and direction allowing price manipulation
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-413](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-413)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- getPrice (UniswapPriceOracle)
- Description
- The getPrice() view reads reserves from an external Uniswap pair stored in the contract state variable`pair`and selects which reserve is input/output using the contract state variable`direction`. If`pair`or`direction`can be changed after deployment, an attacker or privileged account can point`pair`at a malicious/controlled pair or flip`direction`to produce an arbitrary or inverted price. If both`pair`and`direction`are immutable (set once at construction and cannot be changed), the function does not rely on modifiable external configuration and is safe with respect to the stated property.
- Root cause
- getPrice relies on state variables (`pair`and`direction`) that influence which external contract is queried and how its reserves are interpreted; if those variables are mutable after deployment, the function’s output depends on modifiable configuration rather than only immutable code and inputs.
- Impact
- If mutable, an attacker or admin could cause getPrice() to return an attacker-chosen price by (1) changing`pair`to a pair they control whose reserves yield a desired ratio, or (2) toggling`direction`to swap numerator/denominator and invert/amplify the reported price. Downstream consumers of this price (liquidations, oracle-based transfers, pricing logic) could be manipulated, leading to financial loss, incorrect collateral calculations, or unauthorized fund transfers.

## [F-414] Tokenomics.sol issues (lower confidence)
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-414](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-414)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Batch allows skipping unitIds -> pending incentives can remain unfinalized/stuck
- Targets
- accountOwnerIncentives (Tokenomics)
- Description
- accountOwnerIncentives enforces that unitIds are strictly increasing per unitType but does not require them to be consecutive. Because per-unit incentive state (mapUnitIncentives[unitType][unitId].lastEpoch, pendingRelativeReward, pendingRelativeTopUp) is tracked per unitId and finalized only when that exact unitId is processed (via _finalizeIncentivesForUnitId), callers can submit ascending but non-contiguous unitId batches (e.g. [1,3]). Any skipped unitIds that have pendingRelative values and an old lastEpoch will not be finalized by that call and remain with pendingRelative* and lastEpoch > 0, effectively leaving incentives unconverted/unclaimable until the skipped IDs are processed in a future call.
- Root cause
- The function only checks unitIds[i] > lastIds[unitTypes[i]] and updates a local per-call lastIds[] array; it does not require unitIds[i] == lastIds[unitTypes[i]] + 1 (contiguity). There is no per-unit-type last-processed id in storage; finalization is per specific (unitType, unitId).
- Impact
- Owners who (intentionally or accidentally) submit non-consecutive unitId batches can cause incentives for skipped IDs to remain unfinalized and unclaimable, effectively locking funds. This leads to inconsistent per-owner vs epoch-level accounting, delayed or lost payouts for skipped units, and potential denial-of-service to rightful claimants who never include the skipped IDs. While this does not directly enable theft, it can cause permanent or long-lived stuck incentives and inconsistent state across epochs.
- Refund Function Increases Effective Bond Instead of Decreasing
- Targets
- refundFromBondProgram (Tokenomics)
- Description
- The refundFromBondProgram function adds the refunded amount to effectiveBond. Since effectiveBond tracks the currently reserved bond amount, refunds should decrease that reserve. By adding the amount, the function inverts the intended accounting and inflates the effective bond balance.
- Root cause
- Using addition instead of subtraction when adjusting effectiveBond during refunds.
- Impact
- Mis-accounting of the bond reserve can cause downstream logic that relies on effectiveBond to overestimate reserved amounts, potentially leading to incorrect allocations or economic imbalances in the bond program.
- totalDonationsETH downcast truncates large ETH donations
- Targets
- trackServiceDonations (Tokenomics)
- Description
- The function aggregates the current ETH donation amount with the epoch’s cumulative total and then stores it as a uint96. Because the intermediate sum is a uint256, any epoch whose total donations exceed 2^96-1 will be truncated when assigned to uint96, causing the recorded donation total to wrap and become incorrect.
- Root cause
- Storing the cumulative donation amount in a uint96 without validating that the value fits within 96 bits.
- Impact
- Large donation totals silently wrap, corrupting accounting for the epoch. Incentive distributions that rely on the recorded donation amount become wrong and can break the protocol’s economic assumptions.
- Targets
- changeTokenomicsParameters (Tokenomics)
- Description
- The function emits TokenomicsParametersUpdateRequested(epochCounter + 1, …) claiming the supplied parameters will take effect next epoch, but it applies some inputs immediately (devsPerCapital, codePerDev, epsilonRate) while only epochLen and veOLASThreshold are staged into nextEpochLen/nextVeOLASThreshold. The event therefore reports an incorrect/ambiguous view of which values are staged for the next epoch.
- Root cause
- Inconsistent handling of inputs: devsPerCapital, codePerDev and epsilonRate are written directly to their live storage variables when validated, while epoch length and veOLASThreshold are written to dedicated “next” variables. The function nevertheless emits a single event that unconditionally attributes all five parameters to epochCounter + 1, creating a semantic mismatch between storage updates and the event payload.
- Impact
- Off-chain consumers (indexers, dashboards, governance tooling, automated scripts) that rely on TokenomicsParametersUpdateRequested to learn what parameters will be active next epoch will be misinformed. Consequences include incorrect accounting, stale or wrong UI values, erroneous automation decisions, or governance signals based on wrong future values. This is a correctness/semantic bug (not directly a funds-loss exploit), but can produce operational and integrity problems for tooling that trusts the event.
- Bitmask-check parsing bug + unconditional flag clear can drop staged tokenomics updates
- Targets
- checkpoint (Tokenomics)
- Description
- The checkpoint function uses a bitmask register tokenomicsParametersUpdated to detect staged parameter changes, but the code performs bit checks without parentheses (e.g. if (tokenomicsParametersUpdated & 0x01 == 0x01)). Because operator precedence can make this expression parsed differently than the intended ( (tokenomicsParametersUpdated & 0x01) == 0x01 ), the function can take the else branch even when a flag bit was set. The else branch copies current parameters into the nextEpochPoint (overwriting staged values). Later in the same function tokenomicsParametersUpdated is cleared unconditionally (tokenomicsParametersUpdated = 0) or via tokenomicsParametersUpdated > 0 branch; additionally the code ORs tokenomicsParametersUpdated with 0x04 mid-function when a year rollover is detected. These behaviors together allow staged updates to be silently discarded: a flag can be set and next* values written, but checkpoint may fail to apply them (or overwrite them) and then clear the flag, so the staged change is neither committed nor preserved.
- Root cause
- Two cooperating issues: (1) missing parentheses around bitmask comparisons causing ambiguous/misparsed flag tests, and (2) unconditional clearing/wholesale overwrite of the flag register (plus modifying flags mid-function), which wipes staged bits even when their corresponding changes were not applied.
- Impact
- Staged governance/operator updates to tokenomics parameters can be lost without notice. Concretely: scheduled changes (epoch length, veOLAS threshold, incentive fractions, staking params, maxBond, etc.) may never be committed even though they were staged — management actions can silently fail. This results in inconsistent epochs, unexpected reward allocations, denial of intended configuration changes, and could be used to race or disrupt planned parameter changes. In severe cases it can break accounting assumptions across epochs, leading to incorrect incentives, mis-set maxBond/effectiveBond calculations, or operator confusion and loss of control over planned updates.
- Inflation-year mismatch in updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions
- Targets
- updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions (Tokenomics)
- Description
- The function computes numYears from the epoch end time (epoch-specific year) but then calls getActualInflationForYear using currentYear instead of numYears. Because the code only requires numYears <= currentYear (not equality), currentYear can be strictly greater than numYears. getActualInflationForYear returns different inflation amounts for different years, so using currentYear can select the inflation rate of a later year than the epoch actually belongs to. This causes inflationPerSecond (and derived values like curMaxBond, maxBond, effectiveBond) to be computed from the wrong yearly schedule, producing over- or under-minting for the epoch and violating the intended inflation schedule.
- Root cause
- A logic mistake: the function uses the global currentYear when selecting the inflation schedule instead of the epoch-specific numYears computed from the epoch end time. The conditional checks allow currentYear > numYears, so the wrong year index can be passed to TokenomicsConstants.getActualInflationForYear.
- Impact
- Incorrect inflationPerSecond leading to over-minting or under-minting tokens for the epoch.
- Incorrect maxBond and effectiveBond calculations, altering bonding and staking capacities.
- Violation of the published inflation schedule and supply constraints (economic risk, token dilution, incentive distortion).
- Potential downstream unexpected behavior in any component that relies on precise inflation timing (auditing, supply cap calculations, governance expectations).
- getUnitPoint returns UnitPoint for inactive unitTypes (no semantic validation)
- Targets
- getUnitPoint (Tokenomics)
- Description
- The function getUnitPoint(epoch, unitType) returns mapEpochTokenomics[epoch].unitPoints[unitType] without verifying that the requested unitType is actually tracked/active for that epoch. TokenomicsPoint.unitPoints is declared as UnitPoint[2], so out-of-range unitType >= 2 is prevented by the fixed-size array, but unitType values 0..1 that are not active in the epoch still return the stored UnitPoint (often zero/default). Callers that treat a returned UnitPoint as indicating an actually-tracked service can be misled: they may perform calculations, distributions, or display logic with zero/default data that should instead be rejected or handled as “not tracked.”
- Root cause
- Missing semantic validation: the function relies only on the array index existing (UnitPoint[2]) and does not check per-epoch activation/state (e.g., unitPoints[unitType].numNewUnits > 0 or an explicit tracked-services flag). The contract enforces global bounds for unitType but does not enforce that the unitType was active in the specified epoch.
- Impact
- Incorrect or misleading results: callers may assume the returned UnitPoint is for an actively tracked service and use zero/default values in accounting, UI, or reward logic.
- Incorrect incentive/reward calculations: consumers that aggregate or divide by per-epoch counts may produce incorrect allocations, potentially skewing rewards or causing unexpected behavior (e.g., division by zero elsewhere if consumers don’t check).
- Logic errors or conditional flows may be bypassed or incorrectly triggered because the function returns a valid struct rather than signalling “not tracked.”
- Potential integrity issues in downstream computations (financial calculations, reporting, entitlement checks).
- getEpochEndTime returns actual finalization time, not the scheduled epoch end
- Targets
- getEpochEndTime (Tokenomics)
- Description
- getEpochEndTime(uint256 epoch) returns mapEpochTokenomics[epoch].epochPoint.endTime. That endTime is set when checkpoint() finalizes an epoch via tp.epochPoint.endTime = uint32(block.timestamp). checkpoint() only requires block.timestamp >= previous_end + epochLen (and <= MAX_EPOCH_LENGTH). If checkpoint() is executed after the scheduled end (previous_end + epochLen), tp.epochPoint.endTime records the actual checkpoint time (>= scheduled end) instead of the scheduled end. As a result, getEpochEndTime may return a later timestamp than the intended/scheduled epoch boundary.
- Root cause
- When finalizing an epoch, the code records block.timestamp (actual finalization time) into epochPoint.endTime instead of the scheduled end time (previous_end + epochLen). The invariant that epoch endTime equals the scheduled end is assumed but not enforced by the implementation.
- Impact
- Any caller or off-chain logic that expects epoch endTime to equal the scheduled end (previous_end + epochLen) may get an unexpectedly later timestamp. Consequences include: incorrect epoch-length assumptions, miscalculated inflation or reward distributions that rely on stored endTime, scheduling or accounting errors for time-gated actions, and logical inconsistencies across components that use getEpochEndTime. The bug is primarily correctness-related but may enable subtle mis-timings or economic discrepancies if systems rely on a deterministic scheduled end. In some designs, repeated delays in checkpoint could shift subsequent epoch boundaries and inflation calculations, amplifying the effect.
- Checkpoint accumulates old effectiveBond on top of newly computed maxBond
- Targets
- checkpoint (Tokenomics)
- Description
- During checkpoint the code recomputes maxBond for the upcoming epoch but then sets effectiveBond to (new maxBond + previous effectiveBond) instead of aligning effectiveBond to the new maxBond. Concretely, after computing curMaxBond for the next epoch the function executes`curMaxBond += effectiveBond; effectiveBond = uint96(curMaxBond);`. Because effectiveBond already contains the prior epoch’s balance (and may have been modified earlier in checkpoint), effectiveBond ends up equal to (newMaxBond + oldEffectiveBond). This violates the intended realignment of effectiveBond to the new cap and allows the depository to operate against an inflated effectiveBond balance that can exceed the intended maxBond cap. The correct behavior is to overwrite effectiveBond with the newly computed curMaxBond (i.e.`effectiveBond = uint96(curMaxBond);`) without adding the old effectiveBond.
- Root cause
- Logic bug in checkpoint: the final assignment accumulates the previously stored effectiveBond into the newly computed maxBond (curMaxBond += effectiveBond) before writing effectiveBond, instead of replacing it. This mistaken addition both ignores the earlier conditional adjustment semantics and produces an ever-increasing effectiveBond.
- Impact
- effectiveBond is intended to represent the current available bond balance/cap. Because checkpoint adds the previous effectiveBond to the newly computed maxBond, effectiveBond can grow unbounded across epochs. Consequences include:
- The depository can reserve or refund amounts against a larger-than-intended pool, bypassing the intended maxBond cap and draining inflation/top-up budgets or enabling excessive bond reservations.
- Incentive accounting and emitted EpochSettled values will reflect incorrect curMaxBond/effectiveBond, misleading off-chain accounting.

## [F-415] Incorrect post-year-ten loop bounds halt supply growth projection
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-415](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-415)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- _calculateSupplyCapAfterYear10 (TokenomicsConstants)
- Description
- The projection that extends supply caps beyond year ten fails because only`lastYear`is offset by nine while`firstYear`keeps the original year index. For typical post-year-ten calls (e.g.,`firstYear ≥ 10`), the loop condition`i < lastYear`immediately fails, the loop never executes, and the function always returns`SUPPLY_CAP_YEAR10`. Consequently, all dependent getters report a flat cap/inflation after year ten instead of the intended compounding growth.
- Root cause
- Mismatched year offset:`lastYear`is reduced by nine but`firstYear`is not, so the for-loop condition becomes false for normal inputs.
- Impact
- Projected supply caps and inflation amounts after year ten remain constant at the year-ten value. Any downstream logic relying on growth schedules is broken, potentially affecting mint limits, emissions, or economic assumptions.

## [F-416] NeighborhoodScanner issues (lower confidence)
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-416](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-416)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Neighborhood search can return liquidity above amount0-only cap
- Targets
- _neighborhoodSearch (NeighborhoodScanner)
- Description
- pickLoMaxUtil computes an amount0-derived liquidity cap using getLiquidityForAmount0(…) and passes a capped liqBest into _neighborhoodSearch. _neighborhoodSearch, however, recomputes liquidity for candidate (i,j) ranges via LiquidityAmounts.getLiquidityForAmounts(…) and assigns liqBest = liquidity when utilization improves — but it never re-applies the original amount0-derived cap. For some candidate ranges (notably with smaller upper tick j < hi) the amount0-only liquidity for that candidate range can be larger than the original amount0-only liquidity computed for the original upper tick. As a result, _neighborhoodSearch can return a liqBest larger than what the provided amount0 could support for the originally considered range.
- Root cause
- Missing enforcement of the original amount0-derived liquidity cap inside _neighborhoodSearch: candidate liquidity computed by getLiquidityForAmounts(…) is assigned directly to liqBest without min-ing with the initial liquidity parameter passed into the function.
- Impact
- The function can return an inflated liquidity value that exceeds the liquidity the provided amount0 can support for the original range. Callers or downstream logic that trust the returned liquidity may miscalculate token amounts, allocate or mint positions with insufficient amount0 backing, or otherwise suffer incorrect accounting. Depending on callers, this may lead to unexpected reverts, token loss, or incorrect position sizing.
- _raiseLow Can Return Tick With Zero Intermediate
- Targets
- _raiseLow (NeighborhoodScanner)
- Description
- The helper is meant to raise the lower tick bound until the pair (lo, hi) yields a non-zero intermediate value in`_hasNonZeroIntermediate`. However,`ans`is initialized to`loMax`before any feasibility check. If`_hasNonZeroIntermediate(loMax, hi)`is false—as can happen for near-minimum ticks where the product of sqrt ratios is still below`Q96`—the search loop immediately terminates and returns`loMax`even though it violates the non-zero requirement. Downstream routines that rely on`_raiseLow`to guarantee a non-zero intermediate will receive an invalid tick and can perform incorrect liquidity math or follow-on decisions.
- Root cause
- `ans`is preset to`loMax`instead of being updated only after finding a tick that passes`_hasNonZeroIntermediate`, so the function can return an unchecked default when no candidate succeeds.
- Impact
- Callers can be given a lower bound that still produces a zero intermediate. This breaks the intended invariant, leading to inaccurate analytical outputs and potentially causing subsequent liquidity calculations or position constructions to fail or rely on wrong parameters.

## [F-417] null
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-417](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-417)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- constructor (LiquidityManagerProxy)
- Description
- The constructor stores the provided liquidityManager address in storage and then performs a delegatecall to liquidityManager with liquidityManagerData, executing initialization logic in the proxy’s context with the deployer as msg.sender. Whether this is safe cannot be determined from the proxy alone: the delegatecalled initializer (in liquidityManager) may assume a different caller and storage layout. Potentially dangerous outcomes include the initializer assigning privileged roles to msg.sender (the deployer), corrupting proxy storage via layout collisions, or making external calls that grant allowances or transfer assets that the deployer can later exploit.
- Root cause
- Performing an unverified delegatecall from the constructor using the deployer as msg.sender without guaranteeing that the target initializer is safe for delegatecall (i.e., compatible storage layout and benign initialization behavior). The proxy lacks constraints or checks on the initialization bytecode and relies on external code assumptions.
- Impact
- If the initializer is malicious or incompatible: (1) the deployer could become a privileged account (owner/operator), enabling control over protocol functions; (2) proxy storage (including the stored PROXY_LIQUIDITY_MANAGER slot) could be overwritten, breaking invariants or enabling takeover; (3) the initializer could cause the proxy to approve/move tokens or interact with external contracts on the proxy’s behalf, allowing the deployer or others to withdraw or redirect assets. All of these can lead to loss of funds, denial of service, or complete protocol compromise.

## [F-418] LiquidityManagerCore issues (lower confidence)
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-418](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-418)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Incorrect decoding of Uniswap V3 slot0 observation index
- Targets
- _getPriceAndObservationIndexFromSlot0 (LiquidityManagerCore)
- Description
- The function attempts to extract the observation index from the Uniswap V3 pool’s slot0 return data but reads from the wrong offset. Instead of loading the third 32-byte word (offset 64) that contains observationIndex, it reads the fourth word (offset 96), corresponding to observationCardinality. This mis-decoded value is propagated to callers expecting a current observation index.
- Root cause
- Assembly decoding uses mload(add(returnData, 96)) instead of mload(add(returnData, 64)) when reading observationIndex from slot0 return data.
- Impact
- Callers receive observationCardinality in place of observationIndex, leading to incorrect assumptions about pool observation state. Any logic relying on an accurate observation index (e.g., detecting stale observations or ensuring TWAP consistency) may malfunction, weakening safety checks or allowing state-dependent operations to proceed under unsafe conditions.
- Utility fee handling skipped when utilizationRate equals MAX_BPS
- Targets
- collectFees (LiquidityManagerCore)
- Description
- `collectFees`always calls`_manageUtilityAmounts(tokens, MAX_BPS, true)`after fetching position fees. However, within`_manageUtilityAmounts`, the`amounts`array that determines how much OLAS is burned and how much of the counterpart token is forwarded to the treasury is only populated when`utilizationRate < MAX_BPS`. When the rate equals`MAX_BPS`(10,000), the branch that computes positive`amounts`is skipped, leaving both`olasAmount`and`tokenAmount`at zero. Consequently, no tokens are burned or transferred even though the contract just collected fees and holds non-zero balances. The fees remain trapped in the contract, defeating the purpose of fee collection and distribution.
- Root cause
- `_manageUtilityAmounts`initializes the`amounts`array to zero and only assigns non-zero values inside a conditional block guarded by`if (utilizationRate < MAX_BPS)`. Calling the function with`utilizationRate == MAX_BPS`skips this block, so the computed transfer and burn amounts remain zero.
- Impact
- All collected fees stay in the contract instead of being burned or sent to the treasury, resulting in fee accumulation and preventing the intended revenue distribution/burning logic from executing. Funds are effectively stuck unless another function is used to withdraw them, causing loss of expected protocol revenue and mis-accounting of utility token burns.
- convertToV3 proceeds with zero token amounts after utility burn/transfer
- Targets
- convertToV3 (LiquidityManagerCore)
- Description
- convertToV3 initially verifies that both token balances are non-zero, then (when olasBurnRate > 0) calls _manageUtilityAmounts(tokens, olasBurnRate, true) and replaces the local amounts array with the returned updatedBalances. _manageUtilityAmounts burns/transfers portions of the tokens according to utilizationRate and returns the remaining balances. When utilizationRate == MAX_BPS (or in other cases where the callee reduces balances to zero), updatedBalances will be zero for one or both tokens. convertToV3 performs no post-call check for zero balances and continues to approve and call _calculateTicksAndMintPosition or _increaseLiquidity using possibly zero amounts. As a result conversion can proceed with one or both token amounts equal to zero.
- Root cause
- convertToV3 assumes the initial pre-check (amounts != 0) guarantees non-zero balances for the remainder of the function. It fails to account for the fact that _manageUtilityAmounts can burn/transfer token amounts and return zero updated balances (in particular when olasBurnRate == MAX_BPS). There is no post-_manageUtilityAmounts validation to prevent zero-amount operations.
- Impact
- A caller can trigger cases where one or both token amounts become zero after utility management, leading to: unintended attempts to mint/increase a Uniswap V3 position with zero token amounts (which can revert or produce incorrect behavior); loss of tokens that were burnt or transferred to the treasury with no guard; wasted gas; and potential broken state transitions (e.g., mapping of pool->positionId set even when no liquidity was actually deposited). In short: funds can be moved to treasury/burn unexpectedly and position operations may fail or behave incorrectly.
- Post-liquidity call with MAX_BPS drains full contract balances to treasury
- Targets
- _manageUtilityAmounts (LiquidityManagerCore)
- Description
- When _manageUtilityAmounts is called with utilizationRate == MAX_BPS (the maximum basis points), it does not compute the intended fraction of token balances to transfer or burn. Because the function only reduces amounts when utilizationRate < MAX_BPS, the local amounts variables remain equal to the full contract token balances. The subsequent logic treats those amounts as the utility deductions (olasAmount and tokenAmount) and transfers/burns them — resulting in the entire remaining balances being sent to the treasury (or burned) instead of doing nothing or taking only the intended fraction.
- Root cause
- Incorrect conditional logic: the function only handles the case utilizationRate < MAX_BPS by scaling balances down. There is no branch for utilizationRate == MAX_BPS (intended to mean “no deduction”), so amounts remain the full balances and are used directly for transfers/burns. updatedBalances is only set inside the < MAX_BPS block and therefore unused/zero for the MAX_BPS case.
- Impact
- Immediate and deterministic draining of all remaining token balances from the contract to the treasury (or burning in the olas case) whenever _manageUtilityAmounts is invoked with utilizationRate == MAX_BPS. In the observed call path (increaseLiquidity calls _manageUtilityAmounts(tokens, MAX_BPS, false) after minting), remaining tokens are fully transferred to the treasury instead of being left in-contract. Consequences include loss of funds from the expected pool of tokens, mis‑accounting of utility-token deductions, broken post‑liquidity balances, and potential disruption of subsequent operations that expect tokens to remain in the contract.
- Constructor fails to persist oracleV2, balancerVault, and bridge2Burner addresses
- Targets
- constructor (LiquidityManagerCore)
- Description
- The constructor accepts _oracleV2, _balancerVault, and _bridge2Burner and checks they are non-zero, but the LiquidityManagerCore contract does not declare state variables named oracleV2, balancerVault, or bridge2Burner. As a result, the provided addresses are not stored in contract storage for future use. Subsequent functions that expect these addresses to be set will instead operate with unset (zero) addresses or otherwise fail, breaking functionality and potentially causing availability or safety issues.
- Root cause
- Missing state variable declarations for oracleV2, balancerVault, and bridge2Burner in LiquidityManagerCore. The constructor performs checks and assignments but there is no storage slot declared in this contract to hold those values.
- Impact
- Functions that rely on oracleV2, balancerVault, or bridge2Burner may: read address(0) and revert, skip expected external calls, or behave incorrectly. This can cause loss of functionality (e.g., inability to fetch TWAPs, interact with Balancer vaults, or route bridge funds), denial of expected services, and potentially stuck funds or unexpected fallback behavior. Depending on how callers handle zero addresses, this may also open availability or logical attack vectors if checks assume these addresses were correctly initialized.

## [F-419] DefaultTargetDispenserL2 issues (lower confidence)
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-419](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-419)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Unpause function fails to clear paused state
- Targets
- unpause (DefaultTargetDispenserL2)
- Description
- The`unpause`function is supposed to lift the contract pause, but it sets`paused`to`1`, the likely value used to denote the paused state. As a result, calling`unpause`does not change the contract to an active state and may leave it permanently paused.
- Root cause
- `unpause`assigns`paused = 1`instead of resetting it to`0`(or the value representing “unpaused”).
- Impact
- The owner cannot truly unpause the contract, preventing normal operation once the pause is activated. This results in a permanent denial of service after the first pause.
- Permanent reentrancy lock on revert causes DoS of maintenance processing
- Targets
- _processData (DefaultTargetDispenserL2)
- Description
- The function sets the internal reentrancy lock _locked = 2 at entry and only resets it to 1 at the very end. Inside the processing loop it makes external calls (IToken(olas).approve and IStaking(target).deposit) which can revert. If any such external call reverts, _processData reverts before clearing _locked, leaving _locked > 1 permanently. Subsequent calls to _processData (and any entrypoints that check the same lock) immediately revert with ReentrancyGuard(), causing a denial of service of the maintenance/processing functionality — even the contract owner cannot recover by calling processDataMaintenance.
- Root cause
- Holding a reentrancy lock across unrecoverable external calls without a safe rollback/cleanup path. External calls (which may revert) are performed while _locked = 2 and there is no try/catch or finally-like logic to ensure the lock is cleared on failure, so a revert leaves the lock set and blocks future calls.
- Impact
- High — An attacker or a misbehaving external contract (a staking target or token implementation) can trigger a revert during approve/deposit and permanently block processing. Effects include: processing/maintenance becoming unusable, queued or withheld accounting left inconsistent, inability for owner to call processDataMaintenance to recover, potential disruption of staking/distribution flows and economic effects on users relying on these operations.
- Under-accounted withheldAmount when _sendMessage returns leftovers
- Targets
- syncWithheldAmount (DefaultTargetDispenserL2)
- Description
- syncWithheldAmount reduces the contract’s withheldAmount by the full normalizedAmount before calling the bridge helper _sendMessage. _sendMessage can return leftovers (an ETH value) which the function refunds to msg.sender. When leftovers > 0 the actual amount forwarded across the bridge is normalizedAmount - leftovers, but withheldAmount has already been decreased by normalizedAmount, so the contract undercounts the remaining withheld funds by leftovers. With getBridgingDecimals() == 18 (normalizedAmount == amount) this reduces withheldAmount to 0 even though leftovers may exist; the function then refunds those leftovers to the caller and leaves the contract state inconsistent.
- Root cause
- State update (withheldAmount = amount - normalizedAmount) happens before the external/implementation-specific call _sendMessage returns and before observing leftovers. The code assumes the entire normalizedAmount will be consumed by the bridge, but the concrete implementation may return unused ETH (leftovers), so the preemptive subtraction incorrectly reduces withheldAmount by the full normalizedAmount rather than by the actual bridged amount.
- Impact
- Accounting discrepancy where withheldAmount becomes smaller than it should be by the leftovers amount. Consequences include misallocation or apparent loss of withheld funds, incorrect future behavior relying on withheldAmount (e.g., wrong available balance or enabling double-spend logic), and potential fund inconsistencies across bridge operations. If owner (the only caller) or someone who controls the owner key repeatedly triggers this, the contract may permanently lose track of some funds or incorrectly report zero withheld funds.
- unpause sets paused = 1 but emits TargetDispenserUnpaused() — state/event mismatch
- Targets
- unpause (DefaultTargetDispenserL2)
- Description
- The unpause() function enforces owner-only access, then sets the paused state variable to 1 and emits TargetDispenserUnpaused(). Because paused = 1 represents the contract being paused, the implementation leaves the contract paused while emitting an “unpaused” event. This produces a state/event mismatch and prevents the owner from actually unpausing the contract.
- Root cause
- A logic/assignment mistake: unpause assigns the value representing the paused state (1) instead of the unpaused value (0). There is also no guard that the state is changing (e.g., require(paused != 0)), so the event may be emitted even when no transition occurs.
- Impact
- Functional denial-of-service: the owner cannot transition the contract to the unpaused (operational) state, breaking any functionality gated by paused. Off-chain monitoring and indexers will be misled by the emitted “unpaused” event while the contract remains paused. This can disrupt normal operation, prevent withdrawals/processing, and harm user trust. The issue is not an immediate fund-theft vector, but it is a high-severity availability and integrity bug for contract operation.
- Unauthenticated redeem allows arbitrary OLAS transfers to staking targets
- Targets
- redeem (DefaultTargetDispenserL2)
- Description
- The external function redeem(target, amount, batchHash) can be called by any address (no msg.sender == owner check). If a matching tuple (target, amount, batchHash) has been queued (queuedHashes[queueHash] == true) and the contract holds >= amount OLAS, redeem approves the target and calls IStaking(target).deposit(amount), thereby moving OLAS out of the contract to the staking target. Because redeem lacks an owner-only check, non-owners can trigger these token transfers and clear queued entries, violating the property that value-extraction processes succeed only when invoked by the current owner.
- Root cause
- Missing access control on the redeem function. The function authorizes transfers only by the presence of a queuedHashes entry, but does not require that the caller is the current owner. queuedHashes is treated as sufficient authorization to move funds, but ownership checks are omitted.
- Impact
- An attacker (or any external caller) can execute redeem for any queued tuple and cause the contract to transfer OLAS to the specified staking target. This can result in: unauthorized loss or redirection of contract OLAS balance to attacker-controlled staking contracts, bypassing owner-only drains/migrations; clearing queued entries so intended owner workflows cannot later recover or re-route funds; disruption of withheldAmount/bridging flows if expected deposits are consumed. The exploit is straightforward whenever queued tuples exist and the contract balance covers the amount.

Full Finding Details:
- This V12 finding was marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- buyBack (BuyBackBurner)
- Description
- The buyBack function reads the contract’s balance of the provided secondToken and, if the caller-provided secondTokenAmount is 0 or greater than the contract balance, replaces secondTokenAmount with the contract’s balance (if (secondTokenAmount == 0 || secondTokenAmount > balance) secondTokenAmount = balance;). This causes the function to proceed with a smaller swap than the caller requested rather than aborting when the contract lacks the requested amount. The function only reverts when the resulting secondTokenAmount is 0. The swap logic is then executed via _buyOLAS/_performSwap using the adjusted amount.
- Root cause
- A deliberate assignment replaces caller-specified nonzero amounts larger than the contract’s token balance with the contract’s available balance instead of reverting. The function therefore silently truncates the requested amount instead of enforcing that the contract actually holds the requested amount.
- Impact
- Callers who expect the contract to swap the exact amount they requested can be surprised: their requested amount will be silently reduced to whatever the contract holds and the swap will still execute. Consequences include incorrect accounting, unexpected partial execution, unexpected slippage or price impact for callers, and logic errors in callers that assume the exact amount was used. If callers relied on the function aborting when the contract lacked funds, funds may be moved when they did not intend. (If balance == 0, the function still reverts.)

- Description
- The function approves olasAmount of the OLAS token to l2TokenRelayer via IToken(olas).approve(l2TokenRelayer, olasAmount) and then calls IBridge(l2TokenRelayer).relayTokens(…). It never resets or revokes the allowance after the relayer call. This relies on two dangerous assumptions: (1) the relayer will always transfer exactly olasAmount from this contract, and (2) the token behaves like a standard ERC‑20 that reduces allowance on transferFrom. If either assumption is false (fee‑on‑transfer tokens, a buggy or malicious relayer that transfers less, or a non‑standard token that does not decrease allowances), a residual allowance remains for l2TokenRelayer to pull additional tokens later. In short: successful execution can leave an unintended lingering approval to l2TokenRelayer.
- Root cause
- The code issues a single approve for the full balance and does not clear or check the remaining allowance after calling the external relayer. It assumes exact consumption and standard ERC‑20 approval semantics, creating a non‑atomic approval + external call pattern that can leave residual allowance.
- Impact
- An attacker controlling l2TokenRelayer (or a compromised/malicious relayer) can withdraw more tokens later than intended by calling transferFrom on the leftover allowance, potentially draining token balance from the contract. Even if l2TokenRelayer is honest, bugs, token fees, or non‑standard token implementations can produce a residual allowance that becomes exploitable. Loss of funds or unauthorized token transfers are the likely consequences.

## [F-423] Zero Value Guard Failure
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-423](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-423)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- migrate() requires pause and can permanently revoke ownership and lock guarded functions
- Targets
- migrate (DefaultTargetDispenserL2)
- Description
- The migrate(address) implementation contains multiple interacting logic errors that make migration only callable while the contract is paused, and — upon a successful call — permanently remove administrative control and leave the contract in a locked state. Concretely:
- The paused-state check is inverted: the contract represents unpaused as paused == 1 and paused == 2 means paused. migrate reverts when paused == 1, so it only executes when the contract is paused (paused == 2). This forces the owner to pause the contract before migrating.
- migrate sets the internal reentrancy guard _locked = 2 at function entry but never resets it to 1. Other guarded functions expect _locked to be restored to 1; leaving _locked at 2 causes many guarded functions to revert on subsequent calls.
- migrate unconditionally sets owner = address(0) before returning. Because changeOwner prohibits setting owner back to address(0), and owner-only functions check msg.sender == owner, the contract cannot be recovered on-chain after owner is cleared.
- Together these bugs make migrate effectively one‑shot and irreversible: a single successful migrate call can zero out ownership and leave the reentrancy lock set, permanently disabling owner-only maintenance and many guarded code paths.
- Root cause
- Three implementation mistakes that interact to create an irreversible state:
- Logical inversion of paused-state evaluation (migrate reverts when paused == unpaused value), allowing migrate only when the contract is paused.
- Incorrect reentrancy-guard handling: _locked set to a non-unlocked state on entry and not restored on all code paths.
- Unconditional clearing of owner to address(0) with no on-chain path to reassign ownership (changeOwner forbids address(0)).
- Impact
- High — permanent denial of administrative control and potential irrevocable contract malfunction.
- Owner must pause the contract to perform migrate (contrary to intended semantics).
- A successful migrate call can zero the owner and leave _locked > 1, making owner-only functions (changeOwner, drain, pause/unpause, maintenance, etc.) unusable and causing many guarded functions to revert due to the lock. This can brick recovery paths and maintenance tools.
- ETH reception or other flows that depend on owner or unlocked guard states may be blocked (e.g., receive() may revert), possibly causing funds to become stuck.
- Because migrate can succeed even with zero transferred amount, an accidental or malicious call could still produce the destructive state.
- Overall, this is an urgent, high-severity availability/administrative risk requiring immediate remediation.
- Targets
- reserveAmountForBondProgram (Tokenomics)
- changeTokenomicsParameters (Tokenomics)
- Description
- Two separate functions treat zero inputs or zero-like sentinel values inconsistently, producing misleading events and preventing legitimate zero-valued configuration changes:
- Tokenomics.reserveAmountForBondProgram accepts amount == 0 as a valid request. Because it only checks eBond >= amount, a zero request passes, performs no state change, returns success, and emits EffectiveBondUpdated(epochCounter, eBond). This creates spurious “successful” events and allows an authorized depository to spam successful-no-op calls.
- Tokenomics.changeTokenomicsParameters treats an input _veOLASThreshold == 0 as a sentinel meaning “do not change”. The function overwrites the local input with the current committed value when zero is passed and emits TokenomicsParametersUpdateRequested using that overwritten value. The checkpoint/commit path also ignores staged zero (nextVeOLASThreshold > 0 guard), making it impossible to stage and later commit an explicit zero threshold. As a result, callers cannot set the parameter to 0 and events misrepresent what was (not) staged.
- Root cause
- Inadequate and inconsistent handling of zero values:
- Missing positive-value guard in reserveAmountForBondProgram: the function only checks eBond >= amount and does not require amount > 0, so zero is treated as a valid change even though it is a no-op.
- Use of 0 as a sentinel combined with asymmetric guards in changeTokenomicsParameters and commit logic: inputs of 0 are interpreted as “no change” at staging time, and the commit path ignores staged zeros, while the emitted event uses the overwritten local value, making the event misleading.
- Impact
- Confusion, event/monitoring integrity issues, and an inability to set meaningful zero configurations:
- Off-chain consumers and automation that interpret Successful return values or EffectiveBondUpdated events as indicating a non-zero state change can be misled, causing analytics corruption, false-positive triggers, or incorrect downstream actions.
- An authorized depository can spam zero-amount calls that repeatedly emit successful events without changing state, producing event noise and potentially obscuring real events.
- Protocol operators cannot stage and commit an explicit veOLASThreshold of 0 via the documented staging/commit flow; attempts to pass 0 produce misleading events and leave the parameter unchanged. If zero is a meaningful value (e.g., to disable a behavior or lower a threshold to zero), this inability is a correctness/governance bug that may prevent intended configuration.
- Overall severity: moderate — affects correctness, observability, and governance/upgradeability workflows rather than direct theft of funds, but can disrupt automation and policy changes.
- Ambiguous zero/failure handling in slot0 price read causes immediate revert and TWAP fallback DoS
- Targets
- checkPoolAndGetCenterPrice (LiquidityManagerCore)
- Description
- checkPoolAndGetCenterPrice in LiquidityManagerCore treats a zero instantaneous pool price (sqrtPriceX96 == 0) as a fatal error and reverts immediately (ZeroValue()), but the helper that reads pool.slot0 (_getPriceAndObservationIndexFromSlot0) returns (0,0) both when the low-level staticcall to slot0 fails and when the pool legitimately reports a zero price. Because the function never attempts the TWAP fallback (getTwapFromOracle) when the instantaneous price is zero, any pool that causes the slot0 staticcall to revert/fail or legitimately reports sqrtPriceX96 == 0 will force checkPoolAndGetCenterPrice to always revert, preventing the TWAP recovery path and producing a denial-of-service for callers relying on this price retrieval.
- Root cause
- Ambiguous error semantics and improper handling of a zero return: the low-level slot0 reader conflates two distinct conditions (call failure vs legitimate zero price) by returning zeros for both, and the caller (checkPoolAndGetCenterPrice) treats a zero instantaneous price as an unrecoverable error instead of falling back to TWAP. There is no distinction or retry/fallback logic triggered when slot0 reading fails or yields zero, so the TWAP path is never reached in these cases.
- Impact
- High — denial-of-service of price reads and any dependent protocol flows. Concretely:
- Any pool that causes the slot0 staticcall to fail (maliciously or due to incompatibility) will cause checkPoolAndGetCenterPrice to revert with ZeroValue(), blocking callers from obtaining a price.
- Pools that legitimately report sqrtPriceX96 == 0 will also trigger the same immediate revert, disabling the TWAP fallback even though a fallback could provide a usable price.
- Callers and downstream logic that depend on this function for rebalances, swaps, or safety checks may revert, preventing normal protocol operations until the pool address is changed or the contract is patched.
- Because the issue is triggered by either a failing slot0 call or a zero price, an attacker controlling a pool or providing an incompatible pool implementation can create a targeted DoS against protocols relying on this function.
- Unchecked previous-epoch index and inconsistent year computation cause reverts in updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions
- Targets
- updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions (Tokenomics)
- Description
- The updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions function contains two interacting robustness bugs that cause owner-invoked updates to revert unexpectedly:
- Unchecked previous-epoch index underflow: the function unconditionally reads mapEpochTokenomics[curEpochCounter - 1].epochPoint.endTime. If curEpochCounter == 0 (e.g., before initializeTokenomics() has been called), the subtraction underflows and Solidity >=0.8 reverts, preventing the owner from calling this function.
- Fragile year-boundary comparison: the function computes numYears using a look-ahead expression (block.timestamp + epochLen - timeLaunch) / ONE_YEAR but computes lastEpochYear using the previous epoch’s stored endTime (mapEpochTokenomics[curEpochCounter - 1].epochPoint.endTime - timeLaunch) / ONE_YEAR. Because these use different reference points (current timestamp vs stored previous-epoch endTime), they can disagree around year boundaries. When numYears > lastEpochYear the function reverts; the mismatch can occur legitimately near year boundaries or be triggered by slight miner timestamp manipulation, causing otherwise-valid owner updates to fail.
- Root cause
- Missing guard when indexing the previous epoch: the code assumes curEpochCounter > 0 and performs curEpochCounter - 1 without checking, enabling an underflow/revert when curEpochCounter == 0. 2) Inconsistent time reference for year computation: numYears is computed from a look-ahead timestamp while lastEpochYear is derived from stored previous-epoch endTime, producing off-by-one/year-boundary mismatches that can trigger spurious reverts.
- Impact
- Moderate — availability and correctness issues for administrative flows:
- Calls by the owner to update inflation rates and fraction parameters can revert unexpectedly, blocking authorized governance or maintenance actions.
- If the function is called before initializeTokenomics (curEpochCounter == 0), it will always revert due to underflow, preventing legitimate parameter provisioning.
- Near year boundaries, valid updates may be rejected due to the inconsistent year computation; miners or slight timestamp differences can be exploited to force such reverts (timing-based DoS of admin updates).
- While this does not directly enable fund theft, it can impair protocol governance and timely parameter management, increasing operational risk during sensitive transitions.
