- Constructor and oracle read-paths lack pool/pair validation and safe checks — wrong indices, forged prices, and DoS
- Targets
- constructor (BalancerPriceOracle)
- constructor (UniswapPriceOracle)
- getPrice (BalancerPriceOracle)
- getPrice (used by updatePrice / validatePrice) (BalancerPriceOracle)
- Description
- Multiple price-oracle contracts (Uniswap- and Balancer-based) derive an immutable index/orientation (a “direction” or implicit token indices) from minimal checks in the constructor and then blindly trust external pool/vault calls at runtime. The constructors typically compare only token0 (or tokens[0]) against the supplied counterpart and never (a) verify that the supplied token actually belongs to the pair/pool, (b) search/record the correct token indices, or (c) enforce that the pool contains exactly two tokens. Runtime price readers (getPrice / validatePrice) then index balances/reserves/cumulatives using the stored direction and perform arithmetic without validating array lengths or non-zero divisors. Additionally, Balancer-based code calls a caller-supplied vault address from state-changing functions without authenticating it or protecting against reentrancy. Together these flaws let misconfiguration or a maliciously chosen pair/pool/vault produce incorrect/inverted prices, forge TWAPs, trigger division-by-zero or out-of-bounds reverts, and in some cases permit reentrancy during price computation.
- Root cause
- Several related issues combine: (1) weak constructor validation — direction is inferred from a single token comparison (token0 != _secondToken or tokens[0] check) without confirming membership, token ordering, or pool size; (2) failure to record explicit token indices or validate tokens.length leads to incorrect indexing assumptions; (3) runtime code trusts externally-supplied Balancer vault/pair addresses and their returned arrays without validating lengths, non-zero balances, or that the callee is the canonical contract; (4) mixing view-style external calls into state-changing flows leaves open reentrancy and forgery of returned data; and (5) some TWAP logic selects cumulative prices inconsistent with the reserve orientation, amplifying inversion errors.
- Impact
- High — realistic and exploitable consequences include: (1) incorrect spot prices (inverted or referencing the wrong token) and corrupted TWAP snapshots, causing downstream systems (liquidations, swaps, strategies) to act on wrong price data and incur financial loss; (2) an attacker or misconfigured deployer can supply a pair/pool/vault that returns crafted balances to arbitrarily set oracle prices or to bypass slippage checks; (3) availability failures — out-of-bounds accesses or divide-by-zero in getPrice can revert and prevent price updates (DoS); (4) reentrancy via untrusted Balancer Vault calls can allow state mutation mid-validation to persist manipulated prices; and (5) because direction is immutable once set in the constructor, errors persist for the oracle’s lifetime, enabling sustained manipulation.
- Unchecked delegatecall initialization & missing implementation validation — proxy takeover, bricking, and immediate compromise
- Targets
- constructor (LiquidityManagerProxy)
- constructor (BuyBackBurnerProxy)
- Description
- Multiple proxy constructors write a caller-supplied implementation/manager address into a persistent storage slot and then immediately perform a delegatecall into the supplied implementation using provided init calldata, while: (a) not checking that the implementation address contains code, (b) trusting the boolean success of delegatecall as sufficient evidence of correct initialization, (c) not protecting or re-verifying the implementation/manager slot after the delegatecall, and (d) omitting a proxy-side irrevocable initialized guard. Because delegatecall runs the callee’s code in the proxy’s storage and execution context, an attacker-supplied implementation or crafted init calldata can (1) cause arbitrary SSTOREs in proxy storage (including clearing or replacing the implementation slot), (2) perform destructive actions such as SELFDESTRUCT or force/forward ETH transfers, (3) re-run or re-trigger initialization via the fallback, or (4) be entirely absent (EOA/no-code) while returning success—leaving the proxy inert.
- Root cause
- Unsafe initialization pattern: constructors set the implementation/manager slot before invoking an untrusted delegatecall, treat delegatecall boolean success as proof of initialization without verifying code presence or post-call invariants, and expose a fallback that forwards calls to the stored address with no proxy-side one-time init guard. This combination allows the initializer to run with full proxy privileges and mutate or destroy proxy state.
- Impact
- Critical / High — an attacker (or mistaken deployer) who controls the implementation address or init calldata at deployment can fully compromise the proxy or render it permanently non-functional. Realistic impacts include: (1) immediate takeover — the initializer overwrites the implementation pointer to an attacker-controlled address, giving full control of future delegations and enabling theft or arbitrary execution in the proxy context; (2) permanent bricking — pointing the implementation slot at an EOA or zero-code address (or clearing it) makes all proxy delegatecalls no-ops or revert, breaking functionality and potentially locking assets; (3) theft during initialization — arbitrary storage/transfer calls executed under delegatecall can set approvals or move funds; (4) destruction/loss of service — initializer can SELFDESTRUCT the proxy or manipulate its balance (force-send then drain); (5) re-initialization risk — absence of a proxy-side one-time initialization guard lets external callers re-run initializers and mutate storage post-deployment if the implementation does not defend itself. These outcomes are persistent and difficult or impossible to remediate on-chain.
- Weak constructor validation of external parameters and dependencies — permanent misconfiguration, forged inputs, and theft/DoS
- Targets
- constructor (UniswapPriceOracle)
- constructor (Bridge2Burner (used by Bridge2BurnerOptimism))
- constructor (BuyBackBurner)
- constructor (BuyBackBurnerBalancer)
- Description
- Multiple contracts accept critical, external addresses and numeric parameters in their constructors (or initializers) but perform only minimal checks (typically non-zero checks or direct assignment). They then blindly trust those values at runtime when calling external contracts, indexing oracle outputs, or enforcing safety checks. The combination of (a) unvalidated addresses (no code/interface checks), (b) unbounded numeric parameters (e.g., maxSlippage), and (c) delegation of pool/oracle validation to external components enables a deployer or an attacker controlling constructor inputs or owner-configured oracles to permanently misconfigure the system, fabricate or bypass safety checks, redirect funds, or cause availability failures.
- Root cause
- Unsafe trust model and weak constructor validation. Contracts accept externally-supplied addresses and numeric limits at construction but fail to: (1) verify that addresses contain code or implement expected interfaces (e.g., ERC20, relayer, router, or oracle selectors); (2) bounds-check and normalize numeric parameters such as maxSlippage; (3) validate that oracle-returned pool identifiers actually correspond to expected token pairs and token orderings; or (4) provide runtime or owner-side safeguards (whitelists, registries, or mutable corrective setters) to recover from misconfiguration. Because many of these values are stored as immutables or relied upon implicitly, incorrect or malicious constructor inputs are permanent and trusted throughout contract logic.
- Impact
- High — realistic and demonstrable impacts include: - Permanent disabling or weakening of safety checks: an attacker or mistaken deployer can set maxSlippage (or equivalent numeric limits) to values or units that effectively bypass slippage/TWAP validation, allowing manipulated trade prices to be accepted. - Direct theft or redirection: constructor-supplied addresses (bridge, treasury, buyback sink, swapRouter, liquidityManager) can be set to attacker-controlled contracts or EOAs to immediately receive protocol funds or to route swaps through malicious pairs. - Fabricated/misleading oracle data: misconfigured or malicious oracles or pool identifiers can cause price reads to reference the wrong token pair, return forged balances/liquidity, or invert price orientation—leading to incorrect swaps, bad accounting, liquidations, or strategic front-running. - Availability and integrity failures: using EOAs or contracts missing expected selectors for token/relayer addresses will cause external calls to revert or return malformed data, breaking flows and potentially locking functionality. - Irreversibility: where values are stored as immutables or no corrective setters/whitelists exist, these issues persist for the contract lifetime and are difficult to remediate on-chain.
- Empty Tokenomics constructor; tokenomics parameters are compile-time fixed in TokenomicsConstants
- Targets
- constructor (Tokenomics)
- Description
- The Tokenomics constructor is empty (constructor() TokenomicsConstants {}) and does not initialize any tokenomics parameters. All tokenomics values (supply caps and inflation amounts for years 0..9, SUPPLY_CAP_YEAR10, MAX_MINT_CAP_FRACTION, etc.) are defined as compile-time constants or hard-coded literal arrays in TokenomicsConstants and consumed by pure functions. As a result, tokenomics are immutable at deployment/runtime and cannot be configured via constructor arguments, setters, or initializers. Rating: clear exploitability = 1 (low); clear flaw = 3 (high).
- Root cause
- Design/implementation choice: tokenomics were expressed as compile-time constants and fixed literal arrays inside TokenomicsConstants, while Tokenomics’s constructor was left empty. Tokenomics-calculation functions are pure and derive values only from these constants, so no runtime path exists to set or override them.
- Impact
- Not a direct funds-theft vulnerability, but a serious correctness/assurance issue: deployers and users cannot supply custom tokenomics at deployment or update them later. Consequences include misconfiguration risk (inability to match advertised or intended tokenomics), governance/upgrade mismatch, reputational and potential legal/regulatory risk if configurability was promised. It may also break expected upgrade/initialization flows for proxy deployments.

## [F-428] Iteration Bounds DoS
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-428](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-428)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Unbounded iteration in supply-cap calculation -> DoS (gas exhaustion) and eventual arithmetic overflow
- Targets
- getSupplyCapForYear (TokenomicsConstants)
- getActualSupplyCapForYear (TokenomicsConstants)
- _calculateSupplyCapAfterYear10 (TokenomicsConstants)
- Description
- The tokenomics constants module exposes public functions (getSupplyCapForYear, getActualSupplyCapForYear) that delegate to an internal helper _calculateSupplyCapAfterYear10 when numYears >= 10. That helper subtracts 9 from the provided lastYear and then executes a for-loop whose iteration count is linear in (numYears - 9). The external parameter numYears is unchecked and effectively unbounded, so an attacker can supply very large values to: (1) force the loop to execute arbitrarily many iterations and exhaust gas (causing out-of-gas reverts and making on-chain callers fail), and (2) cause repeated multiplicative growth of the supplyCap until uint256 overflow occurs (on Solidity >=0.8 this triggers a checked-arithmetic revert; on older compilers it silently wraps and produces incorrect results).
- Root cause
- Missing input validation and unsafe algorithmic complexity: a user-controlled uint256 (numYears) is used directly to compute the loop bound for an O(n) iterative growth algorithm. There are no upper bounds, clamps, or logarithmic/bounded alternatives; the loop both consumes unbounded gas and performs repeated multiplicative arithmetic with no overflow guards or early termination.
- Impact
- Availability / DoS: On-chain callers (other contracts or transactions) that invoke getSupplyCapForYear or getActualSupplyCapForYear with untrusted inputs can be forced to consume excessive gas or hit out-of-gas and revert by providing large numYears. This enables griefing/denial-of-service of flows that rely on these functions (e.g., minting logic, accounting checks, integrator contracts).
- Integrity / Revert: Repeated multiplicative increases eventually exceed uint256. On Solidity >=0.8.0 this causes a checked-arithmetic revert once values grow large enough (estimated threshold ~5,844 iterations given the constants), producing another DoS vector where legitimate calls fail due to overflow. On older compilers the value would wrap silently, producing incorrect supply cap values and breaking protocol invariants.
- Reliability: Even if gas costs make extreme inputs impractical in direct calls, the unbounded arithmetic and iteration expose a logic vulnerability whereby other parts of the system (internal callers, tooling, or off-chain scripts that might pass large values) can trigger failures or incorrect behavior. There is no direct fund theft in the shown code paths, but availability and correctness of supply-cap computations are compromised.
- Missing input validation and bounds checks in NeighborhoodScanner → unexpected panics and reverts (DoS)
- Targets
- _neighborhoodSearch (NeighborhoodScanner)
- pickLoMaxUtil (NeighborhoodScanner)
- optimizeLiquidityAmounts (NeighborhoodScanner)
- Description
- Several public/internal functions in NeighborhoodScanner assume callers supply well-formed arrays and tick values and do not validate those inputs before indexing or passing them to external libraries. These unchecked assumptions lead to two classes of failures: (1) out-of-bounds (OOB) array access when callers provide arrays with length < 2 (causing Solidity PANIC index-out-of-range), and (2) unchecked tick arithmetic that can pass ticks outside TickMath’s supported domain into TickMath.getSqrtRatioAtTick, which reverts. Both cause unexpected, low-level reverts that break caller flows and can be triggered by external actors.
- Root cause
- Missing input validation and improper bounds handling: functions index calldata arrays (ticks, initialAmounts, amounts) at positions 0 and 1 without checking lengths, and the neighborhood search computes a starting tick by subtracting a multiple of tickSpacing from a caller-supplied hi candidate without clamping to TickMath.MIN_TICK. The loop only guards against j >= MAX_TICK and not j < MIN_TICK, so it may call TickMath.getSqrtRatioAtTick with out-of-range ticks.
- Impact
- Availability / Denial-of-Service: External or internal callers can cause the affected public/internal entrypoints to revert unexpectedly by supplying malformed inputs (arrays with fewer than two elements or hi/lo tick candidates near the minimum tick). Expected behaviors are: - Calls to pickLoMaxUtil, optimizeLiquidityAmounts, and related helpers will panic with index-out-of-bounds (Solidity PANIC 0x32) when arrays have length < 2. - _neighborhoodSearch can revert due to TickMath.getSqrtRatioAtTick being called with ticks < MIN_TICK, producing a revert (T()). These failures are low-level and undocumented, making debugging and error handling harder for integrators. There is no direct theft of funds in the shown code paths, but the reverts can break higher-level workflows, disrupt tooling, and allow griefing by malicious actors.

## [F-429] Admin-Only/Privileged Access (Tokenomics)
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-429](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-429)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Targets
- checkpoint (Tokenomics)
- checkpoint ; trackServiceDonations (Tokenomics)
- updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions (reentered via checkpoint) (Tokenomics)
- refundFromBondProgram (Tokenomics)
- Description
- The checkpoint() flow performs many epoch-scoped state writes (staking incentives, effectiveBond/maxBond, next‑epoch parameters, donation snapshots, epoch endTime, IDF, etc.) and only then calls an external, owner-configurable treasury via ITreasury(treasury).rebalanceTreasury(…). epochCounter (the authoritative marker that the epoch is complete) is incremented only after that external call returns. There is no effective reentrancy protection around checkpoint(), and several other privileged entry points (trackServiceDonations, refundFromBondProgram, dispenser.retain/refundFromStaking, updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions) can be invoked by manager contracts that the owner controls. Because these manager addresses (treasury, depository, dispenser) are configurable, a malicious or compromised manager can re-enter Tokenomics during checkpoint and: re-run checkpoint logic on partially-updated storage, mutate totalDonationsETH after settlement snapshot, call refundFromBondProgram to change effectiveBond mid-checkpoint, or trigger updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions to overwrite stakingIncentive using stale epoch indices. The net result is duplicated or corrupted epoch settlements, lost or zeroed incentives, inflated effectiveBond (bypassing intended maxBond), inconsistent event history, and permanent distortion of tokenomics state.
- Root cause
- Violation of checks-effects-interactions and missing/misapplied reentrancy protection combined with owner-configurable privileged manager addresses. checkpoint() commits epoch effects before interacting with an external, configurable treasury and only marks completion (epochCounter increment) after the call. Other manager-callable functions mutate epoch-sensitive globals (totalDonationsETH, effectiveBond, stakingIncentive) and are callable by the same externally-controlled managers during the treasury call. Some updater functions also cache epochCounter or use low-level calls that allow reentry to stomp finalized state. Together these design choices permit reentrancy attacks and TOCTOU races that corrupt epoch accounting.
- Impact
- High — an attacker who controls (or the owner points at) a malicious treasury/depository/dispenser can:
- Re-enter checkpoint() to process the same epoch multiple times or interleave partial updates, leading to duplicated inflation/top-ups and staking incentives (arbitrary inflation increase).
- Mutate totalDonationsETH after checkpoint has computed incentives from the snapshot, causing donations to be excluded from settlement and producing inconsistent historical records.
- Call refundFromBondProgram during checkpoint to change effectiveBond mid-settlement, corrupting maxBond/effectiveBond calculations and emitted events.
- Cause updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions (or dispenser.retain) to overwrite or zero stakingIncentive for an epoch by exploiting cached epoch indices, permanently erasing incentives.
- Inflate effectiveBond across epochs (via owner pre-sets plus checkpoint accumulation) to bypass intended maxBond caps and enable over-reservation by the depository.
- These attacks can lead to overpayment of rewards, permanent distortion of tokenomics, loss of funds, denial-of-service of epoch progression, and broken economic invariants. Exploitation requires manager control (owner misconfiguration or compromise) or a compromised manager implementation.
- Owner/Manager Trust and External Call Failures Allow Incentive Inflation, Wipe, Spoofing, and DoS
- Targets
- changeManagers (Tokenomics)
- updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions (Tokenomics)
- refundFromStaking (Tokenomics)
- checkpoint / refundFromStaking (Tokenomics)
- trackServiceDonations (Tokenomics)
- Description
- Tokenomics relies heavily on owner-configurable manager contracts (treasury, depository, dispenser) and owner-set auxiliary pointers (donatorBlacklist). Several code paths (refundFromStaking, dispenser.retain calls, trackServiceDonations, updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions) trust these external managers to behave correctly but do not make external actions atomic, do not bound or validate inputs, and often perform destructive state writes regardless of external call success. Combined with the inability to revoke a manager slot (changeManagers disallows address(0)), this creates multiple practical attack/abuse scenarios: a compromised or malicious manager can (1) inflate on‑chain incentive accounting without transferring tokens, (2) force owner-level DoS or cause owner actions to silently erase incentives, (3) spoof donor identities to bypass blacklists or misattribute donations, and (4) exploit gas-exhausting loops to prevent owner remediation.
- Root cause
- Excessive implicit trust in owner-configurable manager contracts and unchecked external calls. Key issues include: manager addresses are permanent (cannot be cleared to address(0)), update flows call external managers via low-level or high-level calls without atomic transfer checks or success-handling, owner-only functions unconditionally clear or overwrite epoch-scoped incentive state, and the per-epoch incentive accumulator lacks an enforced cap. These combine to allow misbehaving external managers or malicious owner actions to desynchronize on-chain accounting from real token movements and to sabotage availability.
- Impact
- High — financial integrity and availability are at risk. Practical consequences include:
- Arbitrary inflation of stakingIncentive: a malicious dispenser can call refundFromStaking to increase the epoch’s reported staking incentives without ever transferring tokens, causing later settlement/third-party distributors to attempt to pay non-existent funds or misallocate treasury resources.
- Permanent or transient loss of incentive accounting: failed retain() calls (or deliberate owner calls) can clear stored stakingIncentive (via updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions or the unconditional zeroing after retain loops) even when the dispenser never executed refunds, making incentives unclaimable.
- Denial-of-service and admin-blocking: dispenser.retain can be implemented to consume gas across many iterations or to revert, preventing owner functions from completing and blocking maintenance or refunds. Because managers cannot be revoked (changeManagers forbids address(0)), a compromised manager cannot be promptly disabled on-chain.
- Donor spoofing and blacklist bypass: treasury-supplied donator parameters and owner-controlled donatorBlacklist being settable to address(0) allow a malicious treasury to attribute donations to arbitrary addresses or bypass blacklist enforcement, undermining policy controls.
- Economic distortion: without an enforced maxStakingIncentive, incentives can grow beyond configured caps, risking exhaustion of treasury budgets or unexpected large payouts. Overall result: theft, incorrect payouts, denial-of-service of settlement flows, and long-term corruption of tokenomics state. Exploitation requires control of (or malicious configuration by) manager/owner addresses or a compromised manager implementation.
- Targets
- migrate (DefaultTargetDispenserL2)
- Description
- The migrate(address) function in DefaultTargetDispenserL2 sets the contract’s manual reentrancy sentinel (_locked = 2) on entry but fails to restore it to the unlocked value (_locked = 1) on the normal exit path. Additionally, migrate sets owner = address(0) before returning. Other critical functions (drain, redeem, syncWithheldAmount, _processData, and others) check the sentinel (if (_locked > 1) revert) and therefore will immediately revert while _locked == 2. Because ownership is renounced by migrate, there is no in-contract, owner-gated recovery path to reset the sentinel. A single successful migrate call therefore permanently prevents guarded functions from being executed and effectively bricks the contract while it may still hold funds.
- Root cause
- An ad-hoc uint8-based reentrancy guard pattern is implemented manually. migrate() acquires the guard by writing _locked = 2 but omits the corresponding release write (_locked = 1) on the successful/non-reverting exit path. The function then renounces ownership (owner = address(0)), removing any owner-only remediation path. The combination of acquiring a persistent lock and zeroing owner makes on-chain recovery impossible.
- Impact
- High — permanent, practical denial-of-service of core contract functionality. After migrate() succeeds:
- All functions protected by the manual reentrancy check will immediately revert, preventing normal operations (drain, redeem, syncWithheldAmount, message processing, maintenance, etc.).
- Because owner is set to address(0), no owner-only function can be used to reset the guard or otherwise remediate the state, so the DoS is effectively irreversible on-chain.
- Targets
- _optimizeTicksAndMintPosition (root cause in changeMaxSlippage) (LiquidityManagerCore)
- changeMaxSlippage (LiquidityManagerCore)
- Description
- The owner-only setter changeMaxSlippage(uint16) validates only that the new value is non-zero and does not enforce an upper bound (<= MAX_BPS). Several internal flows compute minima using expressions of the form (MAX_BPS - maxSlippage) (with MAX_BPS = 10_000). If maxSlippage is set greater than MAX_BPS, the subtraction underflows and — under Solidity 0.8+ — triggers a runtime revert whenever those sites execute. This breaks critical liquidity-management functions (minting/increasing/decreasing positions and related helpers that call _optimizeTicksAndMintPosition) and results in a privileged denial-of-service.
- Root cause
- Missing validation in changeMaxSlippage: the function only checks newMaxSlippage != 0 and does not require newMaxSlippage <= MAX_BPS, allowing the owner (or a compromised owner key) to assign an out-of-domain value that causes downstream arithmetic (MAX_BPS - maxSlippage) to underflow and revert.
- Impact
- High — an owner or attacker with owner privileges can set maxSlippage > 10_000 and cause all operations that compute amount * (MAX_BPS - maxSlippage) / MAX_BPS to revert. Affected operations include minting, increasing, and decreasing Uniswap V3 positions and any flows that depend on _optimizeTicksAndMintPosition or the same slippage math. This produces a practical denial-of-service of core liquidity-management functionality (prevents adding/removing positions and related protocol activity) until maxSlippage is corrected; if the owner key is compromised or lost, recovery may be impossible.
- Unchecked push-refund to msg.sender in syncWithheldAmount — ignored failure, misleading events, and unrecoverable leftover ETH
- Targets
- syncWithheldAmount (DefaultTargetDispenserL2)
- Description
- DefaultTargetDispenserL2.syncWithheldAmount attempts to refund leftover ETH to the caller (msg.sender) using a low-level call msg.sender.call{value: leftovers}(““) but ignores the boolean success return. The function proceeds to emit LeftoversRefunded, advance stakingBatchNonce and post messages even when the transfer fails. The contract’s owner-only recovery (drain) also forwards ETH using call and reverts on failure, so there is no on-chain recovery path when the owner address is a contract that cannot accept plain ETH transfers (reverting fallback/receive or gas-restricted acceptor). As a result, leftover ETH from _sendMessage can become permanently stranded in the dispenser and on-chain events/state will incorrectly indicate that refunds occurred.
- Root cause
- syncWithheldAmount uses a push-based refund (msg.sender.call{value: leftovers}()) but ignores the returned (bool success) and does not record or handle failures. The contract emits events and advances state regardless of transfer success. Additionally, the only owner-recovery path (drain) requires a successful ETH transfer to the owner and will revert if the owner address cannot accept ETH, leaving no pull-based or retriable reclaim mechanism.
- Impact
- High — leftover ETH returned from bridging/distribution operations can become irrecoverably locked in the contract when the caller/owner is a contract that rejects ETH transfers. Consequences:
- Permanent loss or inaccessibility of protocol funds (leftovers) held by the dispenser.
- Mismatched on-chain observability: events (LeftoversRefunded) and advanced nonces/messages will indicate refunds that did not actually occur, hindering monitoring and reconciliation.
- Targets
- trackServiceDonations (Tokenomics)
- changeDonatorBlacklist (Tokenomics)
- changeDonatorBlacklist / trackServiceDonations (Tokenomics)
- Description
- Tokenomics exposes an owner-settable donatorBlacklist pointer that trackServiceDonations calls directly via the typed interface IDonatorBlacklist.isDonatorBlacklisted. The setter changeDonatorBlacklist performs no validation (accepts EOAs or arbitrary contracts, and can be invoked after initialization). trackServiceDonations assumes the callee behaves correctly and makes a high-level external call without try/catch, code-size checks, or ABI validation. These choices let the owner (or a compromised owner) or a malicious blacklist contract silently bypass blacklist checks, block all donation processing by reverting or returning malformed data, or arbitrarily mark donors as blacklisted. Because changeDonatorBlacklist can be called repeatedly after initialization, the owner may also opportunistically change the blacklist before donations are tracked.
- Root cause
- Unchecked owner-controlled external pointer and unsafely-invoked interface: changeDonatorBlacklist stores any address without validation or immutability guards, and trackServiceDonations performs a typed external call IDonatorBlacklist(bList).isDonatorBlacklisted(donator) guarded only by bList != address(0). There is no check that bList is a contract, implements the expected selector, or that the call succeeds; there is no try/catch or use of low-level call patterns to handle failures, nor is the pointer write restricted after initialization.
- Impact
- High — multiple practical, high-impact abuse modes exist:
- Denial-of-Service (DoS): Pointing donatorBlacklist at an EOA, a non-conforming contract, or a contract that reverts will cause trackServiceDonations to revert (ABI decode / revert), blocking all donation tracking and any flows that depend on it. This can be triggered accidentally by misconfiguration or deliberately by a malicious owner or compromised owner key.
- Silent bypass or spoofing: Setting donatorBlacklist = address(0) or pointing it to a contract that always returns false disables blacklist enforcement, allowing blacklisted addresses to donate. Conversely, pointing it to a contract that always returns true can censor legitimate donors.
- Malicious misattribution or behavioral manipulation: A malicious blacklist implementation can return values or behave in ways that manipulate donor eligibility or on-chain accounting, undermining policy controls.
- Targets
- updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions (Tokenomics)
- checkpoint (Tokenomics)
- Description
- Multiple Tokenomics flows place critical epoch- and year-scoped economic state (inflationPerSecond, maxBond, effectiveBond, staged next-epoch parameters and the tokenomicsParametersUpdated flag) under inconsistent authority, ordering, and validation. As implemented: (1) the owner can call updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions at arbitrary times to recompute and unconditionally overwrite inflationPerSecond, maxBond, and effectiveBond — including mid-epoch or during year-0 — producing values that differ from checkpoint() semantics (including setting first-year inflation to zero); (2) the function validates/uses a different year source and can revert if a projected epoch year exceeds the last checkpointed year, blocking owner updates until checkpoint() runs; (3) checkpoint() itself is public and mutates a bit (tokenomicsParametersUpdated |= 0x04) used by owner staging logic, letting non-owners influence/clear owner-intended pending-parameter state; and (4) staged parameters (e.g., nextEpochLen) are applied after checkpoint eligibility checks, meaning a freshly-staged epoch length does not prevent or change whether checkpoint() can settle the current epoch. Together these issues break lifecycle invariants and permit both owner-driven and non-owner timing attacks that corrupt inflation schedules, bond caps, and epoch commit behavior.
- Root cause
- A mix of privileged, unconditional state writes, inconsistent time/year bookkeeping, and ordering/authorization errors: updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions unconditionally writes per-second inflation and derived bond caps using getActualInflationForYear(currentYear) / ONE_YEAR rather than following checkpoint()’s lifecycle and sources (including special handling for year-0). currentYear is only advanced by checkpoint(), so the updater may use stale year state or be rejected when projecting an epoch into the next year. checkpoint() is publicly callable and reuses tokenomicsParametersUpdated for an internal year-rollover bit, enabling non-owners to set/clear an owner-intended flag. Finally, staged parameters (nextEpochLen and other next-epoch slots) are written into next-epoch storage but applied after early eligibility checks, producing TOCTOU-like ordering mismatches between staging, eligibility, and commit.
- Impact
- High — these combined problems allow several concrete, materially damaging behaviors:
- Owner can unintentionally or maliciously zero first-year inflation (setting inflationPerSecond = 0) by calling updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions during launch (year 0), depriving all downstream recipients of planned emissions for the remainder of the launch year.
- Owner can change inflationPerSecond and derived bond caps mid-year or mid-epoch, altering maxBond/effectiveBond unexpectedly and enabling or blocking bond reservations, incentive payouts, or other tokenomic flows that assume stability between checkpoints.
- Owner updates may be rejected (revert) during legitimate year transitions if checkpoint() has not advanced currentYear, blocking urgent parameter adjustments until anyone calls checkpoint(). This is an availability/operational hazard.
- Public callers can influence/clear tokenomicsParametersUpdated via checkpoint()’s year-rollover bit, enabling non-owners to interfere with owner staging (prematurely clear pending updates or cause unintended commits).
- Targets
- processDataMaintenance (DefaultTargetDispenserL2)
- syncWithheldAmount (DefaultTargetDispenserL2)
- Description
- DefaultTargetDispenserL2 contains multiple interacting flaws in its cross-chain message handling and batching logic that can lead to permanent DoS of message processing, duplicated or ambiguous outbound messages, and loss of cryptographic provenance for messages sent to the bridge. The issues stem from incorrect ordering of state updates relative to virtual/external calls, unconditional consumption of single-use deduplication tokens during dry-runs, and delegation of final bridge-payload construction to unverified overrides without enforcing inclusion of computed origin fields (batchHash / chain id / contract address). Together these enable (1) one-shot dedupe tokens to be consumed by maintenance/dry-run calls, blocking later legitimate processing; (2) TOCTOU races where two transactions send the same batch/nonce while the global nonce only advances once (lost increment / duplicate messages); and (3) bridge payloads that omit or replace origin-identifying data if an override/misconfiguration is malicious or buggy, making target-chain consumers unable to cryptographically tie messages to this contract and chain.
- Root cause
- A combination of checks-effects-interactions ordering errors, unsafe reuse of finalization helpers for non-finalizing maintenance, and delegation of critical message construction to virtual/overrideable code without validation. Concretely: _processData unconditionally marks batches consumed (processedHashes[batchHash] = true) even when called as a dry-run; syncWithheldAmount reserves/uses stakingBatchNonce only after calling an overridable/internal _sendMessage (so two concurrent transactions can observe the same nonce and send duplicate messages while only one increment is persisted); and the contract computes a canonical batchHash but delegates message construction to _sendMessage without enforcing that the produced bridgePayload includes the computed origin fields.
- Impact
- High — these faults can cause irreversible loss of correctness and availability for cross-chain message flows:
- Permanent DoS for a batch: an owner maintenance dry-run can permanently flip the processed flag for a batch without applying state (updateWithheldAmount == false), causing the legitimate L1-sourced message to revert as AlreadyDelivered and the batch to never be processed. This can lock funds or prevent reconciliation.
- Duplicate/ambiguous outbound messages: a TOCTOU race permits multiple transactions to send identical batchHash/nonce payloads while the global nonce advances only once, producing duplicate messages on the bridge, receiver-side ambiguity, or lost/inconsistent accounting.
- Storage-collision risk in changeManagers when Tokenomics is used via delegatecall (proxy storage corruption)
- Targets
- changeManagers (Tokenomics)
- Description
- changeManagers performs direct assignments to fixed implementation state variables (treasury, depository, dispenser) after an owner check. Tokenomics is intended to be used behind a proxy (it reads/writes a PROXY_TOKENOMICS slot) and therefore runs via delegatecall into proxy storage. When changeManagers executes via delegatecall, its sstore/write operations target the proxy’s storage layout. If the proxy (or another module in the proxy) places critical fields (owner/admin/implementation pointer or other sensitive state) in the same storage slots used by Tokenomics, invoking changeManagers can overwrite unrelated proxy state — corrupting ownership, upgrade pointers, role assignments, or other contract invariants and breaking separation between the implementation and proxy.
- Root cause
- The implementation unconditionally writes to fixed storage variables while assuming it runs in a storage layout compatible with the proxy. There is no enforced shared storage layout, no unstructured-storage wrapper/gap, and no delegatecall-only guard to ensure writes affect the intended proxy slots. As a result, ordinary state assignments in the implementation map to arbitrary storage slots in the proxy when layouts differ, allowing storage collision.
- Impact
- High — a successful collision can let an authorized caller (the owner as recorded in the proxy) inadvertently or maliciously overwrite proxy-critical storage. Consequences include:
- Loss or takeover of administrative control if owner/admin slots are overwritten, enabling privileged actions by an attacker.
- Corruption or replacement of the proxy’s implementation pointer, causing bricking, malicious upgrade, or denial-of-upgrade.
- Loss of role separation by replacing manager addresses or other critical module pointers.
- Service-owner voting power can satisfy donor top-up voting requirement (OR voting check)
- Targets
- trackServiceDonations / _trackServiceDonations (Tokenomics)
- Description
- Top-up eligibility for donations is gated by multiple manager-controlled guards (epoch-level unit-type flags, service deployment state, treasury-only external wrapper and donator blacklist) and a voting-power check that is implemented as a logical OR between the service owner and the donor. Concretely, the code grants voting eligibility when IVotingEscrow(ve).getVotes(serviceOwner) >= veOLASThreshold || IVotingEscrow(ve).getVotes(donator) >= veOLASThreshold. As a result the service owner’s voting power (or manager-controlled configuration/state) can enable or disable donor top-ups regardless of the donor’s own voting power, violating the intended property that eligibility depends solely on the donor’s voting power threshold.
- Root cause
- Composed guards and an incorrect voting check: instead of evaluating only the donor’s voting power, the implementation uses an OR between owner and donor votes and combines this with several manager-controlled gates (epoch flags, service-deployed check, treasury-only wrapper and blacklist), allowing owner/manager-controlled state to substitute for or block donor eligibility.
- Impact
- High — A service owner (or anyone who controls the owner’s voting power) can cause donors who do not meet the veOLAS threshold to receive pending top-ups by ensuring the owner meets the threshold (or by setting epoch/unit flags and ensuring deployed units). Conversely, managers or the service owner can block eligible donors by toggling epoch flags, blacklisting donors, or ensuring the service has no deployed units. This breaks expected donor-centric eligibility semantics and enables circumvention and denial-of-service on top-up eligibility. Potential consequences include unauthorized allocation of incentives to ineligible donors, privileged owner-funded top-ups, and censorship of legitimate donors.
- Unverified sstore in changeImplementation — writes to implementation storage instead of proxy
- Targets
- changeImplementation (LiquidityManagerCore)
- Description
- The function executes an inline assembly sstore into a hard-coded storage slot (PROXY_LIQUIDITY_MANAGER) without verifying that the call is running in the proxy’s storage context (i.e., via delegatecall). Because sstore updates the storage of the contract currently executing the call, an authorized owner who calls changeImplementation directly on the implementation (logic) contract will overwrite the implementation contract’s own PROXY_LIQUIDITY_MANAGER slot rather than the proxy’s implementation pointer. The function then emits ImplementationUpdated, misleading callers into believing the proxy was upgraded when it was not.
- Root cause
- The implementation assumes it executes within the proxy context and unconditionally writes to a fixed storage slot via sstore, but it lacks any runtime guard (delegatecall-only / onlyProxy / address(this) check) to ensure the storage write affects the proxy rather than the implementation contract itself.
- Impact
- High — an authorized owner can be tricked (or intentionally call) to update the implementation contract storage instead of the proxy, producing a false upgrade event. Consequences include failed/ignored upgrades (denial of upgrade), state inconsistencies between proxy and implementation, administrative confusion, and the potential to combine with other flaws to produce larger exploit scenarios (e.g., unexpected behavior if other flows read the wrong slot on the implementation).
- Targets
- getV3Pool (primary); call sites: _buyOLAS, checkPoolPrices (BuyBackBurner)
- getV3Pool (BuyBackBurner)
- updateOraclePrice (BuyBackBurner)
- Description
- BuyBackBurner relies on owner-configurable allowlists and externally-provided/overrideable helpers (a public virtual getV3Pool and external oracle implementations) but fails to verify that returned pool addresses or oracle updates are honest, well-formed, or safe. getV3Pool is declared public virtual and the contract accepts its returned pool address and checks only that the address is present in an owner-controlled mapV3Pools allowlist — without validating that token0/token1/fee match the requested pair or that the pool is the canonical Uniswap V3 pool for the pair. Separately, updateOraclePrice calls an external oracle’s updatePrice() and treats its boolean return as proof that price state changed, but it does not inspect the oracle’s reported price/timestamp and provides no reentrancy protection around the call. These weaknesses allow malicious or buggy derived implementations, whitelisted pools, or owner-misconfiguration to cause swaps/prices to be sourced from arbitrary pools or stale/manipulated oracles, and permit reentrancy via an attacker-controlled oracle to alter contract state or trigger value-moving flows during updatePrice().
- Root cause
- Excessive implicit trust in overrideable/owner-controlled external components and missing on-chain validation or reentrancy defenses: (1) getV3Pool is virtual and callers do not enforce canonical pool metadata (token0/token1/fee) — only an owner-set allowlist is checked; (2) mapV3Pools is owner-controlled so whitelisting is a privileged decision and can be misused; and (3) updateOraclePrice blindly trusts the boolean return of updatePrice() without verifying the oracle’s new price/timestamp/nonce and lacks a reentrancy guard, enabling reentry during the external call.
- Impact
- High — combined, these problems allow several realistic, high-impact attacks: (1) Mispriced or malicious pools: a malicious getV3Pool implementation or an erroneously/maliciously whitelisted pool can cause BuyBackBurner to use an attacker-controlled or misconfigured Uniswap V3 pool for pricing or swaps, enabling manipulated prices, MEV-style sandwiching, or direct token loss during buy/sell operations. (2) Stale or spoofed oracle prices: a malicious oracle can return true without updating on-chain price state (or set arbitrary values), causing the contract to act on stale or attacker-chosen prices and bypass slippage/price-sanity checks. (3) Reentrancy-mediated state corruption and drains: an attacker-controlled oracle can re-enter BuyBackBurner during updatePrice() (no reentrancy guard), invoking external flows like buyBack or other stateful functions to corrupt accounting, trigger unintended transfers, or drain funds. (4) Owner misconfiguration risk: because pool allowlisting and oracle pointers are owner-controlled, an honest-but-mistaken or compromised owner can produce the same outcomes. Overall results include incorrect buyBack behavior, financial loss, and corruption of BuyBackBurner’s internal accounting and protections.
- Owner-overwrite of staged next-epoch parameters allows silent replacement of pending tokenomics before commit
- Targets
- changeIncentiveFractions / changeStakingParams (Tokenomics)
- Description
- changeIncentiveFractions and changeStakingParams write owner-staged parameter sets directly into the next-epoch storage slots (mapEpochTokenomics[epochCounter + 1], mapEpochStakingPoints[epochCounter + 1]) and mark pending categories via a bitmask tokenomicsParametersUpdated. The contract does not provide a write-once guard, separate immutable staging buffer, per-staging nonce, or any locking mechanism. As a result, the owner can call the staging functions repeatedly prior to checkpoint(), with each call overwriting previously-staged values. When checkpoint() executes it commits whatever values are currently present in those next-epoch slots; earlier staged proposals are lost without trace.
- Root cause
- Design conflates a lightweight pending-bit marker with a robust staging mechanism: staged values are stored directly in the next-epoch commit locations and tokenomicsParametersUpdated is only a bitmask indicating categories with pending changes. There is no protection (write-once semantics, staging nonce, separate immutable buffer, or event-anchored proposal) to prevent subsequent owner writes from replacing earlier staged values prior to checkpoint().
- Impact
- High — although only the owner can perform the overwrite, this permits last-minute, silent replacement of pending economic parameters immediately prior to epoch commit. Concrete consequences include: (1) accidental loss of previously-staged parameter sets (surprising behavior for integrators and multisig governance flows); (2) malicious or careless owner manipulation of economic parameters with no on-chain record of the intermediate proposal that was overwritten; and (3) disturbed expectations for users and external tooling that assume staging is an effective pre-commit proposal. These behaviors can materially alter rewards, bond caps, and staking incentives at commit time and undermine trust in governance processes.

## [F-430] Unsafe external trust and state ordering
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-430](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-430)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- These V12 findings were marked as lower confidence during review.
- Inaccurate and spoofable activity accounting in BuyBackBurner.updateOraclePrice — unauthenticated increments and revert-dependent persistence
- Targets
- updateOraclePrice (BuyBackBurner)
- Description
- BuyBackBurner.updateOraclePrice manipulates the same per-account activity counter (mapAccountActivities) that is used by buyBack flows, but its implementation both (a) allows unauthenticated callers to increment their own activity counters without performing a buyBack, and (b) performs the increment before revert-prone checks/external calls so failed updates roll back the increment. Together these behaviors produce inconsistent, spoofable, and manipulable activity accounting: attackers can artifically inflate counters by repeatedly calling updateOraclePrice when the oracle update succeeds, or alternatively avoid increments by provoking a revert, defeating any activity-based gating, quotas, rewards, or telemetry that relies on the counter.
- Root cause
- Two implementation mistakes: (1) shared instrumentation without authorization — updateOraclePrice is an external, unprotected function that reuses the same mapAccountActivities counter intended for buyBack usage, allowing any caller to increment their counter when updatePrice() succeeds; and (2) incorrect ordering of state mutation and external interactions — the function increments the counter before performing zero-address checks and the external IOracle.updatePrice() call, so any revert undoes the increment and makes persistence contingent on external success rather than on the call attempt.
- Impact
- Medium-High (integrity / operational):
- Spoofing/Inflation: An attacker can repeatedly call updateOraclePrice for a token with a working oracle to inflate their mapAccountActivities entry without performing buyBack operations, potentially bypassing rate-limits, accruing undeserved rewards, or gaining privileges tied to activity counts.
- Evasion: By forcing updateOraclePrice to revert (e.g., using a malformed token/oracle or causing the external call to fail), callers can make attempts that intentionally do not increment their recorded activity, enabling evasion of activity-based restrictions or audit trails.
- Misleading telemetry and incorrect enforcement: Systems that rely on this counter for on-chain gating, off-chain analytics, rewards, or penalties will observe inaccurate counts leading to incorrect enforcement decisions, financial misallocation, or broken monitoring.
- Dependence severity: The practical severity depends on how mapAccountActivities is consumed; if used for gating/payments/privileged access the impact is high. If purely cosmetic, impact is limited to telemetry integrity.
- migrate() leaves reentrancy lock set and clears owner — permanent DoS of guarded functions
- Targets
- migrate (DefaultTargetDispenserL2)
- Description
- The migrate() function acquires a manual reentrancy lock by setting _locked = 2 but never restores _locked to its unlocked value on the successful execution path. After taking the lock, migrate() also sets owner = address(0). Multiple external state-changing functions begin with the guard if (_locked > 1) { revert ReentrancyGuard(); } and therefore will permanently revert once _locked remains > 1. Because owner is cleared, there is no administrative actor left that can call recovery functions to reset the guard. A successful migrate() call therefore leaves guarded functionality unusable and can irreversibly disable critical contract flows.
- Root cause
- Checks-effects-interactions / guard-management bug and missing cleanup: migrate() assigns the manual reentrancy guard (_locked = 2) at entry but does not reset _locked back to the unlocked value before returning on the non-reverting path. This omission is compounded by migrate() zeroing the owner, removing the only role that could have fixed the stuck guard via privileged calls.
- Impact
- High — permanent denial-of-service for all externally callable functions protected by the _locked guard (redeem, drain, syncWithheldAmount, _processData, and subsequent migrate calls). Once _locked is left > 1 by a successful migrate(), guarded functions always revert and cannot be recovered because owner is cleared. This can irreversibly block token redemption, draining, maintenance operations, or any flows relying on those guarded functions; funds and user operations may be effectively locked.
- Trusting overridable/internal hooks and caller-supplied contracts allows derived/malicious implementations to bypass validations, corrupt state, or steal funds
- Targets
- changeRanges (LiquidityManagerCore)
- buyBack (via internal _buyOLAS -> _performSwap) (BuyBackBurner)
- checkPoolPrices (BuyBackBurner)
- Description
- Multiple components delegate critical actions to internal virtual functions or to caller-supplied contracts but then trust the results or forwarded addresses without asserting postconditions or canonicality. Specifically: (a) changeRanges persists the return value of an internal virtual _mintV3 into mapPoolAddressPositionIds without verifying positionId != 0, ownership, or metadata; (b) buyBack flow delegates execution of swaps to an internal virtual _performSwap and never verifies that the actual swap used the pre-authorized pool/oracle or that expected transfers occurred; and (c) checkPoolPrices accepts a caller-supplied uniV3PositionManager/factory and forwards the returned pool address to LiquidityManager without confirming the manager/factory are canonical or that the pool is in the contract’s whitelist. These patterns let a malicious or buggy derived contract or an attacker-provided contract cause persistent state corruption, route actions to attacker-controlled pools, or misattribute/lose funds.
- Root cause
- Design and implementation assumptions about overridable/internal hooks and caller-supplied contracts are unsafe: the base contracts assume derived implementations and external contracts will be honest and that returned values are valid. There is no defensive verification of postconditions (e.g., positionId nonzero and owned, swap execution target matches authorized pool/oracle, ERC20 transfer outcomes), nor is there canonical validation of externally-provided manager/factory addresses against an allowlist. This breaks the checks-effects-interactions model because effects (state writes, asset transfers) are committed or relied upon based solely on untrusted returns.
- Impact
- High. A malicious derived implementation or an attacker-supplied contract can: - Persist an invalid or non-owned positionId into mapPoolAddressPositionIds, leading to stuck liquidity, broken collect/decrease flows, reverts when managing positions, or misrouting of future operations that assume ownership. - Execute swaps against attacker-controlled or unauthorized pools (or ignore the intended oracle), siphoning incoming tokens or returning manipulated OLAS amounts while bypassing pre-swap price/oracle checks and whitelists, causing direct financial loss. - Cause LiquidityManager and BuyBack flows to accept forged pools returned by an attacker-provided manager/factory, enabling price manipulation, DoS via unexpected reverts, or silent mis-accounting. Together these can result in loss of funds, persistent corrupted state that disables management operations, and degraded economic integrity of buy/sell and liquidity management functionality.
- Reentrancy via ITreasury.rebalanceTreasury allows duplicate epoch settlement
- Targets
- checkpoint (Tokenomics)
- Description
- The checkpoint() function performs extensive epoch settlement state changes (inflation/top-ups, effectiveBond adjustments, staking incentives, IDF computation, next-epoch copies, endTime, etc.) and then calls the external function ITreasury(treasury).rebalanceTreasury(incentives[1]). epochCounter — the canonical marker indicating the epoch has been settled — is only incremented after the external call returns. The contract has no ReentrancyGuard and the internal _locked variable present in initializeTokenomics is never used. The SameBlockNumber check (lastDonationBlockNumber != block.number) does not mitigate this because checkpoint does not update lastDonationBlockNumber. The ITreasury interface has no implementation in the repo, so the treasury address can point to an arbitrary contract that may call back into Tokenomics.checkpoint(). A malicious or cooperating treasury can re-enter checkpoint during rebalanceTreasury and cause the same epoch to be processed a second time in the same transaction, producing duplicated/misaligned state updates and incorrect accounting.: clear exploitability = 3 (high); clear flaw = 3 (high).
- Root cause
- Checks-effects-interactions violation combined with missing reentrancy protection: critical final state (epochCounter) that prevents duplicate settlement is only written after an external call. There is no active reentrancy guard; the only similar variable (_locked) is unused. The preexisting SameBlockNumber check does not prevent this path because checkpoint does not update lastDonationBlockNumber.
- Impact
- Duplicate epoch settlement within a single transaction: EpochSettled can be emitted twice for the same epoch.
- Monetary/accounting corruption: inflation/top-ups, effectiveBond, staking incentives, and IDF can be applied twice or in inconsistent order, producing incorrect balances and allocations.
- Potential financial loss or manipulation: attackers could skew incentive distributions or other epoch-based rewards/inflation, possibly enabling fund misallocation or downstream exploits.
- Protocol invariants and downstream logic that assume unique settlement per epoch may break, causing broader system instability.

## [F-431] Signature/Domain Binding and Validator Discovery Errors cause broken EIP-712/EIP-1271 flows, invalid signatures, and potential misbound authorizations
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-431](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-431)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- Description
- Two related issues break off-chain signature semantics and domain binding: (A) OperatorSignedHashes enforces a brittle, nonstandard 65-byte signature format and repurposes r to encode the validator address, calling the decoded address as the validator with the fixed 65-byte blob; and (B) PolySafeCreatorWithRecoveryModule computes a Safe (proxy) address for EIP‑712 domain/tx hashing using a factory helper but assumes that computed address always equals the actually deployed Safe address. Together these defects disrupt EIP‑1271/EIP‑712 expectations, causing valid contract-signed operations to be rejected, signatures to be tied to the wrong on-chain contract, and authorizations to be misbound or unusable.
- Root cause
- Incorrect assumptions about off-chain and on-chain signature/address primitives: (1) OperatorSignedHashes assumes contract validators use the same fixed 65-byte EOAs-style format and can be discovered by decoding the r word, instead of using an explicit validator address and accepting arbitrary-length validator blobs per EIP‑1271; (2) PolySafeCreatorWithRecoveryModule trusts the factory's computeProxyAddress(owner) result as the canonical Safe address without ensuring the factory uses identical inputs/initializer/salt/deployment path, and without verifying that the computed address actually hosts the intended Safe instance. Both rely on brittle, implicit conventions rather than robust validation of the validator identity and domain-binding inputs.
- Impact
- High — correctness/availability and potential authorization misbinding:
- Denial-of-service / broken UX: legitimate EIP‑1271 validators that accept variable-length, validator-specific signatures (or any validator that does not expect the r-encoded address) will be rejected by OperatorSignedHashes (length check or unexpected blob), causing valid contract-signed operations to fail.
- Interoperability loss: wallets and external signers expect standard EIP‑1271 semantics; enforcing a 65-byte format or custom encoding forces all validators to implement a nonstandard interface or be unusable.
- Invalid/irrelevant signatures: getEnableModuleTransactionHash can produce EIP‑712 digests bound to a computed proxy address that differs from the real deployed Safe, so signatures created over that digest will be invalid for the actual Safe or, worse, valid for a different contract if an attacker can cause a contract to exist at the computed address.

## [F-433] Withheld Amount Reduction Creates Cross-Chain Accounting Mismatch Causing Permanent Lockout of Staking Incentives
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-433](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-433)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Unknown`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Invalid, OOS, the`Dispenser.sol`contract is not within the scope of this audit contest
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Invalid, OOS, the`Dispenser.sol`contract is not within the scope of this audit contest
Full Finding Details:
- Summary
- The`_distributeStakingIncentivesBatch`function in the Dispenser contract distributes staking incentives across multiple Layer 2 chains by transferring OLAS tokens to deposit processors and sending bridge messages with distribution instructions. The function relies on two separate data structures:`stakingIncentives[i][j]`arrays containing the amounts each staking target should receive, and`transferAmounts[i]`representing the total OLAS to transfer per chain. A critical accounting mismatch occurs because`transferAmounts[i]`is reduced by withheld amounts in`_calculateStakingIncentivesBatch`, while the`stakingIncentives[i][j]`arrays maintain their original calculated values. When building the bridge message payload, the function uses the original`stakingIncentives`values to populate`updatedStakingAmounts`, but passes the reduced`transferAmounts[i]`as the total transfer amount parameter. This causes deposit processors on Layer 2 to receive fewer OLAS tokens than the sum of the distribution amounts specified in the message, creating an impossible state where the deposit processor cannot fulfill the distribution instructions. Affected staking targets permanently lose access to their incentives because the deposit processor has insufficient funds, the incentives have already been cleared from Layer 1 state, and there is no recovery mechanism.
- Vulnerable Code
- The vulnerability spans two functions in`contracts/Dispenser.sol`. The withheld amount reduction occurs in the calculation phase:
- The mismatch manifests during distribution when the function uses the original incentive values:
- Impact
- This vulnerability causes systematic permanent loss of staking incentives across all Layer 2 deployments whenever withheld amounts exist. When a user claims staking incentives for a chain with`mapChainIdWithheldAmounts[chainId] > 0`, the deposit processor receives insufficient OLAS tokens to fulfill the distribution instructions encoded in the bridge message. For example, if three staking targets should receive 100, 200, and 300 OLAS respectively (total 600), but a withheld amount of 150 exists, the deposit processor receives only 450 OLAS while the message instructs it to distribute the full 600 OLAS. When the deposit processor attempts to execute the distributions on Layer 2, it successfully deposits to the first two targets (consuming 300 OLAS), but fails on the third target because only 150 OLAS remains. The affected staking targets permanently lose their incentives because the corresponding epoch ranges have already been marked as claimed in`mapLastClaimedStakingEpochs`on Layer 1, the user's withheld amount balance has been reduced, and the deposit processor has no mechanism to return undeliverable funds or trigger a retry. This systematic failure affects every claim transaction on chains with non-zero withheld amounts, compounding over time as more users claim and more withheld amounts accumulate. The vulnerability creates cross-chain state inconsistency where Layer 1 records show successful distribution while Layer 2 staking contracts never receive the promised funds, breaking the fundamental trust assumption of the cross-chain incentive distribution protocol.
- Recommended Mitigation
- Apply the withheld amount reduction proportionally to each staking incentive value before building the message arrays, ensuring`sum(updatedStakingAmounts)`equals`transferAmounts[i]`:

- Finding description and impact
- The ServiceManager.update() function allows service owners to switch a service's bond token from an ERC20 token to ETH by calling update() with token = ETH_TOKEN_ADDRESS. When this occurs, the function invokes ServiceRegistryTokenUtility.resetServiceToken(serviceId) to clear token metadata. However, this creates a flaw where operator funds become permanently locked.
- The issue exists in the interaction between two operations
- When operators register agents for an ERC20-based service, their tokens are transferred to and held in ServiceRegistryTokenUtility
- When the service owner switches to ETH:
- resetServiceToken() deletes mapServiceIdTokenDeposit[serviceId] (which contains the token address)
- Operator balances in mapOperatorAndServiceIdOperatorBalances remain unchanged
- Physical ERC20 tokens remain in the TokenUtility contract
- When operators attempt to unbond:
- IMPACT Permanent Fund Loss: All operator ERC20 tokens deposited for that service are permanently locked in ServiceRegistryTokenUtility.
- No Refund Path: The unbondTokenRefund() function exits early because the token address is address(0)
- Griefing Vector: Service owners can intentionally lock operator funds by switching token types
- Affects all operators who deposited before the token switch
- Recommended mitigation steps
- Prevent Token Type Switching Modify ServiceManager.update() to prevent switching between ERC20 and ETH:

Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Invalid, once you have terminated a service, you cannot perform reactivation of a specific serviceId as the following check in the`ServiceRegistry.sol`contract will fail
Full Finding Details:
- Finding description and impact
- The ServiceRegistryTokenUtility contract is responsible for managing ERC20 token deposits for services that choose to use tokens instead of ETH for security deposits and agent bonds. The contract maintains a critical mapping`mapServiceIdTokenDeposit`that serves as the source of truth for determining whether a service is token-secured and what deposit amount is required The protocol's design intent specifies that:
- After a service is terminated and the security deposit refunded, the service should no longer be considered "token-secured
- Attack Propagation Path (Unintentional User Impact):
- Pulls 1000 USDC from service owner
- Owner balance: 10,000 USDC → 9,000 USDC
- Owner balance: 9,000 USDC → 10,000 USDC ✓
- Expects to either:
- Re-activate without payment (service becomes ETH-secured), OR
- Interprets service as still being token-secured (incorrect)
- Owner balance: 10,000 USDC → 9,000 USDC (surprising to user!)
- Critical Insight : This is NOT a theft/drainage vulnerability. The service owner always receives full refunds. However, they are forced into unnecessary payment cycles that violate the protocol's intended design and create significant user confusion.
- Impact Explanation
- The impact is assessed as Medium because while the bug creates real problems, it does not result in permanent fund loss or protocol insolvency Detailed justification:
- Architectural Design Violation
- Significant User Experience Degradation
- Gas Cost Waste
- Temporary Capital Lock
- 100 active services
- Average 3 activation cycles per service
- Recommended mitigation steps
- Add the missing state cleanup in`ServiceRegistryTokenUtility.terminateTokenRefund()`

- The V3 buyback flow in BuyBackBurner._buyOLAS() (lines 208-234) only performs a pre-swap check via`checkPoolAndGetCenterPrice()`at line 231. Unlike the V2 path which validates price bounds post-swap (lines 197-198), the V3 path has no post-swap validation.

## [F-446] LiquidityManagerETH permanently reverts if maxSlippage is configured below 1%, causing Denial Of Service
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-446](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-446)
Review: `Accepted`
Validity: `Valid`
Sufficiency: `Sufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: This issue is missing the root cause mentioned in F-175, that is there is a mismatch in scaling between the LiquidityManagerCore`maxSlippage`parameter (4 decimals) and the derivation computed within the UniswapOracleContract (16 decimals). So the key issue here is not the precision loss but the incorrect precision between the two parameters given if maxSlippage is scaled up to the required slippage (18 decimals), such precision loss would not be possible
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: This issue is missing the root cause mentioned in F-175, that is there is a mismatch in scaling between the LiquidityManagerCore`maxSlippage`parameter (4 decimals) and the derivation computed within the UniswapOracleContract (16 decimals). So the key issue here is not the precision loss but the incorrect precision between the two parameters given if maxSlippage is scaled up to the required slippage (18 decimals), such precision loss would not be possible
Full Finding Details:
- Finding description and impact
- `LiquidityManagerETH`allows the DAO to configure a`maxSlippage`parameter in basis points (BPS) to protect liquidity operations. However, the`_checkTokensAndRemoveLiquidityV2`logic converts this value to a percentage using integer division before passing it to the Oracle.
- Because Solidity truncates on division, any`maxSlippage`< 100 BPS (i.e. < 1%) is converted to 0. This causes the Oracle to enforce a 0% deviation tolerance, which is practically impossible to satisfy in live AMM pools.
- As a result, configuring`maxSlippage`to any value below 1% causes liquidity operations to revert permanently, creating a Denial of Service and forcing the DAO to choose between operational failure and unsafe slippage parameters.
- Example Scenario
- Configuration:
- This is a standard and recommended setting for stable or correlated assets
- Execution:
- Oracle Behavior:
- Any real pool has minor price drift
- Outcome:
- Liquidity removal becomes impossible
- This failure is permanent until the configuration is changed. The same also occurs in`LiquidityManagerOptimism`
- Impact
- Denial of Service: The protocol cannot operate with`maxSlippage < 1%`which are standard in DeFi
- Recommended mitigation steps
- Add a new`validatePriceBps()`function to oracle interface and pass BPS directly to the Oracle

- Total reward: 109 wei
- Each operator gets: 9 wei
- Total to operators: 9 × 10 = 90 wei
- Over 1000 claims with 109 wei each:
- 100 operators + 1 service owner = 101 total receivers
- Total reward: 1000 wei
- Each operator gets: 9 wei (loses ~0.9 wei per claim)
- Total to operators: 900 wei
- Affected Parties
- Recommended Mitigation
- Distribute the remainder evenly among receivers:
- Gas Optimization Note
- The proposed fix adds minimal gas overhead:
- One comparison per receiver: ~3 gas each
- Total overhead: <50 gas for typical service sizes
- This is negligible compared to the fairness improvement.
- Additional Considerations
- Documentation Update
- Update documentation to clarify:
- Test Cases
- Add comprehensive tests:
- References

- Severity : MEDIUM Likelihood : HIGH (Occurs on every proportional distribution) Impact : LOW-MEDIUM (Unfair but bounded loss) Overall Risk : MEDIUM
- CVSS v3.1 Score : 5.3 CVSS Vector :`CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N`

## [F-197] Timelock ETH drain via unchecked refundAddress overpayment
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-197](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-197)
Review: `—`

Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: False positive. The contract operates on Timelock-only access function control: // Check for timelock access if (msg.sender != timelock) { revert UnauthorizedAccount(msg.sender); } Thus is the DAO decided to hurt itself via the vote, there is nothing can be done. The DAO is trusted by default.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: The contract operates on Timelock-only access function control: // Check for timelock access if (msg.sender != timelock) { revert UnauthorizedAccount(msg.sender); } Thus is the DAO decided to hurt itself via the vote, there is nothing can be done. The DAO is trusted by default.
Full Finding Details:
- `WormholeRelayerTimelock.transferTokens()`is designed as a “token bridge helper”, but because it accepts arbitrary`msg.value`and refunds all overpayment to a caller-supplied`refundAddress`, it effectively becomes a generic ETH payout primitive whenever the timelock executes it with non-zero ETH.
- This is particularly dangerous in the Olas governance flow because scheduling is guarded mostly by (target + selector) allowlisting, while the schedule call’s ETH`value`and sensitive parameters like`refundAddress`are not constrained by the guard layer.
- Root Cause
- 1) _manageFee() refunds overpayment to refundAddress (not msg.sender)
- `_manageFee()`computes`leftovers = msg.value - cost`and transfers it to`refundAddress`.
- File:`autonolas-governance/contracts/bridges/WormholeRelayerTimelock.sol`Lines: 172–191
- 2) transferTokens() uses messageFee() as the only “cost” and calls _manageFee()
- ile:`autonolas-governance/contracts/bridges/WormholeRelayerTimelock.sol`Lines: 263–304 (key lines: 288–296)
- So any timelock call with`msg.value > cost`will pay`cost`to Wormhole and refund`msg.value - cost`to`refundAddress`.
- Why this becomes exploitable in the guarded timelock flow
- This contract is`timelock`-only, but the threat model here is not “random EOAs calling it”. The risk comes from what the guard layer actually constrains when a proposal is scheduled.
- GuardCM decodes schedule data but discards the value field(s)
- In`_verifySchedule()`, GuardCM decodes`schedule()`/`scheduleBatch()`and extracts`targets`and`callDatas`, but ignores the`value`/`values[]`fields entirely (they are decoded into blank slots).
- File:`autonolas-governance/contracts/multisigs/GuardCM.sol`Lines: 189–209 (key lines: 199–209)
- VerifyData allowlists only (target + selector + chainId)
- The downstream check verifies only the selector of the calldata, not the calldata arguments, and not any ETH`value`.
- File:`autonolas-governance/contracts/multisigs/VerifyData.sol`Lines: 23–37
- If the selector for`transferTokens(...)`is allowed, a malicious scheduler can still choose:
- Possible Scenario
- Attacker obtains the ability to schedule a timelock action that passes GuardCM checks (e.g., compromised/malicious CM or governance path intended to be restricted by the guard).
- They schedule a call to`WormholeRelayerTimelock.transferTokens(...)`with:
- Ensure the call does not revert (e.g., the contract already holds the needed token amount).
- On execution:
- Impact
- If`transferTokens()`is allowlisted in GuardCM and executed by the timelock:
- This can result in direct loss of ETH from the timelock, i.e. fund theft.
- Recommendation
