## [F-247] null
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-247](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-247)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: False positive. Agree with invalidity, there is simply no realistic reason to allow a zero bond agent service to be created
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Agree with invalidity, there is simply no realistic reason to allow a zero bond agent service to be created
Full Finding Details:
- Finding summary and impact
- If we look at the comments in`ServiceRegistryTokenUtility::createWithToken`it is clear that passing bonds == 0 is possible when updating a service ServiceRegistryTokenUtility::L307
- However the issue is that due to incorrect checks in the code this action will not be possible and will lead to a revert resulting in unintentional behavior and broken functionality in the protocol.
- Finding Description
- If a service owner wants to update his service, he will be doing it through the`ServiceManager::update`. This function has an incorrect check which leads to the tx being reverted if zero value is passed in`bond`. Lets have a look at the function. ServiceManager::L198 and ServiceManager::L218 (where the issue lies)
- If we observe the`@`marks the check for 0 value in case the`token`address passed in is`ETH`is okay and intended. However the same check should not be there in the else block too in case the token = non ETH or ERC20s. This is because as aforementioned that while updating ERC20 services bonds are allowed to be 0 for agents.
- There are some things worth noting here are: One argument for this could be that when updating, user should pass in slots = 0 too, then the transaction will pass as expected. However if a user does that, then in that case the transaction will still revert due to`WrongThreshold`error in`ServiceRegistry::_setServiceData`this function is called when`update`is called on the serviceRegistry contract since even when updating the ERC20 service, the`ServiceManager::update`calls the update function in the ServiceRegistry.sol as well
- ServiceRegistry::update ServiceRegistry::_setServiceData This is where the tx will revert - in ServiceRegistry::L206. Will paste the links of these above in the`Link To root cause`section as well
- Along with this, there is another function where problem will arise if we pass in slots = 0 and that is the`ServiceRegistry::registerAgents`This is again because of the fact that when`registerAgents`is called on the serviceManager for ERC20 services, the`ServiceRegistry`s update fuction is also invoked. See here ServiceRegistry::registerAgent::L422
- Additionally, We can also see in the`update`function of the ServiceRegistry that there is no restriction for for such bonds with non zero slots which proves the forementioned points in the finding description
- So after observing the above facts, the passing in 0 slots cannot be work around for this issue as the protocol allows for these services to have 0 bonds for some agents if the service owner wants to. So the the service owner should be able to update a service with slots = 1 and bonds = 0 to be in line with the protocol's intentional behavior. But here due to incorrect logic this functionality is broken.
- Recommended mitigation steps
- As forementioned in the`Finding Description`section, there 0 bond check in the`ServiceManager::update`function should not be there in the else block when the token = non eth or ERC20. So remove that check from the else block.

Full Finding Details:
- Finding description and impact
- The`BridgeMessenger`allows batching multiple transactions into one message. However, it implements a strict balance check:
- Impact
- Batch Reversion: If a single transaction in a batch of 10 requires more ETH than the contract currently holds, the entire batch reverts.
- Deadlock: Because the contract balance is checked against a specific value in the loop, if the bridge relayer delivers less msg.value than the total sum of the batch, the bridge delivery becomes impossible to execute.
- Recommended mitigation steps
- Instead of reverting the whole transaction, consider logging the failure of the specific sub-call and continuing with the remaining transactions, or ensure a total balance check is performed at the start of the function.

Full Finding Details:

- The`drainServiceSlashedFunds`function checks if`slashedFunds < minAcceptedETH`and reverts if true. Since`minAcceptedETH`is set to 0.065 ether, any amount accumulated in the`ServiceRegistry`that is less than this threshold can never be drained to the Treasury.

## [F-250] null
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-250](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-250)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Unknown`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Invalid, OOS,`WormholeTargetDispenserL2`is not within the scope of this audit contest
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Invalid, OOS,`WormholeTargetDispenserL2`is not within the scope of this audit contest
Full Finding Details:
- Vulnerability Details Description The vulnerability is an Authorization Bypass in the WormholeTargetDispenserL2 contract, specifically in the receivePayloadAndTokens function. This function allows any address on L1 (not just the authorized l1DepositProcessor) to send cross-chain messages via Wormhole, potentially leading to unauthorized token deposits, fund theft, or system manipulation. The issue arises because the function does not validate that the sourceProcessor (extracted from the VAA) matches the stored l1DepositProcessor address, despite the code's comments indicating this requirement.
- Root Cause: Missing input validation for the sender's identity. The function checks sourceChainId and token details but skips authorization checks. Impact: High severity (CVSS ~8.5). Attackers can spoof messages to execute _receiveMessage, which may handle deposits or transfers, resulting in financial loss or protocol disruption. Exploit Scenario: Attacker on L1 crafts a VAA with a fake sourceProcessor (their own address). Sets sourceChainId to match l1SourceChainId and includes valid OLAS token data. Sends the VAA via Wormhole; the contract accepts it without verifying the sender. _receiveMessage processes the payload, allowing unauthorized actions. Referenced Code Sections Below are links to the relevant sections in the provided Solidity code (assuming it's hosted or mirrored on a GitHub repo like a fork of Wormhole SDK). If the exact repo isn't specified, these are based on standard Wormhole SDK structure. Use Markdown for formatting.
- Function Declaration and Comment Indicating Requirement: The comment states "The sender must be the deposit processor address," but no validation is implemented. Link to code (approximate, as receivePayloadAndTokens is in TokenBase.sol).
- Extraction of processor from sourceProcessor: address processor = address(uint160(uint256(sourceProcessor))); – No check follows this. Link to code (line ~200 in TokenBase.sol for similar logic).
- Call to _receiveMessage with Unvalidated processor: _receiveMessage(msg.sender, processor, data); – Passes processor directly without authorization. Link to code (line ~210 in TokenBase.sol).
- Comparison with Authorized Sender in Other Functions: In _sendMessage, messages are sent to l1DepositProcessor, implying it's the only authorized sender, but reception lacks this check. Link to code (for reference to sending logic).
- Proof of Concept (PoC) in Markdown solidity
- Copy code // Attacker's VAA payload simulation bytes memory fakePayload = abi.encode(100); // e.g., deposit amount bytes32 fakeSourceProcessor = attackerAddress; // Not l1DepositProcessor uint16 correctChainId = l1SourceChainId;
- // Contract accepts without revert contract.receivePayloadAndTokens(fakePayload, receivedTokens, fakeSourceProcessor, correctChainId, deliveryHash); Mitigation Add the following check in receivePayloadAndTokens:
- solidity
- Copy code if (processor != l1DepositProcessor) { revert UnauthorizedSender(processor, l1DepositProcessor); }

## [F-252] Tokenomics.updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions permanently nullifies protocol inflation if called during Year 0
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-252](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-252)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Invalid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge rejection comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- Summary
- The`Tokenomics`contract is responsible for calculating and updating the protocol's inflation rate (`inflationPerSecond`). There is a critical logic inconsistency between how the contract is initialized and how it is subsequently updated by the administrator during the first year of operation ("Year 0").
- Vulnerability Details
- 1. Inconsistent Data Sources for Year 0
- During initialization, the contract sets the starting inflation by calling`getInflationForYear(0)`. This function correctly returns the Year 0 budget of 3,159,000e18 OLAS, as intended by the protocol's economic model.
- However, the administrative function`updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions`uses a different internal logic to recalculate the same variable:
- This function calls`getActualInflationForYear(currentYear)`, which retrieves values from the`inflationAmounts`array located in`TokenomicsConstants.sol`.
- 2. The Hardcoded Zero Constant
- In`TokenomicsConstants.sol`, the`inflationAmounts`array, which serves as the source of truth for the`update`function, is defined with a zero value at index 0:
- Because the array explicitly stores`0`for the first year, any call to`updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions`while`currentYear == 0`will result in the following state change:`inflationPerSecond = 0 / 31536000 = 0`.
- 3. Administrative Trap
- While the`updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions`function is intended to allow administrators to adjust incentive distributions (e.g.,`stakingFraction`), it has the unavoidable side effect of recalculating the global`inflationPerSecond`.
- Since the protocol is expected to be managed and tuned during its first year, an administrator performing a routine adjustment of rewards fractions will unknowingly trigger a recalculation that pulls the`0`constant, effectively "killing" the protocol's inflation for the remainder of the year.
- 4. Consequences for Protocol Logic
- The nullification of`inflationPerSecond`propagates through the entire system:
- Impact
- An administrator's routine parameter update results in the permanent loss of all protocol inflation for the first year. This halts the bonding program and developer rewards, leading to a total failure of the protocol's core economic incentives. Given that Year 0 inflation is a "yield in motion" totaling 3.1M OLAS, its accidental nullification represents a significant loss of planned protocol value.
- Recommendations
- 1. Sync Constant Values (Immediate Fix)
- Update the`inflationAmounts`array in`TokenomicsConstants.sol`to ensure that index 0 reflects the intended Year 0 inflation budget. This ensures that`getActualInflationForYear(0)`returns the same value used during the initial deployment.
- 2. Implement Safeguard in Update Function (Logic Protection)
- Modify`updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions`to prevent recalculation of the global inflation rate if the current year is 0. This protects the protocol from accidental nullification while still allowing administrators to adjust reward fractions.

## [F-254] Missing ETH Balance Verification Enables Permanent Loss of Rewards When OLAS Minting Succeeds
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-254](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-254)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Unknown`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Agree with invalidity, see the following check in the`Treasury.sol`contract
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Agree with invalidity, see the following check in the`Treasury.sol`contract
Full Finding Details:
- Summary
- The`claimOwnerIncentives`function in the Dispenser contract fails to verify ETH reward transfers while correctly verifying OLAS token receipts. When a user has earned both ETH rewards and OLAS top-ups, but the Treasury contract has insufficient ETH balance, the Treasury's`withdrawToAccount`function will skip the ETH transfer (due to the failed condition check) but successfully mint OLAS tokens. Because OLAS minting sets the`success`return value to`true`, the Dispenser interprets this as a complete success and does not revert the transaction. However, the user's incentive balances in Tokenomics have already been permanently cleared to zero before any transfers occurred. This results in the user receiving only the OLAS tokens while permanently losing their entire ETH reward amount, with no mechanism for recovery.
- Vulnerable Code
- The vulnerability exists in the interaction between three contracts. The critical flaw is in`contracts/Dispenser.sol`where only OLAS balance is verified:
- The issue is exacerbated by the Treasury's return logic in`contracts/Treasury.sol`:
- The permanent balance clearing occurs in`contracts/Tokenomics.sol`:
- Impact
- This vulnerability causes permanent and complete loss of user ETH rewards under specific but realistic conditions. When Treasury's`ETHFromServices`balance falls below the user's pending`accountRewards`amount, the ETH transfer is silently skipped. If the user also has OLAS top-ups pending, the OLAS minting succeeds and masks the ETH transfer failure by setting`success = true`. The Dispenser accepts this as valid, emits an event claiming both rewards were paid, and completes the transaction. Meanwhile, the user's balances in Tokenomics have been zeroed permanently. There is no recovery mechanism, retry logic, or refund pathway. The ETH rewards are lost forever while the inflated event data misleads off-chain indexers and the user into believing the transfer succeeded. This can result in 100% loss of the user's accumulated ETH rewards, potentially representing months or years of earned incentives, with the likelihood increasing as Treasury ETH reserves deplete over time or during periods of high claiming activity.
- Recommended Mitigation
- Add ETH balance verification symmetrical to the existing OLAS verification in the Dispenser contract:
## [F-255] GuardCM.pause() Missing Governor Contract Validation

Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Judge Comments. Invalid, OOS, assumes deployer/admin performing deployment will perform a reckless/malicious input error when setting the`governor`variable
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Invalid, OOS, assumes deployer/admin performing deployment will perform a reckless/malicious input error when setting the`governor`variable
Full Finding Details:
- Description
- The`pause()`function allows the`multisig`address to pause the guard if a specific proposal`governorCheckProposalId`is defeated. However, it casts the`governor`address to`IGovernor`and calls`.state(...)`without first validating that`governor`is actually a contract that supports the interface.
- Impact
- If the`governor`variable is incorrectly set (e.g. to an EOA or a contract not implementing`state`), the transaction will revert or behave unexpectedly (in case of EOA, call succeeds with no data, decoding might fail or return default 0 which is`Pending`). If it returns`Pending`(0), it falls to`else`and reverts`NotDefeated`. While the impact is low (transaction reverts), it lacks robustness against configuration errors.
- Recommended Mitigation
- Add a check to ensure`governor`is a contract and optionally supports the interface, or wrap the call in a`try/catch`block to handle invalid governor states gracefully.
## [F-256] Critical Arbitrary Call in DefaultTargetDispenserL2 via Unvalidated Cross-Chain Calldata Manipulation
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-256](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-256)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Unknown`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Invalid, assumes malicious`stakingFactory`contract set by trusted deployer/admin during deployment of the Dispenser contracts
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Invalid, assumes malicious`stakingFactory`contract set by trusted deployer/admin during deployment of the Dispenser contracts
Full Finding Details:
- Finding description and impact
- Root Cause: The vulnerability is located in the _processData(bytes memory data) function within DefaultTargetDispenserL2.sol. This contract is responsible for processing cross-chain messages from Layer 1. The root cause is a lack of input validation on the verifyData bytes, which are subsequently passed into a low-level .call() on the stakingFactory address.
- In DefaultTargetDispenserL2.sol#L251, the code executes: (success,returnData)=stakingFactory.call(verifyData);
- Since verifyData is derived directly from the cross-chain payload provided by the user on the source chain, an attacker can manipulate this payload to include any arbitrary function selector and arguments. The stakingFactory contract will execute this call as if it originated from the Dispenser contract itself.
- Impact: This is a CRITICAL severity issue due to Arbitrary Call / Privilege Escalation.
- Recommended mitigation steps
- To mitigate this vulnerability, the contract must avoid low-level calls with arbitrary data. The following steps are recommended:
- Example of secure implementation: Solidity
- // Decode specific parameters instead of using raw bytes (address target, uint256 amount, bytes memory proof) = abi.decode(verifyData, (address, uint256, bytes));
- // Call a specific, validated function bool isValid = IStakingFactory(stakingFactory).verifyData(target, amount, proof); require(isValid, "Invalid staking data");
## [F-257] Evicted services can still claim accumulated rewards, defeating the inactivity penalty system
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-257](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-257)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Judge Comments. Missing mandatory PoC required to be eligible for rewards in the contest
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Missing mandatory PoC required to be eligible for rewards in the contest
Full Finding Details:
- When a service is evicted for exceeding maxInactivityDuration, the _evict() function removes it from the setServiceIds array but does NOT zero out mapServiceInfo[serviceId].reward or delete the service info struct. Since _claim() only checks that msg.sender == sInfo.owner and sInfo.reward > 0 (never checking if the service is still in the active staking set), an evicted service owner can call claim(serviceId) to extract all accumulated rewards after eviction.
- _evict() only does:
- • Removes from setServiceIds array • Emits ServicesEvicted event • Does NOT touch mapServiceInfo[serviceId] • Does NOT zero sInfo.reward • Does NOT clear sInfo.owner _claim() only checks:
- • msg.sender == sInfo.owner ✓ (still set after eviction) • sInfo.reward > 0 ✓ (never zeroed by eviction) • No check for active staking status This defeats the entire purpose of eviction as a penalty mechanism.
- Recommended Mitigation: In _evict(), zero out sInfo.reward and return funds to availableRewards. Or add a staking state check in _claim() that rejects evicted services.

Full Finding Details:
- Finding Description and Impact
- The function`updateInflationPerSecondAndFractions()`writes incentive fractions to the current epoch's storage (`mapEpochTokenomics[curEpochCounter]`) instead of the next epoch. This is inconsistent with`changeIncentiveFractions()`which correctly targets`epochCounter + 1`.
- The inconsistency allows the owner to retroactively change fraction rules for already-accumulated donations, effectively rugging users who contributed during the current epoch.

## [F-448] null
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-448](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-448)
Review: `Accepted`
Validity: `Valid`
Sufficiency: `Sufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: I would say this is at best QA/low severity, and is more of a design improvement suggestion, given multiple buybackburner contracts can be utilized by the protocol.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: I would say this is at best QA/low severity, and is more of a design improvement suggestion, given multiple buybackburner contracts can be utilized by the protocol.
Full Finding Details:
- Finding description and impact
- The`BuyBackBurner`contract uses a single global`maxSlippage`variable applied uniformly to all V2 pool swaps, regardless of the individual characteristics of each pool.
- The _buyOLAS function relies on this global value in two key areas:
- Post-swap slippage bounds check
- This design assumes all pools exhibit similar liquidity and volatility profiles, which is often not the case. For example:
- A deep pool like OLAS/WETH may tolerate a tight slippage bound (e.g., 0.5%) without issue.
- A thinner pool like OLAS/DAI may experience higher price impact during swaps, causing slippage checks to fail even for expected behavior.
- Impacts of this design include:
- Over-conservative setting: Using a low slippage threshold (e.g., 0.5%) may cause buybacks to fail in low-liquidity pools due to minor price movements.
- Over-permissive setting: Using a high threshold (e.g., 3%) may allow all pools to pass, but increases exposure to MEV sandwich attacks in high-liquidity pools, resulting in fund loss.
- Recommended mitigation steps
- Refactor maxSlippage into a per-pool mapping, allowing each pool to have its own slippage tolerance. This enables:
- Tighter slippage controls for high-liquidity pools to mitigate MEV risk.
- More lenient bounds for low-liquidity pools to avoid unnecessary buyback failures.
- Post-deployment flexibility to adjust slippage per pool as conditions evolve.

In fact, Wormhole Relayer docs indicates a behavior that delivers a specific message via a verified action approval (VAA) from a source chain to a specified destination chain, meaning, the same relayer (or relayer network node) can handle many different source→destination pairs across all Wormhole-supported chains
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: There is no proof in the appeal comment and in the original report that the following is accurate But for Wormhole, this is different: on Ethereum, a single WormholeRelayer contract target address is used to relay messages to multiple destination chains (This is how wormhole infra works, it is not done by olas). The destination in the WormholeRelayer contract is selected as per the caller's provided chainId and then the contract an event with this chain id which is then picked by the off-chain relayers and they deliver it on the destination chain (provided chain Id). In fact, Wormhole Relayer docs indicates a behavior that delivers a specific message via a verified action approval (VAA) from a source chain to a specified destination chain, meaning, the same relayer (or relayer network node) can handle many different source→destination pairs across all Wormhole-supported chains
Full Finding Details:
- Finding description and impact
- SUMMARY :-
- The`GuardCM`contract uses`mapBridgeMediatorL1BridgeParams`to map L1 bridge mediator addresses to their corresponding L2 parameters. However, Wormhole uses a single`WormholeRelayer`contract on Ethereum to relay messages to all destination chains. Since the mapping key is only the L1 address, configuring Wormhole for multiple chains is impossible — each new chain overwrites the previous configuration.
- The`GuardCM`contract acts as a guard module for the community multisig, verifying cross-chain messages before they're sent. For chains with native Ethereum bridges (`Arbitrum`,`Optimism`,`Polygon`), their bridges are used as L1 mediator. For chains without native bridges, Wormhole's infrastructure is used.
- The Guard calls verifier contracts according to the chain the data is being sent to to verify the calldata, like if the call is encoded correctly for the chain and if the call is being made with correct function selector.
- Issue :-
- The problem lies in`GuardCM`s`mapBridgeMediatorL1BridgeParams`mapping key. When`_verifySchedule`processes a scheduled call, it fetches bridge parameters using the target address as the key:
- And look how the wormhole verifier (deployed by olas) verfies the data:-
- the verifier checks if the address in mapping and the provided address in calldata are same.
- For native bridges this works fine — Arbitrum's`Inbox`and Optimism's`L1CrossDomainMessenger`are different addresses, so each gets its own mapping entry.
- But Wormhole is different. There's a single`WormholeRelayer`contract on Ethereum mainnet that handles messages to every Wormhole-supported chain.
- So for ex. first it they configure if for Celo, and then later try add another Wormhole chain (say, Sui or another EVM chain), The second call overwrites the first. Now Celo governance calls will fail because the stored`chainId`and`bridgeMediatorL2`are wrong.
- Impact:-
- According to the sponsors and`governance_bridge.pdf`, Wormhole is intended for multiple chains. With the current design:
- This effectively limits the community multisig's cross-chain governance capability to native-bridge chains plus exactly one Wormhole chain. So the Severity is HIGH .
- Recommended mitigation steps
- To mitigate this issue, use nested mapping with chainId or employ some other mechanism.
## [F-450] Slippage protection in convertToV3 is ineffective

Full Finding Details:
- Summary
- The`convertToV3()`function in`LiquidityManagerCore`calculates minimum amount thresholds based on the optimizer's output amounts, which are themselves derived from the current pool price. This creates slippage protection values are based on potentially manipulated prices, making the protection ineffective.
- Finding Description
- When converting V2 liquidity to V3 positions, the`LiquidityManagerCore`contract attempts to protect against price manipulation through minimum amount thresholds. However, the implementation derives these thresholds from values that are themselves based on the current pool price.
- In`convertToV3()`, the function retrieves the current pool price and passes it to`_optimizeTicksAndMintPosition()`:
- Within`_optimizeTicksAndMintPosition()`, the slippage minimums are calculated from the optimizer's output:
- Scenario:
- The mint executes at the manipulated price
- The slippage check only protects against price movement between the optimizer call and the mint call, which cannot occur since both happen in the same transaction. It provides no protection against the price already being manipulated when the transaction executes.
- Recommendation
- Consider calculating minimum amounts based on the original`inputAmounts`rather than the optimizer's output. This ensures the slippage check compares against the protocol's intended deposit amounts rather than values derived from the current price:
- This change ensures that if the optimizer returns significantly different amounts than originally intended (due to price manipulation), the mint will revert rather than executing at unfavorable terms.
## [F-451] Reentrancy vulnerability allows attacker to steal all funds from ServiceRegistry and ServiceRegistryTokenUtility
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-451](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-451)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Judge Comments. Agree, this as opposed to S-862, does not delegate agent operator signatures to the service owner. The PoC also would rely on a agent operator recklessly performing registration to a service with a malicious token, falling in the OOS section Finally, all vulnerabilities that arise from misconfigured registration from users (e.g. component owners, agent owners, service owners, agents operators) or misuse of the registration logic (e.g. accidental locking of funds, loss of keys to control services, etc.).
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Agree, this as opposed to S-862, does not delegate agent operator signatures to the service owner. The PoC also would rely on a agent operator recklessly performing registration to a service with a malicious token, falling in the OOS section Finally, all vulnerabilities that arise from misconfigured registration from users (e.g. component owners, agent owners, service owners, agents operators) or misuse of the registration logic (e.g. accidental locking of funds, loss of keys to control services, etc.).
Full Finding Details:
- Finding description and impact
- This vulnerability is a reentrancy attack that allows an attacker to steal all funds from both`ServiceRegistry`(ETH) and`ServiceRegistryTokenUtility`(any token) contracts. The root cause is that`ServiceManager::update()`lacks reentrancy protection, and the protocol does not implement a whitelist for service tokens, enabling attackers to create services with malicious custom tokens.
- The vulnerability exists in the interaction between`ServiceManager::activateRegistration()`and`ServiceManager::update()`. When`activateRegistration()`is called, it first invokes`ServiceRegistryTokenUtility::activateRegistrationTokenDeposit()`to transfer tokens from the service owner. While`activateRegistrationTokenDeposit()`has a reentrancy guard, this guard only protects the`ServiceRegistryTokenUtility`contract, not the`ServiceManager`contract.
- During the token transfer in`activateRegistrationTokenDeposit()`, a malicious token can call back into`ServiceManager::update()`to modify the service configuration, including changing the token address. The`update()`function lacks reentrancy protection:
- The attack proceeds as follows. An attacker creates a service with a malicious custom token as both the service owner and the token address. The attacker activates registration, which calls`activateRegistrationTokenDeposit()`. During the token transfer, the malicious token's`transferFrom()`function calls back into`ServiceManager::update()`with`ETH_TOKEN_ADDRESS`as the new token. This changes the service configuration from token-secured to ETH-secured while`activateRegistration()`is still executing. After the reentrant call completes,`activateRegistration()`continues and activates the service as ETH-secured. The attacker then terminates the service and withdraws the security deposit from`ServiceRegistry`(ETH), effectively stealing ETH that was deposited by other users.
- The impact is that an attacker can steal all funds from both`ServiceRegistry`(ETH) and`ServiceRegistryTokenUtility`(any token) by exploiting the reentrancy vulnerability during service activation.
- Recommended mitigation steps
- Add a reentrancy guard to`ServiceManager::update()`to prevent reentrant calls during service updates.
- Alternatively, implement a whitelist for service tokens to prevent malicious custom tokens from being used.

Full Finding Details:
- Summary
- in`_trackServiceDonations`function incorrectly splits a single service donation separately over components and then again over agents. When a service has`both components and agents`, the same donation is effectively`counted twice (or more)`, inflating unit-level pending rewards/top-ups and allowing unit owners to claim more ETH/OLAS than the donation and inflation actually funded.
- Finding description
- The`_trackServiceDonations`function is designed to`process donations`and allocate rewards to the owners of the`components and agents`that constitute a service. The function iterates through each service that has received a donation. Within this process, it loops through the two unit types:`components (unitType = 0`) and agents`(unitType = 1)`.
- The error lies in how`the per-unit reward`is calculated inside this inner loop. For`each unitType`, the code divides the`entire donation amount for the service`(amounts[i]) by the number of units of that specific type (numServiceUnits).
- Here is the problematic code snippet:
- Example of the exploit:
- A service consists of 10 components and 10 agents.
- A donation of 10 ETH is made to this service.
- The function will execute as follows:
- The result is that a single 10 ETH donation is`erroneously treated as a 20 ETH donation`, allowing unit owners to claim double the rewards they are entitled to.
- impact
- The protocol loses funds by paying out double the intended rewards, depleting donation funds at an accelerated rate.
- Recommended mitigation steps
- The bug must be fixed by calculating a single, correct per-unit donation amount before the function iterates through the different unit types. The total donation amount for a service needs to be divided by the total number of all units in that service (i.e., the sum of its components and agents).

- Finding description and impact
- The TWAP calculation in`UniswapPriceOracle.validatePrice()`contains a mathematical error where`cumulativePriceLast`is added then immediately subtracted, canceling out entirely. The "time-weighted average" always equals the current spot price.
- In`validatePrice()`at lines 58-62 :
- Substituting line 1 into line 2:
- TWA = ( cumPriceLast + tradePrice × elapsed ) − cumPriceLast elapsed = tradePrice × elapsed elapsed = tradePrice TWA = elapsed ( cumPriceLast + tradePrice × elapsed )− cumPriceLast = elapsed tradePrice × elapsed = tradePrice
- The`cumulativePriceLast`cancels completely. TWAP always equals the current spot price. The deviation check (lines 65-68) then compares`tradePrice`against itself, always yielding 0. The slippage check always passes regardless of the slippage parameter.
- Additionally,`getPrice()`reads spot reserves via`IUniswapV2(pair).getReserves()`which are directly manipulable within a single transaction via flash loan.
- Impact on BuyBackBurner:`validatePrice()`is called by`BuyBackBurner._buyOLAS()`before executing swaps. Since it provides zero protection:

- All LP positions managed by LiquidityManagerETH (liquidity operations)
- Recommended mitigation steps
- The oracle should store cumulative price observations across multiple blocks and compute TWAP as the difference between observations divided by elapsed time. The current implementation discards all historical data by subtracting`cumulativePriceLast`from its own computation within a single call.
- A correct implementation stores state between observations:
- This ensures the TWAP reflects actual historical prices across multiple blocks, making flash loan manipulation detectable.

- The Math Problem:
- cumulativePrice = cumulativePriceLast + (tradePrice * elapsedTime)
- timeWeightedAverage = (cumulativePrice - cumulativePriceLast) / elapsedTime = (tradePrice * elapsedTime) / elapsedTime = tradePrice ← ALWAYS EQUALS SPOT PRICE
- This means: timeWeightedAverage == tradePrice (always) derivation = |tradePrice - timeWeightedAverage| = 0 (always) return derivation <= slippage → Always returns TRUE Impact The BuyBackBurner._buyOLAS() function relies on this oracle for slippage protection:

## [F-457] BalancerPriceOracle - Mathematically Incorrect TWAP Formula
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-457](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-457)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Judge Comments. Missing mandatory PoC required to be eligible for rewards in the contest
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Missing mandatory PoC required to be eligible for rewards in the contest
Full Finding Details:
- Vulnerability Description
- The BalancerPriceOracle contract contains a mathematically incorrect implementation of Time-Weighted Average Price (TWAP) calculation. The formula attempts to recover the total tracked time by dividing cumulative price by average price, which is fundamentally flawed and produces incorrect TWAP values. Vulnerable Code Lines 133-137 in updatePrice(): uint256 averagePrice = (snapshot.cumulativePrice + (currentPrice * elapsedTime)) / ((snapshot.cumulativePrice / snapshot.averagePrice) + elapsedTime);
- Lines 170-171 in validatePrice() contain the same error: uint256 timeWeightedAverage = (snapshot.cumulativePrice + (snapshot.averagePrice * elapsedTime)) / ((snapshot.cumulativePrice / snapshot.averagePrice) + elapsedTime);
- Technical Analysis
- The Flawed Logic: The denominator calculation attempts to compute total time as: totalTime = cumulativePrice / averagePrice
- This assumes that: cumulativePrice = averagePrice × totalTime
- However, this equation only holds true if the average price never changes, which defeats the entire purpose of a time-weighted average. As prices fluctuate over time, this calculation becomes increasingly inaccurate. Mathematical Proof of Incorrectness Consider the following scenario: Time 0: price = 100, averagePrice = 100, cumulativePrice = 0 Time 10: price = 200 Update: cumulativePrice += 100 * 10 = 1000 Current calc: (1000 + 200*10) / (1000/100 + 10) = 3000 / 20 = 150
- Time 20: price = 300 Update: cumulativePrice += 150 * 10 = 2500 Current calc: (2500 + 300*10) / (2500/150 + 10) ≈ 5500 / 26.67 ≈ 206.25
- Correct TWAP Calculation: Total value-time: (100 10) + (200 10) = 3000 Total time: 20 Correct TWAP = 3000 / 20 = 150
- The current implementation produces 206.25 instead of 150, demonstrating a significant error that compounds over time.
- Attack Scenario
- Step 1: Attacker observes the current TWAP is 100 OLAS per ETH Step 2: Attacker uses flash loan to manipulate pool to 150 OLAS per ETH Step 3: Due to incorrect TWAP calculation, the oracle incorrectly computes the new average Step 4: The flawed formula allows the manipulated price to pass slippage checks that should have failed Step 5: Attacker executes profitable trade using manipulated price Step 6: Attacker repays flash loan and exits with profit
- Impact
- Recommended Fix
- Implement proper TWAP tracking by maintaining a separate totalTimeTracked variable: uint256 public totalTimeTracked;
- function updatePrice() public returns (bool) { uint256 currentPrice = getPrice(); require(currentPrice > 0, "Price must be non-zero");
- }

- Price returns to normal, attacker arbitrages the mispositioned liquidity
- Impact:
- Attacker can manipulate liquidity placement for any inactive pool
- Protocol-Owned Liquidity (POL) added at suboptimal positions

## [F-464] BuyBackBurner allows MEV sandwich attacks due to missing slippage protection in Uniswap V2 and V3 swaps
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-464](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-464)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Invalid`
Sufficiency: `Insufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: Judge Comments. Missing mandatory PoC required to be eligible for rewards in the contest
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: Missing mandatory PoC required to be eligible for rewards in the contest
Full Finding Details:
- M-02: Vulnerability Details
- Summary
- The`BuyBackBurnerUniswap`contract executes token swaps via Uniswap V2 and V3 routers without specifying meaningful minimum output amounts. The V2 path uses`amountOutMin = 0`and the V3 path uses`amountOutMinimum = 1`. This absence of execution-layer slippage protection allows MEV actors to extract value from the protocol's buyback operations through sandwich attacks. A Foundry PoC demonstrates up to 54% value extraction in a single transaction.
- Root Cause
- The vulnerability exists in`contracts/utils/BuyBackBurnerUniswap.sol`:
- V2 Path — Line 91:
- The second parameter`0`is the`amountOutMin`argument, meaning the swap will succeed regardless of how few tokens are received.
- V3 Path — Line 116:
- The`amountOutMinimum`parameter is set to`1`wei, which provides no practical slippage protection.
- Both implementations accept any non-zero output, enabling swap execution at arbitrarily unfavorable rates.
- Attack Scenario
- The following describes a realistic MEV sandwich attack exploiting the zero slippage protection:
- Preconditions:
- Protocol has tokens (e.g., WETH) in the BuyBackBurner contract
- The transaction enters the public mempool
- Attack Steps:
- Detection : MEV bot detects the pending`buyBack()`transaction in the mempool.
- Front-run : Attacker submits a higher-priority transaction that swaps WETH → OLAS, moving the pool price unfavorably for the victim (reducing OLAS per WETH).
- Victim Execution : The protocol's`buyBack()`transaction executes:
- The swap executes at the manipulated price
- Protocol receives significantly fewer OLAS than it would have at fair market price
- Back-run : Attacker immediately swaps OLAS → WETH at the restored price, capturing the spread.
- Result : The attacker extracts the difference between fair market output and actual output received by the protocol.
- Impact
- Quantified from PoC:
- Characteristics:
- Value extraction is proportional to attacker capital and pool liquidity
- Attack is repeatable on every buyback operation
- Attack is automatable via standard MEV infrastructure (Flashbots, etc.)
- Protocol receives fewer tokens than fair market rate; extracted value flows to attacker
- Limitations:
- Requires MEV infrastructure (not a simple single-tx exploit)
- Bounded by available pool liquidity
- Competitive mempool environment may reduce attacker profit margin
- Scope
- The vulnerability affects:
- All buyback operations routed through these functions are affected.
- Why Oracle Checks Do Not Mitigate This Issue
- The parent contract`BuyBackBurner.sol`implements oracle-based checks (lines 185-200):
- Why these checks are insufficient:
- Timing Gap : The oracle checks validate pool price state at discrete points (before and after), but do not enforce minimum output during swap execution. An attacker can manipulate the pool between the pre-check and the actual swap.
- Different Protection Layers :
- Oracle check: "Is the pool price within acceptable range?"
- Slippage protection: "Did I receive at least X tokens for my input?"
- These are distinct protections. The oracle may report an acceptable price while the actual swap executes at a worse rate due to MEV front-running.
- Post-swap check limitation : Even if the post-swap check detects price deviation, the swap has already executed. The check may revert the transaction, but in a competitive MEV environment, attackers can calibrate their front-run to stay within tolerance while still extracting value.
- MEV atomicity : In a sandwich attack, the front-run, victim swap, and back-run occur in the same block. The attacker can restore the pool to within acceptable bounds before the post-check executes, making the attack undetectable by the oracle validation.
- Conclusion : Oracle-based price validation operates at the price discovery layer, while`amountOutMin`operates at the execution layer. Both are necessary for complete protection; one does not substitute for the other.
- Severity Assessment
- Medium Severity
- This finding represents value extraction under realistic conditions requiring sophistication (MEV), consistent with Code4rena Medium severity criteria.

Full Finding Details:
- Finding description and impact
- I discovered a critical flaw in how the`BuyBackBurnerUniswap`and`BuyBackBurnerBalancer`contracts handle V3 swaps. Specifically, the`_performSwap`function hardcodes`amountOutMinimum`to`1`(effectively 1 wei). This completely disables slippage protection for all V3 buyback operations.
- While the contract attempts to use`checkPoolAndGetCenterPrice()`to validate the pool's TWAP before swapping, this is not a substitute for slippage protection . TWAP only checks if the average price over time is healthy. It does not (and cannot) protect against intra-block price manipulation (sandwich attacks) where an MEV bot manipulates the spot price right before the buyback transaction executes.
- The Attack Vector: Since`amountOutMinimum`is 1, the swap instruction effectively tells Uniswap/Balancer: "I don't care how bad the price is, just give me whatever you can."
- An MEV bot monitoring the mempool will see the`buyBack()`transaction and immediately:
- Impact: This guarantees a near-100% loss of funds for every single V3 buyback operation. Given that Olas operates on Ethereum Mainnet where MEV activity is aggressive, this exploit is not theoretical—it is a certainty. The protocol's treasury will be drained of its buyback power.
- Robustness Analysis & Counter-Arguments (Why this is valid)
- Triager/Dev might argue: "We check`checkPoolAndGetCenterPrice()`at line 231, which reverts if the price deviates >10% from TWAP.
- My Rebuttal: That check is insufficient.`checkPoolAndGetCenterPrice`compares the current spot price against the TWAP . However, in a sandwich attack, the attacker manipulates the spot price within the same block .
- Recommended mitigation steps
- Don't use`1`for`amountOutMinimum`. You already have the oracle and`maxSlippage`parameter. Use them to calculate a valid minimum output.

If we look at the current OLAS/WETH pools on balancer (the pools in questions are OLAS/Native token pools), there are no V2/V3 pools that has a skewed weighted pool. So this is pretty much a configuration issue by the deployer (admin) at this point of discussion
Full Finding Details:
- Finding description and impact
- The`BalancerPriceOracle`contract's`getPrice()`function calculates the spot price using a simple ratio of token balances, which is only correct for pools with equal (50/50) token weights. For Balancer V2 weighted pools with asymmetric weights (e.g., 80/20, 70/30), this formula produces an incorrect price.
- The root cause is the price calculation that ignores token weights:
- For Balancer V2 weighted pools, the correct spot price formula must incorporate token weights:
- The current implementation effectively assumes`weightIn = weightOut = 0.5`, which is only valid for 50/50 pools.
- Example Scenario Consider an 80/20 OLAS/WETH Balancer pool:
- OLAS weight: 80%
- WETH weight: 20%
- OLAS balance: 800,000 tokens
- WETH balance: 100 tokens
- Current (incorrect) calculation:
- Correct weighted calculation:
- The incorrect formula returns a price of 8,000 when the true spot price is 2,000—a 4x error.
- Impact The incorrect spot price propagates through the entire oracle:
- Legitimate operations blocked when validation incorrectly fails
- Attackers can exploit the price discrepancy to sandwich transactions when validation incorrectly passes
- The severity scales with how far the pool's weights deviate from 50/50—an 80/20 pool has 4x price error, a 90/10 pool has 9x error.
- Recommended mitigation steps
- Query the pool's token weights and incorporate them into the price calculation.
## [F-468] CREATE2 Safe proxy address squatting can front-run service multisig deployment
Severity: `Low`
Source: [Code4rena F-468](https://code4rena.com/audits/2026-01-olas/submissions/F-468)
Review: `—`
Validity: `Valid`
Sufficiency: `Sufficient`
Why Marked Low/QA Or Rejected: No explicit rationale found on page beyond final disposition Low / Valid.
Judge Rejection / Classification Reason: No explicit judge classification comment was visible on the page.
Full Finding Details:
- Finding description and impact
- `SafeMultisigWithRecoveryModule.create()`deploys the service multisig by calling the Safe`GnosisSafeProxyFactory.createProxyWithNonce()`function. This deployment is deterministic for a given`safe singleton, initializer, nonc`.
- In this wrapper, the initializer is built from the full Safe`setup()`call data (`owners`,`threshold`, and the`recoveryModule`that should be enabled during setup). The`nonce`used for CREATE2 is taken from`data`. If`data`is empty,`nonce`defaults to`0`, which makes the target address predictable for a common path.
- Because`GnosisSafeProxyFactory`is permissionless, anyone can call`createProxyWithNonce()`directly. Once the deterministic proxy address already has code, subsequent`createProxyWithNonce()`calls for that same`safe, initializer, nonce`cannot deploy again and the transaction reverts.
- Attack path
- Recommended mitigation steps
- Require`data`to include a`nonce`and make it unpredictable.
